case_summary.text: Excise & Customs : Ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were not liable to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purposes

Excise & Customs : Where Central Board of Excise and Customs exercising its powers under sections 141(2) and 157 of Customs Act notified Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 and regualtion 6(1)(l) thereof obliged customs cargo service providers not to charge demurrage in certain cases, said regulation did not violate articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution
IT: Section 44B could not be invoked in case of demurrage charges reimbursed by assessee to non-resident for import of crude oil
Refund of demurrage not deniable due to delay in issuance of Detention Certificates by Customs authorities: HC
SC dismissed SLP against HC's order that demurrage charges hadn't accrued to assessee
Demurrage charges to be excluded from value of closing stock; rules ITAT

INCOME TAX: No obligation is cast upon assessee/Indian company to deduct tax at source at time of making of payment towards demurrage charges to a non-resident shipping company, as latters income was liable to be brought to tax under section 44B and consequently under section 172

Customs : Where goods of petitioner though detained initially, were ultimately found to be in line with Bills of Entry and DRI had ordered release on 08.04.2010 on payment of appropriate duty and later on importer was directed to obtain Detention Certificates in order to claim refund of demurrage charges but Detention Certificates were issued by Customs Authorities as late as in 2015, refund of demurrage charges which was due to importer could not be denied for delay due to inaction of custom

IT : Ocean freight, demurrage charge, handling charges or other amount of similar nature which are paid to Indian agents or authorized representative of non-resident shipping company who carry passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at port in India are merely reimbursement of expenses not covered for deduction of tax at source under provision of 194C and 195

INCOME TAX : Handling contractor was not responsible for deducting TDS under section 194C on demurrage and railway siding charges that were charged by Dock authorities on importer for delayed clearance
IT : Demurrage/detention charges were not liable for inclusion in valuation of closing stock
NR buyer not taxable for demurrage exp. reimbursed to it by Indian Co.; beneficiary shipping Co. is taxable instead
IT : SLP dismissed against order of High Court that demurrage/wharfage charges had not accrued to assessee

INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Demurrage paid by assessee-company, engaged in export of iron ore and shipping and ship building, to non-resident buyers of iron ore in terms of relevant sales contract was not income accrued or arisen to said non-resident buyers in India within meaning of section 5(2)(b) read with Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i)
HC directs Co. to process refund of demurrage charges as there was no delay on account of assessee

Customs : Customs Authorities cannot order custodian to waive demurrage for period of seizure/detention, etc.; waiver is grantable only if on conclusion of adjudication, there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by customs authorities

No demurrage charges if delay in receiving consignment was due to compliance of statutory obligations Port Trust Act : Where on failure to lift consignment by original importers, appellant purchased same and demurrage charges was levied due to delay in taking delivery, since delay occurred due to ensuring compliance of various statutory obligations, demurrage charges to be remitted
Case remanded to larger bench to decide applicability of sec. 172 on demurrage charges paid to shipping co.
GST/Cenvat Credit: Assessee was eligible for credit of service tax paid for demurrage charges in respect of goods imported by Air

Port Trust Act : Where on failure to lift consignment by original importers, appellant purchased same and demurrage charges was levied due to delay in taking delivery, since delay occurred due to ensuring compliance of various statutory obligations, demurrage charges to be remitted

Reimbursement of demurrage charges to be excluded from shipping profits while applying sec. 44B

TRANSFER PRICING : Where due to COVID lockdown, goods imported by assessee could not be cleared on timely basis which led to payment of demurrage and detention charges, since demurrage charges were an extraordinary cost, same shall be treated as non-operating in nature

GST : Detention of imported industrial oil declared as Distillate Oil was held unsustainable as CRCL report showed only cloud point deviation and non-definitive diesel-fraction traits, while other parameters were satisfied; mis-declaration not being proved, applying “most akin” test, goods were rightly classifiable as Distillate Oil.
Demurrage paid to non-resident shipping company not liable for deduction of tax at source
INCOME TAX : Provision of section 195 would not be applicable to reimbursement of demurrage charges paid by assessee to a non-resident shipping company and that same would be covered by section 172

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where assessee had made payments in foreign currency to ports outside India claiming to be demurrage charges for storage of goods during period post 1-7-2012 but failed to produce any documentary evidences to prove that such payments were made for storage of goods, same were liable to be taxed under reverse Charge Mechanism.

INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Demurrage paid by assessee-company to non-resident buyers of iron ore in terms of relevant sales contract was not income accrued or arisen to said non-resident buyers in India within meaning of section 5(2)(b) read with Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i)
Demurrage charges paid due to COVID-19 lockdown to be treated as non-operating in nature: ITAT

IT : Where there was nothing in export agreement that only balance after adjusting demurrage and dead freight charges alone would be sale consideration, sale consideration for purpose of claiming deduction under section 80HHC would be whole amount without deduction of demurrage charges

IT/ILT : Where assessee, a Denmark based company, engaged in business of operation of ships in international traffic, earned freight from shipping operations in India which included Inland Haulage Charges (IHC), in view of fact that IHC was not only directly connected with business of shipping but it was also a part of overall international voyage, it could be concluded that IHC was covered within definition of profits from operation of ships in international traffic and, thus, same was taxable
No demurrage charges if delay in receiving consignment was due to compliance of statutory obligations
No sec. 195 TDS on demurrage charges paid to non-resident shipping company

ICD/CFS can levy penal charge on importers where goods remained beyond 'free period' during COVID lockdown: Delhi HC

Inland haulage charges, being part of income from operation of ships in international traffic, not taxable in India

Customs : Deemed addition in respect of 'loading, unloading and handling charges' under rule 9(2)(b) of Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 at 1 per cent of CIF, even where actual charges are available, is ultra vires section 14; hence, said deemed addition at 1 per cent of CIF would apply only if actual charges are not ascertainable
Terminalling charges paid by 'Indian Oil' to avail of infrastructure facilities won't attract Sec. 194C TDS
Demanding ST again on Ocean freight already included in value of goods imported amounts to double taxation: CESTAT

CUSTOMS/EXCISE/ST : Where assessee operated flights on international routes and remnant ATF was filled in aircraft at foreign destination airport to be consumed on return journey to India and at time of arrival of an international flight into India, aircraft may be flown on a domestic route and customs department opined that cost of transportation of remnant ATF that was left over in fuel tank of aircraft to be used for domestic sector was liable to be included in value of remnant ATF for determining transaction value, no amount towards alleged transportation cost was required to be included in value of remnant ATF for determining transaction value

IT: In view of difference of opinion between orders passed by co-ordinate Benches of Tribunal regarding applicability of section 172 in respect of demurrage paid to non-resident shipping company, matter was to be referred to Larger Bench for consideration

GST: IGST on ocean freight under reverse charge for CIF imports was not leviable separately as per Mohit Minerals [2022] 138 taxmann.com 331/92 GST 101/ 61 GSTL 257 (SC) ruling, since freight forms part of composite supply already taxed on import; IGST and interest paid during 2018-19 under Notification No.10/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate) should be refunded though Notifications 11/2023 and 13/2023 omitting Notification No.10/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate) were made effective from 01-10-2023.
EXCISE/ST/VAT : Merchant Shipping Act has no provision for interference with CFSs or ICDs charges - Penal or otherwise

Customs : Merely because importer has cleared goods at enhanced value to save demurrage charges or otherwise, by itself, does not mean that importer is consenting to enhance value; it is right of importer to contest enhancement and fact of clearance of goods, cannot preclude importer from exercising right of appeal
No separate levy on Indian importer for ‘supply of services’ by shipping line in CIF contract: HC
Ocean freight on CIF imports not taxable again under GST in hands of shipping line as freight included in customs duty: HC

ST/GST : Importers of goods under CIF contract were not liable to pay Service Tax/IGST on ocean freight paid by foreign exporters to shipping line for transportation of goods by a vessel from outside India upto Customs station in India on reverse charge basis in terms of Notification No. 16/2017-S.T., dated 13-4-2017 and Sl. No. 10 of Notification No. 10/2017-I.T.(Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

IT/ILT : Where assessee, a Denmark based company, engaged in business of operations of ships in international traffic, earned freight from such shipping operations in India, which included Inland Haulage Charges (IHC), in view of fact that IHC was not only directly connected with business of shipping but it was also a part of overall international voyage and hence it was directly covered within definition of 'profits from operation of ships in international traffic', same was taxable only in Denmark and not in India as per article 9(1) of India-Denmark DTAA

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 14, read with  section 151A, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Levy of, and exemption from, customs duties - Valuation of goods for purposes of assessment - Whether when circular issued by Central Board of Excise and Customs (Board) remains in operation, revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to terms of statute - Held, yes - Whether circular issued by Board in which it was said that demurrage did not form part of assessable value of goods imported, same was binding on revenue and department could not contend otherwise - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent imported various petroleum products and crude oil into India and had cleared the same upon payment of customs duty. The customs authorities having noted that the respondent had paid demurrage charges to the shipowners under the charter party agreements through negotiating bank issued a show-cause notice to the appellant and included the bank charges and demurrage paid in the customs value of the goods and created additional demand of customs duty against the respondent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order. On second appeal, the Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal (CEGAT) allowed the appeal of the respondent on the grounds; (i) that the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) had issued a circular on 14-8-1991 under section 151A of the Customs Act in which it was said that the demurrage did not form part of the assessable value of the goods imported and the circular was binding on the revenue and the department could not contend otherwise, (ii) that the decision of the Supreme Court in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [1999] 113 ELT 358 relied upon by the revenue was not an authority for the proposition that demurrage payable on account of delay in discharging goods from a vessel was includible in the value of goods while assessing the customs duty payable thereon, and (iii) that under section 14 the assessable value of the imported goods must be the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold and the payment of demurrage was not an incident of an ordinary sale and an extraordinary expenditure, like demurrage, could not be included in the assessable value of the imported goods.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: PER RUMA PAL, J. - Although a circular is not binding on a Court or an assessee, it is not open to the revenue to raise the contention that is contrary to a binding circular by the Board. When a circular remains in operation, the revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to the terms of the statute. Despite the decision of the Supreme Court, the department cannot be permitted to take a stand contrary to the instructions issued by the Board. A show-cause notice and demand contrary to existing circulars of the Board are ab initio bad. It is not open to the revenue to advance an argument or file an appeal contrary to the circulars. [Para 10]

The provisions of section 151A are in pari materia with the provisions of section 119 of the Income-tax Act and section 37B of the Central Excise Act. The Parliament introduced section 151A by an amendment to the Customs Act in 1995 but with effect from 27-12-1985 (Act 80 of 1995), when the Supreme Court had already construed identical language in the manner indicated. It may be assumed that the Parliament had legislatively approved the construction by using the exact words so construed again in the Customs Act. There is, therefore, no reason why the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court under the two earlier Acts should not also be determinative of the construction put on the later in respect of a materially similar statutory provision. This was also not argued by the appellant (department). [Para 11]

The relevant circular dated 14-8-1991 provides, inter alia, that 'demurrage' and 'despatch' money may not form a part of assessable value. [Para 12]

The circular dated 14-8-1999 in no uncertain terms excludes demurrage from the assessable value. In the light of the judicial principles enunciated earlier, it was not open to the appellant to either issue the show-cause notice or contend otherwise. The demand based on an assessable value inclusive of demurrage could not be sustained as long as the circular remained operative and as long as the decisions on the issue remain good law. [Para 13]

provider and is, therefore, bound by such responsibilities. The Cargo Regulations, which contain the impugned regulation 6(1)(l), derives its existence from section 141(2) read with section 157 of the Customs Act. Those provisions show that the Central Board of Excise and Customs is empowered to prescribe the responsibilities of persons engaged in the activities of receiving, storing, delivering, dispatching or otherwise handling of imported or export goods in a customs area. [Para 10] Undoubtedly DIAL's functions in relation to operating, maintaining, developing, designing, constructing, upgrading, modernizing, financing and managing of the IGI Airport as conferred by the agreement dated 4-4-2006, except those functions pertaining to the cargo terminal which have been sub-contracted to the proforma fourth respondent by virtue of the concession agreement, are governed by the AAI Act. Nevertheless, the obligations of the customs cargo service provider/proforma fourth respondent is governed by the Cargo Regulations. The court is aware that the Supreme Court in the cases of International & Airports Authority of India v. Grand Slam International 1995 taxmann.com 344 (SC) and Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd. v. C.L. Jain Woolen Mills 2001 (129) ELT 561 (SC) has observed that there was no provision in the Customs Act empowering the customs authorities to direct the custodian of goods to waive the demurrage charges on the goods. However, these decisions were pronounced before introduction of sub-section (2) to section 141 of the Customs Act, which later gave way to the notification of the Cargo Regulations. Therefore, the petitioner's argument that the second respondent exceeded the power delegated to it by the Customs Act must fail. [Para 11]

The contention of the petitioner that the impugned regulation 6(1)(l) violates article 14 of the Constitution of India, as it has no nexus with the object sought to be achieved, is insubstantial because the Cargo Regulations were enacted for the purpose of prescribing the responsibilities of persons engaged in the activities of receiving, storing, delivering, dispatching or otherwise handling of imported or export goods in a customs area and the impugned regulation is as such an obligation cast upon the persons involved in the said activities. DIAL also urged that the regulation contravene article 19(1)(g) inasmuch as it places a blanket ban on the charge of demurrage by the custodian of goods in case of detention, confiscation or seizure of goods by customs. However, such restriction is covered under the premise of article 19(6), by which reasonable restrictions in the interest of general public may be imposed on the right under article 19(1)(g). Investigation being an integral part of working of the Customs Department, the consignments detained by the customs authorities or other investigating agencies cannot be cleared during investigation particularly if such cases involve trade policy, human safety and security, security of State, etc. It is with these considerations that the impugned regulation was included in the Cargo Regulations and it should be viewed in the light of the object with which it has been framed. Therefore, the allegation that the impugned regulation violates article 19(1)(g) does not survive. [Para 12]

The Supreme Court in the case of Maharashtra State Board of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education v. Paritosh Bhupesh Kumar [1984] 4 SCC 27 has upheld the validity of a regulation made to carry out the provisions of the Act. It was held in that case that the regulations had to be judged on a threefold tests namely: (1) whether the provisions of the regulations fall within the scope and ambit of the power conferred on the delegate, (2) whether the regulations made are to any extent inconsistent with the provisions of the enabling Act, and (3) whether they infringe any of the fundamental rights or other restrictions or limitations imposed by the Constitution. In the instant case, the first test is answered in the affirmative and the second and third tests are answered in the negative, which would imply that the Cargo Regulations is well within the scope and ambit of its parent Act, i.e., the Customs Act and is also consistent with the same and does not, in any way, violate constitutional provisions. [Para 13]

The court acknowledges that section 151A of the Customs Act places an obligation upon the officers of customs to follow the orders, instructions and directions of the Central Board of Excise and Customs, as far as they relate to any prohibition, restriction or procedure for import or export of goods. [Para 14]

The Commissioner of Customs (third respondent), a customs officer, is bound by section 151A of the Customs Act. Hence, the court cannot issue directions restraining him from following the orders of the Central Board of Excise and Customs, i.e., constraining the former or any other officer on his behalf from issuing any letter/order/direction/advice/recommendation to the petitioner or its agents or concessionaire to waive the demurrage charges or not to charge the same under the impugned regulation. [Para 15]

DIAL's further argument was that in the event of directions under the regulations, compliance would result in commercial unviability, because its autonomy to charge fully or in part might eventually result in losses. [Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Levy of duty - Valuation of goods - Whether ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purpose - Held, no [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were not liable to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purposes

FACT: The question involved in the instant appeal is as to whether ship demurrage charges paid by the assessee-importer on the import of the goods were to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for purpose of levy of customs duty.

HELD: The demurrage charges are admittedly incurred after the goods reached at Indian ports and, therefore, it is a post-importation event. Such charges, therefore, cannot form part of the transaction value. [Para 5]

In view of the aforesaid, the appeal filed by the revenue was liable to be dismissed.

The regulations framed by the customs authorities stipulate that the same are subjected to any other law for the time being in force and such are subject to the policy framed by the AAI which policy was framed in 2003 and Regulations came into force in 2009 and as such in terms of said policy, no waiver can be granted.

The waiver, if any granted earlier, has been granted on case to case basis.

Issue Involved Whether CELEBI is bound by the HCCAR or by the Policy for Waiver of Demurrage Charges notified by the Airports Authority of India in 1999 ("Policy for Waiver") and further whether the two can be harmoniously construed ?

Whether the CELEBI is entitled to charge demurrage/detention charges for the period the goods were detained by the customs authorities and for which the customs authorities have issued a certificate advising CELEBI to waive off demurrage charges in terms of section 6(1)(l) of the Handling of Cargo under Customs Area Regulations, 2009 ?

HELD: . Analysis of law :

Section 45 : Section 45 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that all imported goods unloaded in the customs area shall remain in the custody of a person approved by the Commissioner of Customs till the time they are cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped in accordance with chapter VIII which deals with goods in transit. The person to whom the custody of such goods is handed over by the Commissioner of Customs is liable to keep record of the same and keep the same in the customs area and not to permit removal of the same except with prior permission and in case of any pilferage etc. the said person is liable to pay duty on the said goods. [Para 24]

Sections 49 and 57 to 73 : Under section 49, the Customs Authorities on an application of the importer, if satisfied, that the goods entered for home consumption cannot be cleared within a reasonable time, permit the importer to deposit the goods in a public area or a private warehouse for a specified period. The period may be extended from time to time by the Commissioner of Customs. Section 49 further stipulates that goods so warehoused on an application by the importer shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods for the purposes of this Act and provisions of chapter IX shall not apply. Section 57 lays down that the Assistant Commissioner/Deputy Commissioner of Customs may appoint public warehouses wherein dutiable goods may be deposited. Section 58 empowers the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs to licence private warehouses wherein dutiable goods imported may be deposited where the facilities for deposit in a public warehouse are not available. Sections 59 to 73 of chapter IX deal with the general provisions under which an importer may warehouse the imported goods and stipulates the period for which the goods may be warehoused and general conditions for removal/clearance of the goods. [Para 27]

Section 141 : Section 141 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that the conveyances and goods in a customs area are subjected to the control of the officers of customs and are to be handled in a customs area in such a manner as may be prescribed and responsibilities of a person engaged in the receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and otherwise handling import or export goods in customs area shall be such as may be prescribed by the customs authorities. [Para 29]

Goods are within control of customs authorities : The above noted sections of the Customs Act postulate a scheme or a procedure whereby goods which are imported into a customs area immediately come into the control and power of the officers of the customs. The customs authorities are empowered under the Act to appoint persons or officers who are responsible for receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and handling goods in the customs areas. Under certain circumstances, the customs authorities may permit storage of imported goods in a warehouse pending clearance on a application by the importer, where goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time (section 49) or warehoused in a public or private warehouse (sections 60, 61). [Para 30]

AAI : The Airports Authority of India, is an authority established under the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 in terms of the said Act, all rights, powers, authorities, privileges and ownership in respect of all property movable or immovable airports of India. The functions and powers of AAI include establishment of warehouses and cargo complex at the airports for storage and processing of the goods at the terminals. [Para 32]

AAI Act : Under the provision of the AAI Act, AAI is empowered to make lease of premises of Airport to carry out some of functions under the Act. AAI, for overall public interest granted some of its functions, being the functions of operating, maintaining, developing, designing, construction, upgradation, modernisation, finances and managing the airport to the Delhi International Airport Private Limited, (DIAL for short) under the operation, management and developing agreements (OMDA) dated 4.4.2006 which agreement further empowers DIAL to sub-contract any activity covered by OMDA. [Para 33]

The circular dated 14-8-1999 in no uncertain terms excludes demurrage from the assessable value. In the light of the judicial principles enunciated earlier, it was not open to the appellant to either issue the show-cause notice or contend otherwise. The demand based on an assessable value inclusive of demurrage could not be sustained as long as the circular remained operative and as long as the decisions on the issue remain good law. [Para 13] The submission of the appellant that the respondent had not acted on the basis of the circular and, therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel did not apply is misconceived. The circulars issued by the CBDT under the Income-tax Act and the CBEC under section 37B of the Central Excise Act have been held to be binding primarily on the basis of the language of the statutory provisions buttressed by the need of the adjudicating officers to maintain uniformity in the levy of tax/duty throughout the country. [Para 14]

The stand of the appellant that the Supreme Court had taken the view that demurrage was includible in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) both in the adjudication order and before the Tribunal appears to have been abandoned in the written notes of submission. Apart from the decision of the Constitution Bench in Collector of Central Excise v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 143 ELT 19 on the binding nature of the circulars, in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) the decision was on landing charges. It did not construe the 1988 Rules. The circular on the other hand was issued on a re-examination of the issue in the light of the GATT Valuation principles as incorporated in the 1988 Rules. [Para 17]

Therefore, demurrage was wrongly included by the adjudicating officer in the assessable value contrary to the directive of the CBEC at a time when the circular had not been withdrawn. [Para 18]

PER P. VENKATARAMA REDDI, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW) : The revenue's appeal is liable to be dismissed in the light of the circular dated 14-8-1991 issued by the CBEC which is traceable to the power conferred on the Board by section 151A of the Customs Act. The purpose of this separate opinion is only to highlight certain doubts as to the correctness of the proposition laid down in the two Dhiren Chemical Industries' cases (supra) - one decided by the Constitution Bench and the other by a three Judge Bench. [Para 20]

The circulars issued by the Board under section 151A of the Customs Act or section 37B of the Central Excise Act are generally binding on the revenue. However, when there is a statutory mandate to observe and follow the orders and instructions of the Board in regard to specified matters, that mandate has to be complied with. It is not open to the adjudicating authority to deviate from those orders or instructions which the statute enjoins that it should follow. If any order is passed contrary to those instructions the order is liable to be struck down on that very ground. Extending this principle which flows from the statutory provision contained in section 151A of the Customs Act or a pari materia provision in other fiscal enactments, the Supreme Court also held that it is not open to the department to file an appeal against the order passed in conformity with the circular. To this extent one has no difficulty in understanding the rationale of the decisions of the Supreme Court leaving apart for the time being the decisions in which a somewhat different note was struck. However, one is unable to reconcile to the view that even after the highest Court settles the law on the subject, the view expressed by the Central Board on the same point of law should still hold the field until and unless it is revoked. [Para 21]

As is evident from section 151A the Board is empowered to issue orders or instructions in order to ensure uniformity in the classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty. The need to issue such instructions arises when there is a doubt or ambiguity in relation to those matters. The possibility of varying views being taken by the customs officials while administering the Act may bring about uncertainty and confusion. In order to avoid this situation, section 151A has been enacted on the same lines as section 37A of the Central Excise Act. The apparent need to issue such circulars is left when there is no authoritative pronouncement of the Court on the subject. Once the relevant issue is decided by the Court at the highest level, the very basis and substratum of the circular disappears. The law laid down by the Supreme Court will ensure uniformity in the decisions at all levels. By an express constitutional provision, the law declared by the Supreme Court is made binding on all the Courts within the territory of India (vide Article 141), Proprio vigore the law is binding on all the Tribunals and authorities. [Para 22]

HEADNOTE: Section 141, read with section 157, of the Customs Act, 1962 and regulation  6 of the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 - Conveyances and goods in customs area - Whether where Central Board of Excise and Customs exercising its powers under sections 141(2) and 157 of Customs Act notified Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 and regualtion 6(1)(l) thereof obliged customs cargo service providers not to charge demurrage in certain cases, said regulation did not violate articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution - Held, yes [Paras 10, 11 and 12] [In favour of revenue]Excise  Customs : Where Central Board of Excise and Customs exercising its powers under sections 141(2) and 157 of Customs Act notified Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 and regualtion 6(1)(l) thereof obliged customs cargo service providers not to charge demurrage in certain cases, said regulation did not violate articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution

FACT: Pursuant to the provisions of section 12A of the Airports Authority of India Act (AAI Act), the Airports Authority of India (AAI) and the Delhi International Airport (P) Ltd. (DIAL), i.e., the petitioner here entered into an agreement on 4-4-2006, whereby the latter was granted exclusive right and authority for performing the functions of operating, maintaining, developing, designing, constructing, upgrading, modernizing, financing and managing of the Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi [IGI Airport]. Thereupon DIAL took over the operations of the IGI Airport from AAI and was empowered under the provisions of the agreement to exercise powers under section 12A(4) of the AAI Act and was also empowered to exercise AAI's statutory powers under the Regulations framed in 2003, with regard to levy of demurrage charges at the IGI Airport.

On 17-3-2009, the Central Board of Excise and Customs [CBEC], i.e., the second respondent exercising its powers under section 141(2) read with section 157 of the Customs Act notified the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 (Cargo Regulations) and regulation 6(1)(l) thereof obliged the customs cargo service providers not to charge demurrage in certain cases if directed not to do so.

Further DIAL executed a Concession Agreement dated 24-8-2009 with Celibi Delhi Cargo Terminal Management India (P.) Ltd. [proforma fourth respondent, hereafter Celibi], which enabled it to upgrade, modernize, finance, operate, maintain and manage the cargo terminal at IGI Airport.

Thereafter the Commissioner of Customs (third respondent) started issuing directions to DIAL and Celibi to waive demurrage charges in accordance with the impugned regulation 6(1)(l). These directions were not complied with. Consequently the third respondent issued show cause notices to the petitioner and Celibi as to why the impugned regulation was not complied with and as to why action should not be initiated against them.

The petitioner filed a writ peetition challenging regulation 6(1)(l) of the Cargo Regulations on the plea that the CBEC exceeded the power delegated to it by the Customs Act and also contended that said regulation violated articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India.

HELD: Regulation 6 of the Cargo Regulations fixes the responsibilities of a customs cargo service provider, defined under regulation 2(1)(b). The proforma fourth respondent, by virtue of the concession agreement, comes within the purview of customs cargo service provider and is, therefore, bound by such responsibilities. The Cargo Regulations, which contain the impugned regulation 6(1)(l), derives its existence from section 141(2) read with section 157 of the Customs Act. Those provisions show that the Central Board of Excise and Customs is empowered to prescribe the responsibilities of persons engaged in the activities of receiving, storing, delivering, dispatching or otherwise handling of imported or export goods in a customs area. [Para 10]

FACT: The assessee, a non-resident shipping company, received detention/demurrage charges on containers. The Assessing Officer took the receipt as income in the hands of the assessee-company, and after deducting some estimated expenses, made addition. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the amount received against detention/demurrage charges should be treated at par with freight and, therefore, only 7.5 per cent thereof be treated as profit of business from operation of ships. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that nothing could be taxed as no income accrued in India.

On reference :

HELD: According to Explanation to section 44B(2) inserted retrospectively, the demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature should be taxed in the same way as the amount in clause (i ) or clause (ii) of section 44B(2). Accordingly, demurrage charges or freight charges should be taxed in the same way as freight taxable under section 44B.

Section 44B provides how the income from shipping business can be taxed in the case of non-residents and the section starts with a non-obstant clause, i.e. ‘Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A of the Act’. Thus, whatever is provided in the provisions contained in sections 28 to 43A, that will not come in the way of the provisions contained in section 44B as to how the income from shipping business in the case of non-residents will be computed, whether the income will be computed or not or what will be the rate of that income. However, the question was where an income of a non-resident had accrued outside India by way of demurrage charges, could that be taxed in India? There was no specific finding by the Tribunal as to what part of the demurrage income accrued to the assessee in India or outside India. Therefore, it was necessary to have the finding whether the demurrage income accrued in India or outside India and if not the entire income of demurrages, as to what part of the income of demurrages accrued in India or outside India.

Hence, the matter was remitted back to the Tribunal to give a finding on the above issue and decide the issue afresh.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Restrictions on custody and removal of imported goods - Demurrage - Show cause notice discharged--liability of payment of demurrage and ground rent must be borne by the Customs Department from the date of filing of the bill of entry till the release of goods. Custodian--Inland Container Depot, being custodians of Customs is bound to release the goods after the issuance of detention certificate

FACT: The petitioner imported 71 cartons and the Bill of Entries were presented on February 27, 1988 and the Customs Authorities issued a show cause notice on December 15, 1988, which was discharged by the Assistant Collector of Customs. The petitioner stated that since the show cause notice had been discharged, the petitioner had no liability to pay demurrage charges and/or ground rent charges and that after issuance of the Detention Certificate, the Inland Container Depot being custodian for Customs was under obligation to release the goods without payment of demurrage and ground rent charges.

HELD: Demurrage charges--ICD being custodian for customs is bound to release the goods to the petitioner after issuance of Detention Certificate and the Customs Department is liable to pay demurrage and ground rent charges after Bills of Entries were submitted till the goods were released. ".......in the present case, the Container Corporation of India through the Inland Container Depot is the custodian of goods under section 45 of the Customs Act. As the Inland Container Depot is the custodian for the Customs authorities and the detention certificate has been issued by the Customs, then the Inland Container is bound to release the goods to the importer and with regard to the demurrage charges and ground rent charges, it is the Customs Department which is liable to the Container Corporation of India.........The demurrage charges prior to the date February 27, 1988, will be borne by the importer on which date the Bill of Entries were submitted by the petitioner and after February 27, 1988, till the goods are released, the Customs Department would be liable for the payment of demurrage charges and ground rent charges to the Container Corporation."

HEADNOTE: Section 44B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Shipping business in case of non-residents -  Assessee, a non-resident shipping company, claimed that demurrage charge received was in nature of insurance and not taxable - Whether since demurrage income had accrued in India and also received in India, same was taxable - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a non-resident shipping company of Japan, claimed that the demurrage charge received by it was not part of the taxable income as the same was in the nature of insurance and not taxable under the Act. The Assessing Officer rejected that claim in view of the provisions of section 44B. But the Tribunal allowed the claim holding that the demurrage was received on account of carriage of goods.

On reference :

HELD: Since the fact was that the demurrage income had accrued in India and was also received in India, the Tribunal had committed an error by allowing the claim of the assessee.

Regulations of AAI are specific provisions : The regulations of the AAI of which the policy for waiver of demurrage charges is a part specifically deals with the storage and processing of cargo, courier and express goods and postal mail. The Airport Authority fixes the charges for processing of the Cargo and has thus formulated the Policy for Waiver of such demurrage charges. [Para 41]

II. Analysis of this case : Customs authorities are issuing certificate of waiver on regular basis : The customs authorities it appears issues certificate for waiver in every type of case irrespective of the fact whether the importer is at fault or not. The customs authorities have issued certificate for waiver of the demurrage charges in both the cases at hand. In one case the release of the goods are on provisional basis pending adjudication and in the other there is imposition of both fine and penalty. These are not cases where the importer has been held to be not at fault. In one case the Importer has been found to be at fault and penalty and fine imposed. The importer has accepted the said order. In the other case adjudication proceedings are pending and are yet to be finalised. [Para 42]

Apparent overlapping but harmonious construction : There is an overlap in the Policy for Waiver framed by AAI and the HCCAR. Though initially there appears to be a conflict between the policy and the regulations but on closer scrutiny it is apparent that they can both be harmoniously construed and coexist. [Para 43]

AAI Policy of Waiver distinguishes between innocent and culprit importers - Said policy overrides : The policy makes a distinction between the cases where the importer is innocent but his imported goods are seized and detained pending an enquiry and adjudication and the cases where the importers have indulged in mis-declaration, mis-description, under valuation or concealment and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities. Importers who are innocent cannot be equated with the importers who violate the law and be given the same treatment. The AAI policy makes a distinction between the two. [Para 44]

HCCAR subject to policy of waiver : The regulations framed in 2009 themselves stipulate that they are subject to any law for the time being in force and as such the regulations would be applicable in terms of the Policy for Waiver framed by the AAI in 2003. [Para 45]

Faulty importers cannot get benefit of waiver : In case the HCCAR were to be made applicable in all cases then the result would be that in no case where there is a fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning imposed by the customs authorities CELEBI would be able to charge demurrage charges. Customs authorities are issuing waiver directions even in cases where the importers are clearly at fault and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning has been imposed by the customs authorities. Even in cases of mis-declaration, undervaluation and concealment, the certificates are being issued. This is clearly giving premium to dishonesty. The waiver should be granted in genuine cases where the importers are ultimately found not at fault. It cannot be that all importers honest and dishonest are treated equally. [Para 46]

Innocent importer - Demurrage may be waived : In cases where the importer is found innocent and there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by the customs authorities, the policy for waiver would be applicable and the importer would be entitled to be considered for its benefit provided a certificate entitling him to be so considered is issued by the customs authorities. The importer would not be automatically exempt but would be covered under the policy for waiver and eligible for waiver which would be granted subject to other compliances. [Para 47]

Policy of waiver not overridden by superdginama of CELEBI : The execution of the superdginama by CELEBI that it would not claim any storage charges for the safe custody of the goods charge would also not be in conflict with the policy for waiver. The policy has been framed by the Airports Authority of India and the execution of the Superdginama by an employee would not override the policy. It would be applicable in cases where no fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities. In cases where the importer is found eligible for the benefit of the Policy, the Superdginama would automatically become applicable. [Para 48]

No waiver if importer is at fault - HCCAR not overrides : Where the importer is clearly at fault and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities, making the regulations applicable and granting the benefits of waiver would be clearly unreasonable and would grant benefit of waiver, with the person who has provided space suffering. This was and is not the intention and purpose behind HCCAR. Regulation recognises and accepts that any other law in force is not abrogated or repealed . The existing provision applicable stands protected. [Para 49]

III. Conclusion :

Conclusion as to principle of law :

(1)

In cases where on conclusion of the adjudication proceedings there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by the customs authorities :

(i)

the Policy for Waiver would be applicable; and

(ii)

with reference to section 145A, the same deserves to fail. This is as even if the detention/demurrage charge is considered as not arising on account of a contractual obligation, but a statutory one, i.e., as in the nature of a levy or impost (which would though need to be established), it would stand to be included under section 145A only where it represents a qualifying cost - which have found as not, and not otherwise. [Para 3.1] The opening stock for the year under reference would include demurrage charges, while the closing stock would not, and which would itself become a source of distortion. Though normally both the opening and the closing stock are to be valued on the same basis, it cannot also be denied that the valuation of the opening stock has to agree with that of the closing stock for the immediately preceding year. It is not in dispute that the value of opening stock, as assumed by the assessee, is the same as adopted in respect of the closing stock for the immediately preceding year. Any change would lead to a distortion - to the extent of the change - in the year the same is effected, so that the same is incidental thereto, and the fundamental question that would need to be addressed and answered is if the change is valid. It is found as so. Further, altering the value of the opening stock would amount to effectively modifying the closing stock and, thus, the income for the immediately preceding year, which stands assessed. The change thus gets effectively shifted to that year. The argument qua uniformity in the valuation of opening and closing stock would then stand to be assumed for that year, leading to a modification in the value of the opening stock for that year, and so on, thus causing a ripple effect. The argument is, thus, to no moment, and inasmuch as a change has been validated for the current year, an exception to the principle of uniformity in the valuation of the closing and opening stock for that year would have to be drawn. These and the like arguments would thus suggest non-disturbance of the value of the (opening) stock as carried forward from the preceding year, even though the same may not be valid, subject of course to the change in the method of valuation being bona fide. [Para 3.3]

The Assessing Officer having adopted the same method of valuation for the closing stock, i.e., as for the opening stock, being in fact consistently followed, the question of validity of the revision by the assessee arose for consideration. The same, as by the first appellate authority, approved on the basis of the accounting principles, which would govern the matter in the absence of any specific provision/s in the Act toward the same, with section 145A being inapplicable, also relying on the decision in the case of CIT v. British Paints India Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 44/54 Taxman 499 (SC), wherein the same issue arose; the Apex Court therein reiterating its professed stand in the matter refer: S.N. Namasivayam Chettiar v. CIT [1960] 38 ITR 579 (SC) and CIT v. A. Krishnaswami Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 122 (SC).

However, integral thereto is the question of a corresponding change in the value of the opening stock, which would otherwise continue to be valued per the old method, since held as invalid. It is axiomatic that determination of correct profit would require proper valuation of inventories, both as at the beginning as well as the end of the relevant accounting period, as stands clarified by the Apex Court in, among others, British Paints India Ltd. (supra) and Chainrup Sampatram v. CIT [1953] 24 ITR 481 (SC). This is also in essence the rule of the non obstante provision of section 145A, since statutorily mandated. The issue is legal, and goes to the root of the matter. The same would accordingly get decided on the basis of legal precedents, including an analysis thereof. The issue arising directly out of decision validating the change by the assessee, having not been dealt with by the Commissioner (Appeals) - who in fact approved the change in the first instance, with no specific arguments in the matter. It is considered to be fit and proper to refrain from deciding the matter, and only consider it proper to restore the same back to the file of the Commissioner (Appeals), who shall decide the same in accordance with law per a speaking order after allowing reasonable opportunity of hearing to both the parties before him.

HEADNOTE: Section 141, read with sections 45 and 49, of the Customs Act, 1962 and Regulation 6 of the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 - Clearance of Imported Goods - Demurrage - Custodian demanded demurrage even for period during which goods were seized by department and could not be cleared - Department issued certificate favouring assessee that demurrage could not be levied - Assessee claimed that said certificate of department had overriding effect under Regulation 6 of Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 (HCCAR) - Custodian claimed that it was governed only by Policy for Waiver of Demurrage Charges notified by Airports Authority of India (AAI) - HELD : HCCAR Regulations themselves stipulate that they are subject to any law for time being in force and, therefore, HCCAR and directions of customs authorities thereunder do not override 'Policy for Waiver' framed by AAI - In cases where on conclusion of adjudication proceedings there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by customs authorities demurrage for period when goods were seized, detained or earlier confiscated would be waived as per Policy of Waiver - However, in any other case, demurrage would not be waived for period of seizure, etc. and provisional release order would be subject to furnishing of bond and/or security that in case any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by customs authorities, importer would pay demurrage charges [Para 50] [In favour of revenue]Customs : Customs Authorities cannot order custodian to waive demurrage for period of seizure/detention, etc.; waiver is grantable only if on conclusion of adjudication, there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by customs authorities

FACT: Facts

The assessee imported mobile phones "Made in China" of different brands.

The Director of Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, Delhi Zonal Unit, seized the goods on the ground of mis-declaration. During investigation, it was found that the address given in the import documents of the petitioner was incorrect and 2000 pieces of memory cards of 4GB capacity were concealed in the mobile phones.

The Department released the goods provisionally on execution of a provisional duty bond guarantee.

Pursuant to the direction for release of the goods, the assessee approached the Deputy Director of Directorate of Revenue Intelligence for issuance of directions to the custodian viz. M/s. Celebi Delhi Cargo Terminal Management India (CELEBI) to waive off demurrage charges on the detained goods.

The Commissioner of Customs advised CELEBI to waive of the detention charges in terms of Regulation 6(1)(l) of Handling of Cargo under Customs Area Regulations, 2009 ("HCCAR").

Despite that, CELEBI refused to waive off the demurrage/detention charges.

The assessee filed present petition seeking waiver of the said charges in terms of the direction/advise issued by the customs authorities.

Assessee's Arguments

CELEBI has acted contrary to the provisions of law inasmuch as demurrage incurred for the period of detention/seizure by Customs should have been waived off as directed by the Customs Department.

In similar circumstances, CELEBI and AAI have waived of the charges where customs authorities have so directed in terms of the regulations.

Arguments of Customs Department (favouring assessee)

As per regulation 6(1)(l) of HCCAR, no detention/demurrage charges are leviable and more so in view of the fact that there is a direction issued by any customs authorities to CELEBI to waive off the said charges.

The action of CELEBI to not to allow the clearance of the shipment without the payment of demurrage charges is contrary to the provisions of Handling of Cargo in Customs Area Regulation 2009.

Arguments of CELEBI viz. custodian

CELEBI is bound by the policies, instructions, guidelines, circulars, notifications and regulations formulated by Ministry of Civil Aviation or Airport Authority of India or AERA and it is not bound by any contrary regulations of the Customs department with respect to waiver of any charges levied by CELEBI. As per the policy formulated by AAI no waiver of any charges has to be granted in cases any fine/penalty/personal penalty/warning is imposed by the customs authorities.

The regulations framed by the customs authorities stipulate that the same are subjected to any other law for the time being in force and such are subject to the policy framed by the AAI which policy was framed in 2003 and Regulations came into force in 2009 and as such in terms of said policy, no waiver can be granted.

The waiver, if any granted earlier, has been granted on case to case basis.

HEADNOTE: Section 172 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Non-resident - Shipping business of - Whether demurrage payable to non-resident owner of charterer of ship on account of delay in loading goods sold to non-resident would not be taxable - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioners entered into an agreement to sell ore to foreign buyer. The agreement was in the nature of FOB contract. The ships were chartered by the foreign buyer of ore for the purpose of conveying the ores purchased from the seller. The seller was paid price at the rate specified in the agreement and the quantity of the ore was quantified with reference to their loading into the ship. In case there was delay in loading, the seller had to pay demurrage and similarly in case time was saved in loading, the seller was entitled to receive dispatch money. The ITO held that this demurrage was essentially an extended freight payable towards the carriage of the goods and was taxable in the same manner, as the receipt towards freight was taxed.

On writ, the Single Judge held that the demurrage was not an extended freight at all; that section 172 covered the field of taxing a non-resident owner or charterer of a ship who was not engaged in the business of operation of shipping and section 5 was inapplicable to the facts of the instant case.

On writ appeal :

HELD: Section 172(1) identifies the subject of taxation. That subject is to be taxed only as provided under section 172(2) to (7). There is no question of any residuary income attributable to that subject being taxed elsewhere. That will be amending section 172(1) by reading into it a supposed intention of the law-maker; such a course is impermissible.

Section 172(1) is not attracted to the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of operation of ships. A non-resident owner of charterer of a ship which carries passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India only, is covered by section 172.

Since section 172 is a complete code by itself, the levy and collection of tax in respect of the subject on which the tax is levied thereunder has to be only as provided therein. For whatever reason, the concept of total income of a non-resident person coming within section 172(1) is confined to the specified income under section 172(2). There is no scope at all to travel outside section 172 to impose tax on such a person's income derived in the manner stated in section 172(2).

Thus, if the payment is to be made not on account of carriage of goods, etc., then section 172(2) is not attracted and, therefore, such a receipt or payment is not taxable under section 172.

A perusal of the agreements showed that that demurrage payable was to prevent delay in loading the goods. In other words, the payment was to speed up the activity of delivering the goods to the purchaser in whom the title vested on delivery into the ship. If the seller expedited the delivery and loading, then he gets "dispatch money". While dispatch money was receivable by the seller, i.e., the petitioners, the demurrage was receivable by the purchaser. The carriage of goods by the ship commenced on completion of the loading work till then the goods were in the process of delivery on board the ship. The demurrage payable in the instant case at the most was on account of deley in the delivery of the goods on board the ship. If so, certainly section 172(2) was inapplicable.

The demurrage paid or payable under the said two agreements could not be taxed in the manner pleaded by the revenue.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(6A), read with Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Foreign companies - Income by way of royalty/fees for technical services - Petitioner-company entered into an agreement with 
a foreign company for mooring job of floating dock - Having regard 
to delay, foreign company claimed additional payment for extra period 
of work - Whether only because foreign company in debit note used expression ‘demurrage’ instead of ‘fee for technical services’ benefit of section 10(6A) could be denied to assessee - Held, no

FACT: The petitioner-company entered into an agreement with a Singapore based company in terms whereof the mooring job of the Floating Dock was entrusted to the latter. The work was to be completed within 16 days. As there was delay in the work, the said company was paid additional amount for extra period. According to the petitioner, although expression ‘demurrage’ had been used in debit note, in truth and substance, it was fee for technical services, which was supported by the Singapore based company. The IAC, however, treated such payment under the heading ‘Any other payments’ and held that the provisions of section 10(6A) were not applicable. On appeal, the Commissioner affirmed the order of the IAC.

On writ :

HELD: The Singapore based company also clarified in its letter that the expression ‘demurrage charges’ had been used having regard to the provisions normally made in a marine contract although in effect and substance, the same came within the purview of ‘fee for technical services’. [Para 8]

A bare perusal of section 9(1)(vii) would clarify and show that the same carries definite import. The transaction entered by and between the petitioner and the Singapore-based company was, therefore, required to be considered in the light of the afore-mentioned provision. The question was not considered from that angle. By reason of the impugned order, the IAC as well as the Commissioner had failed to exercise their jurisdiction vested therein by law and a jurisdictional error had been committed. By reason of the said order, the respondent had failed to perform its statutory duties to which it was otherwise obliged to. [Para 10]

The impugned order was, accordingly, set aside. The matter was remitted back to the competent authority for fresh consideration.

HEADNOTE: Section 47 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Clearance of imported goods for home consumption - Cannot be withheld when import lawful and correct value declared/accounted. Demurrage/Ground rent waived as goods were not being released

FACT: The petitioners imported components of electric typewriters in September 1985 and filed B/E and also deposited duty. The goods were, however, detained by the Customs and were finally directed to be confiscated by the Collector. On appeal to the Tribunal, the import was held to be lawful. However, the matter was remanded to the Collector for valuation. The Collector held the declared value to be the correct value and directed that the goods be cleared. The goods were not, however, released despite the Collector's order, hence this appeal.

HELD: Clearance--Once the import of goods has been held to be lawful and the declared value accepted, there is no reason for not releasing the goods. Consequently importer not liable to demurrage/ground rent charges/container charges from the date of filing the B/E. "........when the import was lawful, the goods could not be confiscated and when the valuation has also been finally determined by the Collector.......the declared value as accepted by the Collector, then there was no occasion for not releasing the goods and the petitioner cannot even be held liable for demurrage in these facts and circumstances. In our opinion, therefore, the petitioner is entitled to a direction for the release of the goods without payment of any demurrage/ground rent charges/container charges in respect of the period from the date of filing of the bill of entry."

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 145A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Valuation of closing stock (Demurrage charges) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee had not included demurrage charges paid to Port Authorities in valuation of closing stock as at year-end, in departure with its consistent past practice of valuing its closing inventory by including same as an element of cost, alluding to section 145A - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's method of valuation of its closing stock - Whether demurrage/detention charges, being toward cost for delay in removal of goods could only broadly be said to be a holding cost, and it would be more appropriate to consider it as a cost for delayed removal of goods, i.e., beyond stipulated period same was thus, only a revenue expenditure of period to which it related and, hence, not liable for inclusion in value of goods from any stand point - Held, yes - Whether therefore, revision made by assessee in method of valuation of closing stock was approved on basis of accounting principles, which would govern matter in absence of any specific provision/s in Act toward same, with section 145A being inapplicable - Held, yes - Whether thus, valuation of opening stock which would continue to be valued as per old method was invalid - Held, yes [Paras 3.1 and 4] [In favour of assessee/matter remanded]IT : Demurrage/detention charges were not liable for inclusion in valuation of closing stock

FACT: The assessee had not included the demurrage charges paid to the Port Authorities in the valuation of the closing stock as at the year-end, in departure with its consistent past practice of valuing its closing inventory by including the same as an element of cost, alluding to section 145A.

The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's method of valuation of its closing stock.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) had accepted the assessee's claim on the ground that the said change in its method of accounting by the assessee is a bona fide change and, thus, could not be validly objected to by the revenue.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: Storage cost is neither a cost of purchase nor of conversion nor can it be considered as toward bringing the inventory held in stock to its present location or condition. It is in the nature of a holding cost, which could be considered as an element of cost only where the goods have to be necessarily held in a particular manner, entailing cost, for a defined period, prior to their further processing, i.e., itself represents a process integral to their conversion, so that it represents a process and, thus, conversion cost. There is accordingly no question of the same being added to its value. A simple question would clarify the issue, i.e., whether rent, were the goods, instead of lying at the port, removed expeditiously to a rented premises, saving demurrage, or the cost of the staff attending thereto (godown) or otherwise supervising the storage, etc. be said to form part of the acquisition or conversion cost of the goods or otherwise incurred in bringing the same to their present location and condition, so as to be included in their valuation? Surely not. The third element of cost, i.e., other than toward acquisition and conversion, it would be noted, is broadly worded, so that it could in fact be said to include the cost of acquisition and conversion as well. It is only the direct cost incurred toward so bringing that could be included in as much as it adds value. In fact, the demurrage/detention charges, being toward the cost for the delay in removal of the goods, can only loosely/broadly be said to be a holding cost, and it would be more appropriate to consider it as a cost for the delayed removal of goods, i.e., beyond the stipulated period. The same thus is only a revenue expenditure of the period to which it relates and no more and, thus, not liable for inclusion in the value of the goods from any stand point.

As regards the objection by the revenue with reference to section 145A, the same deserves to fail. This is as even if the detention/demurrage charge is considered as not arising on account of a contractual obligation, but a statutory one, i.e., as in the nature of a levy or impost (which would though need to be established), it would stand to be included under section 145A only where it represents a qualifying cost - which have found as not, and not otherwise. [Para 3.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 44B, read with section 172, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Shipping business in case of non-residents - Petitioners were mine owners and exporters of iron and manganese ore, who entered into export agreements with foreign buyers who sent their ships either owned by them or chartered by them - It was provided in contract that for detention of ships for unforeseen circumstance petitioners had to bear demurrage charges and pay same to owner or charterer of ships - Whether payments of such demurrage could fall under section 44B or 172(2) - Held, no

FACT: The petitioners were mine owners mining, among other things, manganese and iron ores, which they exported. The petitioners entered into an agreement with a foreign buyer to supply on credit basis iron and manganese ore and the foreign buyers sent their ships either owned by them or chartered by them for carriage of the goods. Contracts provided that in case of detention of a ship in the port for unforeseen reasons, petitioners had to bear the demurrage charges and pay the same to the owner or charterer of the ship. Payments for such demurrage were being paid with the approval of the RBI through the regular bank channels. In February, 1988, the first respondent - Dy. Controller of RBI - issued a Circular dated 22-2-1988 to all the exporters requiring them to obtain income-tax clearance certificate for remittance of demurrage payments. By yet another communication dated 11-10-1988, all the exporters had been informed by the first respondent that all demurrage amounts payable in respect of foreign vessels attract Indian Income-tax. Therefore, the exporters were advised to ensure that all applications for remittances towards demurrage payable to foreign vessels should be duly supported by income-tax clearance certificates or documentary evidence that tax was withheld along with a no-objection certificate from the department.

On writ, the petitioners disputed the circular instructions and prayed that these be quashed.

HELD: There is this difference between section 44B and section 172. In section 44B no procedure for assessment and collection of tax is provided. The use of non obstante clause refers only to sections 28 to 43A and not to the other provisions of the Act as contemplated under sub-section (1) of section 172. Section 28 and the following sub-sections up to 43A are to be found under the heading - D - 'Profits and gains of business or profession' in Chapter IV of the Act. In other words, income from shipping accrued or deemed to have accrued to a non-resident shipowner or charterer falls outside the scope of trade and business normally so understood. The incidence of tax under section 44B is on a non-resident engaged in the business of operation of ships owned or chartered by him or it, and if such income constituted the amounts earned on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from any port in India and the amount so received or deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods etc.

In contrast section 172 does not refer to a non-resident assessee. It only refers to levy and recovery of tax in case of any ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident which carries passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from a port in India. If this difference is borne in mind, then the want of special procedure for levy and collection under section 44B becomes patent and obvious. In the result, a non-resident engaged in shipping business subject to the qualification of carrying goods, passengers, livestock, mail or goods etc., being an assessee shall be assessed in accordance with section 143 and not in accordance with the procedure prescribed for a non-resident shipowner or charterer covered by section 172(1) and (2) of the Act. Therefore, the inevitable conclusion is that the shipowner or charterer in section 172(1) is not an assessee as defined in clause (7) of section 2 of the Act.

A person who is required to be covered and controlled by the provisions contained in section 172 is, therefore, not an assessee. He is a mere shipowner who is a non-resident or a charterer of a ship, also a non-resident. In other words, the heading under H in Chapter XV assumes some significance in interpreting section 172 of the Act. The Court is bound to take notice of it. That heading is as follows:

"H — Profits of non-residents from occasional shipping business." [Emphasis supplied]

Regulations framed by AAI : The AAI has framed regulations in exercise of powers conferred under the AAI Act. The regulations relied upon by the respondent CELEBI as applicable to the present case are the Airports Authority of India (storage and processing of cargo, courier and express goods and postal mail) Regulations, 2003. As per the said Regulation, the Airport Authority fixes the charges for processing of the cargo and also formulates policy for waiver of such demurrage charges. (b) Delay arose by reason of dispute in the assessable value or for revalidating or correcting the license in ordinary course of appraisal. [Para 36]

Policy of Waiver of AAI : The Policy framed by the AAI lays down that the authorities specified are authorised to sanction, in consultation with the finance and accounts department, remission/waiver of demurrage charges regarding cargo operation. Power of customs is to control storage, removal and handling : Section 156 of the Customs Act lays down the general rule making power of the central government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act and section 157 lays down the power of the board to make regulations to carry out the purposes of the Act. Under the Customs Act, the custom authorities are concerned with the setting up of public or private warehouses and for storage, removal and handling of imported goods in a customs area. [Para 38]

HCCAR : The Handling of Cargo under Customs Area Regulations, 2009 have been framed to provide for the manner in which the imported goods/export goods shall be received, stored, delivered or otherwise handled in a customs area. HEADNOTE: Section 53 of the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 - Exemption from and remission of rates or charges - Demurrage charges - Original importers failed to clear goods - Appellant agreed to buy consignments - Due to delay in taking delivery, demurrage charges were levied - Such delay occurred because of time taken in ensuring compliance of various statutory obligations such as amendment of IGM etc. - Appellant cleared goods after making payment towards demurrage, under protest - In a meantime, Government of India notified 'Statement of Guidelines for Remission of demurrage charges' where goods detained by custom were to be considered for grant of remission from payment of demurrage for period goods were being so processed by custom authorities - However, Port rejected request of petitioner for complete remission - Whether where no reasons were demonstrated for declining complete remission as claimed by appellant, Port's decision to decline remission was to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 53]Port Trust Act : Where on failure to lift consignment by original importers, appellant purchased same and demurrage charges was levied due to delay in taking delivery, since delay occurred due to ensuring compliance of various statutory obligations, demurrage charges to be remitted

FACT: During the period November 1991 to January 1992, 78 shipments of zinc ingots and copper iron bars were imported by 5 different consignees from one MDL. These consignments were landed at the Bombay Port. The consignees filed bills of entry for 37 out of the 78 consignments, but, subsequently, failed to lift the consignments and, thus, they came to be stored at by the Port of Bombay. Facing a grave loss MDL requested the present appellant, if they were interested in purchasing the goods.

The appellant applied to the Customs Authorities to have the Bills of Entry substituted in their name for the 37 consignments for which the original consignees had filed Bills of Entry, and also applied to file Bills of Entry for the remaining 41 consignments lying unclaimed.

The clearing agent of the petitioner wrote to the Customs Authorities seeking an amendment of the Import General Manifest so that the goods could be cleared. The appellant was granted a detention certificate by the Customs Authority for the 41 consignments.

Government of India vide Statement of Guidelines for Remission of Demurrage Charges', notified that goods/consignments detained by Customs for 'ITC Facilities' were to be considered for grant of remission from payment of demurrage for the period the goods were being so processed by Customs Authorities. However, in the meantime, the Respondent levied a total of Rs. 2.81 crore as demurrage charges, the total remission granted by the Port of Bombay was Rs. 90 crore and, therefore, demanded a balance of Rs. 1.91 crore for the period of 23-3-1992 till 9-9-1992, on the ground that no remission could be granted prior to date of noting.

Aggrieved by the order of the respondent, the appellant, filed writ petition. The appellant, however, cleared the goods after making payment of the amount under protest.

By the judgment under appeal, the High Court dismissed the writ petition.

On appeal:

HELD: The dispute in this case centres around demurrage. The expression "demurrage" is not defined under the Act. The expression demurrage in the world of shipping meant a sum agreed by the charterer to be paid as liquidated damages for delay beyond a stipulated or reasonable time for loading or unloading, generally referred to as the laydays or laytime. Where the sum is only to be paid for a fixed number of days, and a further delay takes place, the shipowner's remedy is to recover unliquidated "damages for detention" for the period of the delay. The phrase "demurrage" is sometimes loosely used to cover both these meanings.' [Para 24]

In Trustees of the Port of Madras v. Aminchand Pyarelal [1976] 3 SCC 167, it was opined that the "Board has used the expression "demurrage" not in the strict mercantile sense but merely to signify a charge which may be levied on goods after the expiration of free days".[Para 25]

Regulation 2(g) of the International Airports Authority (Storage and Processing of Goods) Regulation, 1980 made under the provisions of the International Airports Authority Act, 1971, defined the expression 'demurrage' to mean, the rate or amount payable to the airport by a shipper or consignee or carrier, for not removing the cargo within the time allowed. [Para 26]
