The assessee contends that the payment is made to a non-resident/foreign company and, therefore, there may be an obligation to deduct the tax at source in terms of sub-section (1) of section 195 but the overriding provision in section 172 will come to its assistance. [Para 44] The shipping business of non-residents is an aspect dealt with by section 172. While considering the levy and recovery of tax in case of such business which is carried on with the aid of any ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident which carries passengers etc. shipped at a port in India, then, it is to compute the tax and recover it in relation to such business of a non-resident that section 172 is incorporated in the Statute Book. There are special provisions for computing profits and gains for shipping business in the case of a non-resident and enacted by section 44B which falls in Chapter IV - 'Computation of Business Income'. [Para 45]

A bare perusal of section 44B would indicate as to how this provision covers the case of an assessee who is a non-resident and engaged in the business of operation of ships. That stipulates a sum equal to 7½ per cent of the aggregate of the amount specified in sub-section (2) of section 44B as deemed to be profits and gains of such business chargeable to tax under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession'. It is the Explanation which refers to the demurrage and for the purpose of sub-section (2) of section 44B. It clarifies that the amount paid or payable or received or deemed to be received, as the case may be, by way of demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature shall for the purposes of sub-section (1) deemed to be the profits and gains of the business, namely, shipping business chargeable to tax under that head.

The amounts which are paid or payable whether in or out of India to the assessee or to any person on his behalf on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India and the amount received was deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port outside India shall be deemed to be the profits and gains. On that the tax is payable by virtue of sub-section (1) of section 172. That has to be levied and recovered in terms of the sub-sections of section 172.

Once section 172 falls in Chapter XV titled as Liability in Special Cases - Profits of Non-residents, then section 172 is referable to section 44B. Both provisions open with a non obstante clause and whereas section 44B enacts special provisions for computing profits and gains of shipping business in case of non-residents, section 172 dealing with shipping business of non-residents is enacted for the purpose of levy and recovery of tax in the case of any ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident operated from India.

These sections and particularly section 172 devise a scheme for levy and recovery of tax. The sub-sections of section 44B denote as to how the amounts paid to or payable would include demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature. The sub-sections of section 172 read together and harmoniously would reveal as to how the tax should be levied, computed, assessed and recovered. Therefore, there is no warrant in applying the provisions in Chapter XVII of Act for collection and recovery of the tax and its deduction at source vide section 195. [Para 46]

It is the recipient's position and the perspective in which the recipient's income would be taxed will have to be borne in mind. The non-resident shipping company in respect of its income would be in a position to rely upon section 44B and consequently section 172. However, one does not see how there is an obligation to deduct tax at source on the resident assessee/Indian company in the instant case. While computing the income of the non-resident Indian / foreign company, assistance can be derived by such non-residents from section 44B if they are in shipping business. It would also be in a position to rely upon section 172 but the responsibility of the person making payment to a non-resident in sub-section (1) of section 195 cannot be avoided in the manner set out in other cases. The scheme as above operates only to cases covered by section 172 and none else. [Para 48]

The question referred is answered accordingly.

The case of the Assessing Officer was that the IHC was not covered under section 44B. The assessee had placed reliance on the Explanation to section 44B to contend that IHC would be covered within its Explanation. [Para 6] A plain reading of the Explanation to section 44B reveals that the demurrage charges or handling charges or other amounts of similar nature have been brought within the ambit of 'business income' for applying the rate of 7½ per cent. The very nature of items prescribed in the Explanation being demurrage charges or handling charges, which precede 'any other amount of similar nature', show that the latter category has to draw a colour from the items referred to in the earlier part. The expression 'any other amount of similar nature' cannot be read in isolation by disregarding the nature of items preceding it. The meaning of the succeeding expression has to be understood in the context of the preceding words. Since the demurrage charges or handling charges have been mentioned in the Explanation prior to 'any other amount of similar nature', 'any other amount' has to be considered, which is similar to or closely resembles with the nature of demurrage or handling charges. Handling charges are the charges paid for loading/unloading/stacking, etc., of the containers and the demurrage charges are in nature of penalty for non-removal of the cargo in time. On the contrary, the IHC are towards transport of the goods from the exporter's place to the port. The very nature of inland transportation charges clearly differentiates it from handling or demurrage charges, which are of a different genus. Therefore, there was no substance in the submission of the assessee that inland haulage charges were covered under section 44B, as these were equal to or part and parcel of the amount on account of carriage of goods shipped at any port in or outside India, and, hence, were automatically covered under Article 8. [Paras 7 and 8]

Section 90(2) gives an option to an assessee to whom the DTAA applies either to be governed by the regular provisions of the Act, or take recourse to the DTAA. The option is with the assessee to be ruled by either of the two options which is more beneficial to it. In the instant case, the assessee had opted to go by the DTAA and the Assessing Officer had also accepted the same. [Para 9]

The DTAA is the main document and has to be considered for examining the taxability or otherwise of an item of income in the respective States. If the language of the DTAA is clear and does not admit of any doubt, there is no need for referring to the OECD Model and commentaries, etc. [Para 10]

The case of the assessee was that it was covered under Article 8(2)(b)(ii ) as well as under Article 8(2)(c). On the contrary, the plea of the revenue was that the assessee was not covered under any of the above said clauses and, hence, the Assessing Officer was justified in putting the IHC to tax. Article 8(2)(b)(ii ) defines the income derived from the 'operation of ships in the international traffic to mean the income derived from the transportation by sea of goods carried on by the owners or lessees or charterers of the ships including 'any other activity directly connected with such transportation'. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Pilfered goods - Demurrage - BPT must remit if Customs issue certificate or Court allows it. Such certificates have binding effect--However the remission can apply only to 80%, and the maximum period allowable is 150 days

FACT: Goods imported by the petitioners were detained at the Bombay port on the ground that the licences produced did not adequately cover the goods. Petitioners' appeal was allowed, and the Customs authorities were instructed to clear the goods forthwith and to issue a detention certificate for waiving of port trust charges. Bombay Port Trust, however, refused to release the goods without payment of demurrage charges which petitioners paid under protest. After clearance of the goods the Petitioners applied for remission and/or refund of demurrage charges, which was rejected. Their contention in this petition is that goods were detained by mistake by Customs authorities for which the petitioners cannot be made to suffer, and that they should be allowed remission of 80% of demurrage charges for the full period of 225 days. It is also argued that the order passed by the B.P.T. authorities was invalid and bad in law for having been passed without a personal hearing.

HELD: Remission of demurrage charges--rule of law is binding on executive authorities. Action of B.P.T. in rejecting remission of demurrage charges, in spite of the High Court order, held to be wrong and arbitrary and it was passed without assigning any valid reasons. "As I have pointed out heretofore in the order of the Secretary of the B.P.T. Authorities dated 27.8.1986, no reasons at all have been assigned for rejecting the claim for remission made by the Petitioners. I have dealt with the reasons given in the affidavit-in-reply, and I have come to the conclusion that the reasons given are such that no reasonable person would arrive at the conclusion arrived at by the Secretary. The order of the Bombay Port Trust authorities, therefore, is certainly not one which is informed by reason and hence the same is perverse. On that ground the order needs to be struck down".

2. Demurrage charges--remission of demurrage charges is allowable only up to the limit of 80% of charges and for a maximum period of 150 days, the remaining 20% of which is to be detained as handling and storage charges. B.P.T. policy statement, paragraphs 4, 10 & 4.11. "I am afraid it is not possible to accept this submission of Shri Mehta in view of the Policy Statement of the B.P.T. Authorities, Respondent No. 4, stated heretofore in paragraphs 4.10 and 4.11, which ultimately became part of Resolution No. 635 of 1975. Under those rules, the B.P.T. Authorities decided that the remission of the demurrage charges would be only to the tune of 80%, keeping the 20% towards service charges including handling costs and storage charges. Paragraph 4.11 laid down that the concession of remission would be applicable only to the extent of 150 days. The Remission Committee was empowered to decide each case on merits. The petitioners, therefore, under the policy decision of the B.P.T. Authorities, Respondent No. 4, would be entitled only to 80% of the demurrage charges for a period of 150 days."

3. Natural justice is not isolated if the aggrieved party has not asked for a personal hearing, consequent to which no personal hearing is given by the Remission Committee. "In the instant case also, I find that the Petitioners at no stage had asked the Remission Committee to give a personal hearing. This being the case, I do not think that Shri Mehta's contention can be accepted that in the absence of a personal hearing the order passed by the B.P.T. Authorities dated 28.7.1986 was bad."

HEADNOTE: Section 44B of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 8 of Model OECD Convention - Non-resident - Shipping business of (Reimbursement of expenses) - Assessee engaged in business of refining crude oil, entered into contracts with non-resident for supply of equipment, designs and drawings and project management and supervision contract - Demurrage charges incurred by non-resident on behalf of assessee were reimbursed - Said charges were brought to tax under section 44B - Whether in present case, both conditions envisaged by sub-section (1) of section 44B were not fulfilled and, thus, section 44B was not applicable - Held, yes [Paras 4  5] [In favour of assessee]IT: Section 44B could not be invoked in case of demurrage charges reimbursed by assessee to non-resident for import of crude oil

FACT: Assessee engaged in business of refining crude oil, entered into contracts with non-resident for supply of equipment, designs and drawings and project management and supervision contract. Demurrage charges incurred by non-resident on behalf of assessee were reimbursed.

Said charges were brought to tax under section 44B.

HELD: The case of the Department is that the Assessee has remitted/ paid the amount for design and drawing contracts. It is in such situation and the facts peculiar to the present case, firstly, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer was in error in applying both Section 44B and Section 195. The facts as set out are not found to be so by both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal. In fact the question of law arises out of payment of demurrage. That is reimbursed to the supplier of crude oil. It is in the nature of reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal found that this reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee cannot be brought within sub-section (1) of Section 44B. That is special provision for computing the profits and gains of shipping business in the case of a non-resident. That envisages the profits and gains of business of operation of ships. The sum to be covered by this provision should be of the nature referred to therein. In the present case, what has been paid is the sum for reimbursing the expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee by a non-resident. The amount referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 44B and which are deemed to be profits and gains of the business of operation of ships chargeable to tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" shall be the amount firstly, paid or payable, whether in or out of India, to the Assessee or to any person on his behalf on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port in India and secondly, received or deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the Assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port outside India. [Para 4]

In the present case, the finding of fact is that both conditions envisaged by sub-section (1) of Section 44B are not fulfilled. The provision has been invoked in case of reimbursement of demurrage charges paid or reimbursed by Assessee for import of crude oil. It is such a finding of fact which is recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) and which has been confirmed by the Tribunal in the impugned order. The reasons assigned in Tribunal's order would, therefore, go to show that the view taken is in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case at hand. The view taken, therefore, is possible one. It cannot be termed, by any stretch of imagination, as perverse or vitiated by error of law apparent on the face of the record. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: II. Section 172 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Non-resident - Shipping business in case of (Demurrage payments) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had paid demurrage to various non-resident companies with whom India did not have DTAA, without deducting tax at source - Assessing Officer disallowed said expenditure in view of section 40(a)(i), as no tax had been deducted on said amount - Commissioner(Appeals) deleted disallowance holding that these payments were not demurrage payments made to owner of ships as applicable under section 172 - Whether for bringing a case under section 172, one has to establish a case of profits of non-resident from occasional shipping business and since in instant case assessee had not earned profit from occasional shipping and was not a non-resident, section 172 did not have application in relation to assessee - Held, yes [Para 17] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: Assessing Officer noted that assessee had paid demurrage to various non-resident companies with whom India did not have DTAA, without deducting tax at source.

Assessing Officer disallowed said expenditure in view of section 40(a)(i), as no tax had been deducted on said amount.

On appeal, the Commissioner(Appeals) deleted the disallowance holding that these payments are not demurrage but payments made to purchasers of iron ore and not to the owner of ships as applicable under section 172 and these payments are taxable under section 195 (1).

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: The issue in the instant case is duly covered by the decision of the High Court in the case of CIT v. Orient Goa (P.) Ltd. [2010] 325 ITR 554/[2009] 185 Taxman 131 wherein the Bombay High Court held that for bringing a case under section 172, one has to establish a case of profits of non-resident from occasional shipping business and since assessee had not earned profit from occasional shipping and was not a non-resident, section 172 did not have application in relation to assessee and since the facts of the case were governed by section 40(a)(i), order passed by Assessing Officer was legal, proper and in accordance with scheme of Act. Thus, respectfully following the aforesaid decision of the High Court the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside and that of the Assessing Officer is restored.[Para 17]

HEADNOTE: II. Section 9, read with sections 40(a)(ia), 172, 194C and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India [Business connection] - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee-company reimbursed demurrage charges for delayed loading, payable by foreign buyers to shipowners, as assessee had to export goods on FOB basis, which was disallowed under section 40(a)(ia) for non-deduction of tax at source - Whether, such payment was in nature of expenditure incurred for sales in view of contract with foreign buyer - Held, yes - Whether, since Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) provides that no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to a non-resident, through or from operations confined to purchase of goods in India for export, amount of demurrage could not be deemed as income in hands of foreign buyer, and no disallowance could be made under section 40(a)(ia) - Held, yes [Para 33.1] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company remitted the demurrage amount for delayed loading, payable by the buyers of its iron ore to the ship owners as the assessee had to export goods on FOB basis. The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount under section 40(a)(i) for remittance without deduction of tax at source. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance.

HELD: The assessee has paid the demurrage charges to the non-resident in respect of delay in loading the ship. The sum was reimbursed by the assessee to the foreign buyer to compensate the foreign buyer for paying demurrage to the ship owner when ship came to Indian port and the assessee could not load the goods on to the ship within the limited time period. The export sales were made to the foreign Pakistani buyer on FOB basis. In view of the contract with the Pakistani buyer the assessee was bound to compensate the Pakistani buyer in respect of demurrage paid by the Pakistani buyer to the ship owner. This payment can be regarded to be the expenditure incurred by the assessee for the sale of the goods and was not akin to price deduction due to fault in product/service and was equivalent to discount/rebate which can be adjusted against the sale price. [Para 31]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of the goods in India for the purpose of export. The non-resident buyer got the compensation towards the demurrage incurred through the operation which was confined to the purchase of the goods, i.e. in relation to the ship which it had arranged for taking the delivery of the goods from the assessee/seller from India. Therefore, this income cannot be deemed to accrue or arise in India in the hands of the foreign buyer, and therefore, it cannot be taxable in India and is not liable to tax deduction at source. On this basis, no disallowance can be made under section 40(a)(ia), and accordingly, the disallowance is deleted. [Para 32]

From a perusal of the Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995, it is apparently clear that the provisions of sections 194C and 195 relating to tax deduction at source are not applicable where the provisions of section 172, relating to shipping business are applicable. The circular issued by the CBDT is binding on the department. In view of the circular, the assessee was not obliged to deduct TDS on the payment made as demurrage charges and the demurrage charges are also liable to be taxed under section 172. The assessee, since, is not liable to deduct tax at source, no question arises for making any disallowance under section 40(a)(i). [Para 33]

-state supply of goods or services or both. The proviso to sub-section (1) of section 5 provides that the integrated tax on goods imported into India shall be levied and collected in accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, on the value as determined under the said Act at the point when the duties of customs are levied on the said goods under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962. [Para 208] Thus, the goods imported into India are subjected to the integrated tax under section 5(1) read with section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. [Para 210]

The writ-applicant imports the goods on CIF basis and thus the amount charged by the foreign exporter includes the freight amount till the place of customs clearance in India. The writ-applicant discharges the basic customs duty on the value of goods under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962. In addition, the writ-applicant also discharges the IGST on such value under section 5, read with section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1972. [Para 211]

The impugned Notification No. 8/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate), read with Notification No. 10/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017 seek to levy and collect the integrated tax again on the amount of freight as a supply of service by deeming the importer in India as the recipient of supply of transportation service. [Para 212]

It is a fundamental principle of construction of tax statutes that if the words of the Act on one construction results into double taxation of the same transaction, that result will be avoided by adopting another construction which may reasonably be open. Further, double taxation, by way of delegated legislation, when the statute does not expressly provide, is not permissible. [Para 213]

In the case of United Shippers Ltd. v. CCE [2015] 57 taxmann.com 429 (Mum. - CESTAT) the Tribunal held that there can be no levy of service tax on barge charges and the handling charges which is part of the import transaction into India and form an integral part of the transaction value on which the customs duty is leviable. The judgment of the Tribunal has been affirmed by the Supreme Court in the case of CCE v. United Shippers 2015 (39) STR J369. [Para 214]

Thus, having paid the IGST on the amount of freight which is included in the value of the imported goods, the impugned notifications levying tax again as a supply of service, without any express sanction by the statute, are illegal and liable to be struck down. [Para 215]

Purpose/object for which tax is levied will not validate an ultra vires or unconstitutional tax

Prior to 1-6-2016, the services of transportation of goods in a vessel from a place outside India up to the customs station of clearance in India were exempted from service tax. As a result, the Indian Shipping Lines were unable to avail the input tax credit of tax paid on the goods and services and such tax formed part of their transportation cost. To provide them the level playing field, service tax was imposed on the service of inward transportation of goods to enable the Indian Shipping Lines to avail the input tax credit. Further, the services of the outward transportation of goods were treated as export of service and thus the credit of the excise and service tax was available. It is further stated that subsequently, many FOB contracts were being converted into CIF contracts. In order that the tax is suffered by both, the foreign shipping line and the Indian shipping line, the services of the inward transportation of goods provided by a person in a non-taxable territory to a person in a non-taxable territory were made liable to service tax. [Para 217]

History of taxation of international transportation service prior to Finance Act, 2016

Chapter V of the Finance Act, 1994, for the first time, introduced taxation of services in India. Till 1-7-2012, the service tax was levied on selected categories of services. Thus, the services which were specifically included within the tax ambit, were only taxable. Section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994, defined the term 'taxable services'. Clause (zzzzl) was introduced in section 65(105) with effect from 1-9-2009 which provided levy of service tax on the service of transportation of coastal goods, transportation of goods through national waterways and through inland waterways. [Para 218]

Thus, only the service of transportation of coastal goods or through national waterways or inland waterways was made taxable. The service of international transportation was not leviable to service tax. [Para 219]

With effect from 1-7-2012, the negative list regime was introduced for levy of service tax and all services were made taxable except those provided under the negative list of service. Section 66D of the Finance Act, 1994, provided such negative list of services. [Para 220]

HEADNOTE: Section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [corresponding to section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961] - Business expenditure - Goods unauthorisedly imported by assessee-firm confiscated by customs authorities - Option to assessee to get import regularised on paying Rs. 22,000 as fine - Matter unsuccessfully agitated before higher authorities for four years - Assessee finally took delivery of goods after paying fine and substantial demurrage charges for use of port facilities beyond permissible free period - Whether tribunal was justified in law in disallowing demurrage charges as admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) - Held, on Facts, No

FACT: The assessee-firm ran a rolling mill where iron bars were manufactured out of billets and plate cuttings, etc. Certain goods imported by it were confiscated by customs authorities, by an order dated 10-02-1959, on finding that these were not covered by its import licence. The assessee, however, had the option to pay Rs. 22,000 as fine and clear the goods for home consumption subject to adjustment thereof against the licence held by him. After unsuccessfully agitating the matter before various authorities for four years, it finally cleared the goods by paying not only the fine but also a sum of Rs. 19,119 as demurrage charges for use of the port facilities beyond the permissible free period during the litigation period. The assessee claimed the deduction of these demurrage charges as business expenses under section 10(2)(xv) but the same was disallowed by the ITO. Its appeal before the AAC and the Tribunal were unsuccessful. The Tribunal held (i) that the demurrage was paid not for business reasons but for breach of the Import Control Order, and (ii) that there was no essential difference between the "fine" paid and the "demurrage" paid.

On reference :

HELD: 1. Demurrage charged by port authorities is in the nature of compensation for delay in clearing the goods from the godowns of the port authorities. It includes amount chargeable for storage and safe custody of the goods by the port authorities beyond the free period allowed under port rules. In the instant case, the demurrage paid by the assessee was not a fine paid for any criminal act but compensation for use of the port facilities beyond the permissible free period.

2. Once the unauthorized import of goods had been regularized on payment of fine, commercial expediency dictated the assessee to take delivery of the goods after paying the demurrage failing which its stock-in-trade would have been auctioned by the port authorities to realise their dues. The payment was, thus, made by the assessee to preserve its stock-in-trade and to utilise it for its manufacturing business.

3. The impugned expenditure was, therefore, held to be a permissible revenue deduction under section 70(2)(xv).

HEADNOTE: Section 49 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Storage of imported goods in warehouse pending clearance - Detained goods - Plea for storage of goods in warehouse--Assistant Collector is empowered under Section 49 to order storage of goods in a warehouse pending determination of dispute regarding duty liability of goods--Petitioner accordingly directed to file application to Assistant Collector

FACT: Release of a consignment of goods from the Inland Container Depot (Railways) at New Delhi was requested by the petitioners who pleaded that detention of goods was causing them great loss and that if the goods could not be released, they should be stored or deposited in a public or private warehouse. The respondents urged that a proper application should be filed by the owner before the Assistant Collector who had the power and authority under Section 49 to order the storage of goods in a public or private warehouse pending a decision on whether the goods had been legally imported or whether they were leviable to duty.

HELD: Jurisdiction: Application for storage or deposit of goods in a public or private warehouse should be filed before the Assistant Collector who is empowered under Section 49 to order storage pending determination of whether goods have been legally imported or are liable to duty, as clearly provided for in Section 49. "In view of the clear language of Section 49, it is imperative for the petitioner to seek his relief under Section 49 from the Assistant Collector concerned by making a proper application. I hope and trust that if an application under Section 49 is made by the applicant, the same shall be disposed of without any delay or loss of any time keeping in view of the huge losses which are being suffered by the petitioner in the form of payment of demurrage."

III. Conclusion :

accepted the contentions of the assessee so far as ocean freight of Rs. 49.39 lakhs paid by the assessee to these Indian agents of non-resident shipping companies towards the ocean freight while rest of the amount of Rs. 9.60 lakhs paid towards other service charges were disallowed by the Commissioner (Appeals) by invoking provision of section 40(a)(ia) as assessee had not deducted tax at source on such payments..

On appeal to the Tribunal: HELD: The non-resident shipping companies have confirmed vide freight certificates to have received the same amount of other service charges which are mainly terminal handling charges, documentation charges, demurrage etc. from these agents. It is observed that provision of section 172(8) also stipulate that other charges such as demurrage or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature are also covered by provision of section 172(2) by virtue of provisions of section 172(8), which by virtue of CBDT Circular No 723, dated 19-9-1995 shall also take it out of provision of section 194C for deduction of tax at source. As discussed, the non-resident shipping companies have given two freight certificates with respect to each bill raised by BS Corporation, the first pertain to ocean freight which is already accepted by Commissioner (Appeals) while granting relief to the assessee and revenue is not in appeal against relief granted by the Commissioner (Appeals), and the second freight certificate is with respect to THC charges and documentation charges which are acknowledged to be received by non-resident shipping companies, thus it leaves no doubt that these are merely reimbursement of expenses as also claimed by BS Corporation vide debit note and are in the nature of payment referred to in section 172(8) and hence are covered by provision of section 172(2) and no income tax was required to be deducted at source under section 194C keeping in view special provisions relating to taxability of non-resident shipping companies who have to discharge their liabilities towards income tax before leaving port or to make satisfactory arrangements for payment of taxes as are contained in section 172 and section 44B. The circular no. 723 issued by the CBDT on 19-9-1995 also supports the stand of the assessee that with respect to the ocean freight, demurrage charge, handling charges or other amount of similar nature which are paid to the Indian agents or authorized representative of non-resident shipping company who carry passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at port in India are not covered for deduction of tax at source under provision of sections 194C and 195. Thus, keeping in view ratio of decision in the case of CIT v. V.S Dempo & Co. (P.) Ltd. [2016] 381 ITR 303/238 Taxman 91/66 taxmann.com 93 (Bombay) and in the light of the provision of section 172(8), Explanation 2 to sub-section 2 to section 44B read with aforestated Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995, it is held that the issue is covered in favour of the assessee and the deletion of the disallowance of Rs. 9.60 lakhs under section 40(a)(ia) as made by the Assessing Officer which was later confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. The assessee succeeds on this ground. It is ordered accordingly. [Para 7]

The appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 40(a)(i), read with section 172, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business disallowance - Interest, etc., payable outside India - Assessee, an Indian company, claimed deduction on account of demurrage payable to a non-resident company - Assessing Officer considered same as non-deductible claim in view of section 40(a)(i), as no tax had been deducted on said amount - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) observed that demurrages debited by assessee in hands of recipient were in nature of profits of non-resident from occasional shipping business under section 44B, read with section 172, and, therefore, disallowance made by Assessing Officer was incorrect - Tribunal upheld order of Commissioner(Appeals) - Whether for bringing a case under section 172, one has to establish a case of profits of non-resident from occasional shipping business and since in instant case assessee had not earned profit from occasional shipping and was not a non-resident, section 172 did not have application in relation to assessee - Held, yes - Whether facts of instant case were governed by section 40(a)(i) and order passed by Assessing Officer was legal, proper and in accordance with scheme of Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company claimed deduction of certain amount on account of demurrage payable to a non-resident company 'M'. As no tax had been deducted on that amount, the Assessing Officer considered said amount as non-deductible claim in view of section 40(a)( i). On appeal, the Commis-sioner (Appeals) observed that demurrages debited by the assessee in the hands of the recipient were in the nature of profits of non-resident from occasional shipping business under section 44B, read with section 172. He also referred to the provision of section 172(8) which had been brought on the statute by the Finance Act, 1997 with effect from April 1, 1976 and the CBDT Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995 and allowed the assessee's appeal holding that disallowance made by the Assessing Officer under section 40(a)( i) was incorrect. The Tribunal dismissed the revenue's appeal.

On the revenue's appeal to the High Court :

HELD: Section 172 comes under sub-title 'H - Profits of non-residents from occasional shipping business'. Title of section 172 is 'Shipping business of non-residents'. For bringing a case under Chapter XV-H, one has to establish a case of profits of non-residents from occasional shipping business. 'Non-resident' is defined under section 2(30 ), as a person who is not a 'resident' and for the purpose of sections 92, 93 and 168, includes a person who is not ordinarily resident within the meaning of clause (6) of section 6. The assessee, being a company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956, could not be said to be non-resident. The assessee could not lay fingers on section 172, since profits of non-residents were not to be dealt with. The other aspect is that such profits of non-residents should be from occasional shipping business. It was not the case that the assessee had earned some profits from occasional shipping business and was a non-resident. The tax liability of the foreign company, i.e., 'M', Japan which was recipient of demurrages was not being examined. Section 172 did not apply to the facts of the instant case wherein the assessee was an Indian company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. The Tribunal had recorded a perverse observation/finding regarding application of sections 44B and 172. [Para 8]

The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal had wrongly interpreted the circular dated 19-9-1995 issued by the CBDT. That circular could not be considered in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, in aid of the assessee. The Assessing Officer, in fact, had passed a legal, proper and reasoned order, holding that the provisions laid down under section 40(a )(i) applied to the case in hand. [Para 10]

In the instant case, there were no pleadings or material brought on record to show that the case was governed by occasional shipping within the meaning of section 172 and said section applied. [Para 11]

The facts of the instant case were governed by section 40(a)(i ). The order passed by the Assessing Officer was legal, proper and in accordance with the scheme of the Act. Therefore, the appeal deserved to be allowed by quashing and setting aside the orders passed by the Commissioner(Appeals) and the Tribunal. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 172, read with section 195 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Non-resident - Shipping business of (Demurrage charges) - Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 - Whether in view of difference of opinion between orders passed by co-ordinate Benches of Tribunal regarding applicability of section 172 in respect of demurrage paid to non-resident shipping company, matter was to be referred to Larger Bench for consideration - Held, yes [Para 13] [Matter referred to Larger Bench]IT: In view of difference of opinion between orders passed by co-ordinate Benches of Tribunal regarding applicability of section 172 in respect of demurrage paid to non-resident shipping company, matter was to be referred to Larger Bench for consideration

FACT: The assessee company filed its return claiming deduction of demurrage paid to a non-resident shipping company.

The assessee's case was that there was no obligation to deduct tax at source as the amount was paid to non-resident shipping company engaged in operation of ships and, therefore, governed by section 172.

The Assessing Officer, however, opined that assessee was required to deduct tax at source under section 195 while making payment to non-resident shipping company. In view of assessee's failure to do so, Assessing Officer disallowed payments in question.

Reliance was also placed upon the Circular No. 723 dated 19-9-1995 issued by CBDT which interalia provides that Section 172 is a self contained code for levy and recovery of taxes ship wise and journey wise in case of ships owned or chartered by non-residents. Therefore, the requirement of deducting tax at source would not be applicable in such a case thus the consequent disallowance of expenditure under Section 40(a)(i) was not warranted.

However, the CIT(A) did not accept the contention of the assessee and held section 44B would apply as it related to computation of profits and gains and from shipping business. In the above view, the appeal of the assessee was dismissed.

The Tribunal allowed assessee's appeal by following decision in DCIT v. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. [2009] 185 Taxman 131. The impugned order specifically held that section 172 was a charging as well as a machinery provision in respect of non-resident shipping companies. It provided for determination and collection of tax. Thus Chapter XVII of the Act in respect of deducting tax at source would not apply in such cases. Consequently, the disallowance of expenditure on account of section 40(a)(i) Act was deleted.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: This Court in CIT v. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. [2010] 325 ITR 554/[2009] 185 Taxman 131 held that section 172 is applicable only in respect of non-resident carrying on shipping business while assessee i.e. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. was admittedly a resident and therefore section 172 could not be applied. Thus the expenditure of demurrage charges could not be allowed in the absence of tax being deducted at source. [Para 10]

The above view of this Court in Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. (supra) cannot be accepted. This is for the reason that the assessee placed reliance upon section 172 in respect of payments made by it to a non-resident shipping company by way of demurrage charges. The tax which is deducted at source by the assessee company is on behalf of the recipient of the charges. The issue before the Court was whether demurrage charges which are paid by the assessee to a non-resident company would be allowed as an expenditure in the absence of deduction of tax at source in view of section 40(a)(i) of the Act.

Although the Court was concerned with the issue in an appeal concerning a resident company. The introduction of section 172 by the assessee was to determine whether in view thereof, was there any obligation to deduct tax at source by the payer-assessee. Section 172 has to be examined through the prism of the non-resident shipping company in respect of its income. It is in the above view that section 172 and Circular No. 723 issued by the CBDT was relied upon by the assessee to point out that as section 172 provides a complete code itself for recovery of tax ship wise and journey wise. Thus there is no occasion to deduct tax under Chapter XVII of the Act. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962 Trade Notices or advice - no reliance can be placed on such notices--Sample tests can afford guidance only--Demurrage can be waived only for the period goods are specifically detained by Customs. Woollen rags not having been proved to be textiles, demurrage payable. ICT Item 49 (4).

FACT: The petitioner-firm utilised woollen rags for manufacturing shoddy woollen yarn and blankets. The GOI permitted import of woollen rags and garment rags (rags from woven woollen fabrics and rags from knitted woollen material) and exempted woollen waste and rags from levy of customs duty by a notification dt. 20.4.1966. The importers have to claim the said exemption under Item 49(4) of Indian Customs Tariff read with the notification before clearing and consignment of woollen rags from the customs. Since 1966, the STC has been given monopoly in licences for importing woollen rags, which are not granted individually but allotted a quota on recommendation of the Textile Commissioner. The petitioners were allotted a quota of 37 bales of woollen hosiery rags which were imported from foreign suppliers by STC. The Customs Authorities carried out a visual inspection by taking samples, and later decided to have a chemical test. In spite of these two tests the Authorities decided to resort to the core-drilling test. On the basis of this the department held that the wool content of these bales was less than 50 per cent and therefore not eligible for exemption under the notification dt. 20.4.1966 and though clearance of goods was allowed they were charged to appropriate duty. The goods were kept in the sheds of the Port Trust of Bombay and it was not permitting clearance without payment of demurrage charges.

HELD: Exemption: Customs Authorities cannot rely upon trade advice and levy duty on the ground that the content was not according to the advice. Trade advice is not statutory and as such reliance cannot be placed on it. "The Exemption Notification dated April 20, 1966 totally exempted woollen wastes and woollen rags from the whole of the duty of customs leviable thereon. The Exemption Notification does not restrict the advantage only to those woollen wastes and woollen rags containing wool of more than 50%. In absence of any such provision in the Notification, it is not permissible for the Customs Authorities to levy duty on the imported woollen rags on the ground that the wool content was found less than 50 per cent. It is now well settled that the trade advice issued by the Government of India has no statutory force and it is not permissible for the Authorities exercising quasi judicial function to place reliance upon such trade advice to hold that the petitioners are liable for payment of duty."

2. Exemption: Physical and Chemical tests offer guidance and assistance only. "Merely because the different analysis show different conclusions it is not permissible to select that conclusion which suits the authorities to levy the duty. .........The procedure adopted by the Customs Authorities was entirely misconceived and cannot be sustained either in law or by principles of natural justice. In my judgment, the finding of the Customs Authorities that the import of woollen rags by the petitioners is not eligible for duty exemption is totally incorrect and deserves to be set aside. Natural Justice: High Court's order not imposing any condition for safeguarding of interests of the Port Trust is erroneous since the Port Trust was not a party to the Writ Petition and since in the absence of a notice, would not have been able to recover full demurrage charges after the goods were cleared under Detention Certificates. "It is, however, to be observed that before compelling the Customs authorities to issue a Detention Certificate, the High Court should have issued notice as regards the demurrage charges recoverable by it under law. This was necessary because on the production of the Detention Certificate issued by the Customs authorities the Port Trust was under an obligation to permit the clearance of the goods without payment of full demurrage charges. If ultimately the party concerned is found to be at fault and becomes liable to pay the full demurrage charges the Port Trust may no: he in a position to recover such full demurrage charges from the party concerned, since it would have no longer any lien as provided by section 59 of the Act on the goods which are already cleared. The Port Trust being a body corporate constituted under the Act is entitled to be heard by the Court before any order which affects its interests prejudicially is passed. ......The orders passed by the High Court in the proceedings to which the Port Trust was not a party which had the effect of prejudicially affecting the interests of the Port Trust would. not be binding on it in view of the violation of the principles of natural justice. The High Court erred in not imposing any condition on the 1st Respondent for protecting the interests of the Port Trust even in the Writ Petition to which it was a party. HEADNOTE: Section 44B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Profits And Gains of Shipping Business in Case of Non-Residents Computation Of - Assessment year 1986-87 - Assessee, a non-resident company, was engaged in business of operation of ships - Whether detention/demurrage charges received by assessee for retention of containers beyond agreed period could be treated as on account of carriage of goods so as to be includible in total income of assessee- Held, no

FACT: The assessee, a non-resident company, was engaged in the business of operation of ships. For the assessment year 1986-87 the assessing officer held that the entire receipts from detention/demurrage were the income of the assessee and therefrom allowed deduction of 5 per cent as expenses on estimate basis. On appeal, the assessee contended before the Commissioner (Appeals) that the detention/demurrage charges were part and parcel of the carriage of goods within the meaning of section 44B. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee's claim and directed the assessing officer that like freight only 7.5 per cent of the detention/demurrage charges should be treated as profits of the business of operation of ships.

On further appeal by the revenue:

HELD: Receipt from detention/demurrage, in the present case, was nonetheless during the course of the business of operation of ships and, therefore, even if it was treated as income of the assessee, for argument sake, it could not be assessed under sections 28 to 43A. The provisions of sections 30 to 43C are not attracted for computation of income in respect of these receipts. The assessing officer, therefore, committed an error in treating the receipts from demurrage as income independent of carriage charges and further committed an error in estimating the expenses at 5 per cent. At the best, he could have treated those receipts as amount on account of carriage.

However, as laid down in CIT v. Pestonji Bhicajee [1977] 107 ITR 837 (Guj.), dead freight is an agreed sum to be paid in respect of space not filled according to charter or damages provided for by a charter, in the event of the freighter not loading a full cargo. It has been held by the High Court that 'dead freight' cannot be treated as payment made on account of carriage of goods in a ship. That was considered with reference to section 172, a provision analogous to section 44B. In context with the same, i.e., section 172 the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Gosalia Shipping (P.) Ltd. [1978] 113 ITR 307 held that the amount which the time charterers were required to pay to the owners of the ship was not payable on account of the carriage of goods but was payable on account of the use and hire of the ship. In this view of the matter, the detention/demurrage charges received for retention of the containers beyond the agreed period could not be treated as on account of the carriage of goods.

Accordingly, no part of the impugned receipts could be included in the total income of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation of imported goods - Duty rate - Relevant date is date of entry inwards of the vessel, even if Bill of Entry has been presented before that date - Ultra vires--Section 15 is not ultra vires, as it lays down a procedure, and following that procedure cannot be termed arbitrary. Discrimination--Different rates of duty for different categories of importers are not violative of fundamental rights. Constitution or India: Art. 14

FACT: The petitioners imported a consignment of edible oils. The vessel carrying the goods approached Bombay and made its "prior entry" on July 4, 1981. It actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay on July 11, 1981, at which time the rate of duty applicable to the petitioners' goods was 12.5%. As there was no berth available and the vessel was under heavy pressure from the parties whose goods she was carrying, she left Bombay for Karachi for unloading other cargo intended for that port. The vessel returned after discharging the Karachi cargo, arrived in the Port of Bombay on July 23, 1981 and waited for a berth. On August 4, 1981 she was allowed to berth and the Customs Authorities made the "final entry" on that date. The petitioners contend that when the vessel made its original journey to Bombay and was waiting in the waters of the Port they presented the Bill of Entry to the Customs authorities on July 9, 1981, and that the Bill of Entry was accepted by the Import Department and an order was passed by the Customs Officer on the Bill of Entry on July 18, 1981 directing the examination of the consignment. The Customs authorities imposed duty on the edible oils at the rate of 150% on the footing that the import was made on July 31, 1981, the date of "Inward Entry". The case of the petitioners is that the rate of duty leviable on the import should be that ruling on July 11, 1981, when the vessel actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay, and that but for the fact that a berth was not available the vessel would have discharged its cargo at Bombay, and would not have left that Port and proceeded to Karachi to return to Bombay towards the end of July, 1981. Alternatively, the case of the petitioners is that even if the rate of customs duty found leviable on their goods is 150 per cent, such levy is unconstitutional and void as it violates of Article 14 of the Constitution, inasmuch as customs duty at 5 per cent only was levied on the STC for similar imports. The petitioners have also challenged the validity of section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 under which the rate of duty and tariff valuation are determined.

HELD: Duty rate--Relevant date is date of entry inwards of the vessel, even if Bill of Entry has been presented before that date. "It is urged......that the import of goods must be deemed to have taken place on 11 July, 1981, when the ship originally arrived in Bombay Port and registered itself. The rate of customs duty prevailing on that date was 12.5 per cent..............The provisions of section 15 are clear in themselves. The date on which a Bill of Entry is presented under section 46 is, in the case of goods entered for home consumption, the relevant date for determining the rate of duty and tariff valuation. Where the Bill of Entry is presented before the date of Entry Inwards of the vessel, the Bill of Entry is deemed to have been presented on the date of such Entry Inwards. .............In the present case, "the date of inwards entry" is mentioned as 31 July, 1981. In the absence of anything else, we may take it that the entry was recorded on that date itself. Accordingly, the rate of import duty and the tariff valuation shall be that in force on 31 July, 1981. The contention of the petitioners that the rate of import duty and tariff valuation will be that ruling on 11 July, 1981 cannot be sustained and is rejected."

HEADNOTE: Section 57 read with section 58 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Appointing public warehouse - Baggage - Demurrage--Airport authorities not entitled to claim any demurrage in view of public notice 29/86 specifying that demurrage charges will not be recovered for warehousing baggage detained by the Customs Authorities

FACT: The petitioners are citizens of Nepal. Some of their goods which were being transhipped from Singapore arrived as unaccompanied baggage at the IGI Airport for onward shipment to Kathmandu. Being under the impression that this importation was improper, the Customs Authorities confiscated these goods under section 117 of the Customs Act. The confiscated goods were stored in the customs warehouse of IGI Airport. After the completion of adjudication proceedings, the Deputy Collector of Customs permitted transshipment of the seized goods. The petitioners have filed these appeals being aggrieved by the refusal of the Airport Authorities to release the goods unless the demurrage charges were paid. It is their contention that this claim was illegal as the goods had been stored in the warehouse upon the insistence of the Customs Authorities and not the petitioners. Moreover, in view of the detention certificate issued by the Assistant Collector of Customs, the respondents were bound to waive the demurrage charges.

HELD: Airport Authorities are not entitled to claim any demurrage charges from the petitioners--respondents bound by Public Notice 29/86 which specifies that demurrage charges will not be recovered for warehousing baggage detained by the Customs Authorities. "For the purpose of waiver or remission of the warehouse charges customs authorities have to certify that goods were not cleared up to a certain period for them to make enquiries under the Act. This certification is the detention certificate. The Public Notice 29/86 and the Regulations and guidelines of the Airports Authority, the first respondent, talk of detention certificate to be issued by the customs authorities. Reference may well be made to section 63 of the Act falling under Chapter IX dealing with warehousing. Under sub-section (1) of section 63, the owner of any warehoused goods shall pay to the warehouse-keeper rent and warehouse charges at the rates fixed under any law for the time being in force or where no rates are so fixed, at such rates as may be fixed by the Collector of Customs. We have seen above, rates for warehousing baggage have not been fixed by the first respondent and Public Notice 29/86 in effect specifies under clause (vii) that charges for warehousing baggage for the period it is detained will not be charged by the Airports Authority, the first respondent. ........We are, therefore, of the opinion that the first respondent is not entitled to charge any demurrage in all these cases and the petitioners are entitled to have their goods transhipped to Nepal without payment of any ground rent/demurrage charges."

HEADNOTE: Section 12, read with sections 13, 14, 23 and 47 of the Customs Act, 1962 and rules 3 and 9 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 and rule 3 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 - Charge/levy - Customs Duty - Assessee imported crude oil, which was liable to duty on ad valorem basis - Department demanded duty based on quantity of crude oil mentioned in bills of lading, as assessee had paid price based on said quantity - Assessee argued that since quantity actually received into shore tanks in India was lesser, quantity actually received should be basis for payment of duty - HELD : Customs duty is a duty only on 'goods imported' i.e., goods brought into India from a place outside India - Since act of import is complete only after an order permitting clearance of goods for home consumption is made under section 47, duty can be demanded only on quantity of goods entering for home consumption - In accordance with said principles, no duty is demanded under sections 13 and 23 on goods which are pilfered, lost, destroyed or abandoned before clearance - Customs duty is different from purchase tax and therefore, quantity stated in a bill of lading is merely quantity involved in purchase transaction and can only be validly looked at in case of a purchase tax but not in case of an import duty - Whether customs duty is at a specific rate or is ad valorem makes no difference to above statutory scheme - Under section 14, value is determined only for goods imported and further, transaction value is price that is actually paid or payable only for 'imported goods' - Hence, quantity of crude oil actually received into a shore tank in a port in India should be basis for payment of customs duty - Circular dated 12-1-2006 was held to be contrary to law [Paras 10 to 18] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Customs duty is different from purchase tax and is leviable only on quantity actually imported and entered for home consumption and not on quantity stated in bill of lading; therefore, where goods actually received are lesser than quantity stated in bill of lading, duty would be leviable only on value of goods actually received

FACT: Facts

Assessee imported crude oil, which was liable to duty on ad valorem basis.

Department demanded duty on quantity of crude oil mentioned in bills of lading.

Assessee argued that since quantity actually received into shore tanks in India was lesser, quantity actually received should be basis for payment of duty.

Revenue's Arguments

The department argued that since duty was now levied on an ad valorem basis and not on a specific rate, the duty should be paid on the bill of lading quantity based on the ullage obtained when the goods were loaded on the vessel in the country of export.

Since full payment for the goods has to be made by the importer only on the basis of the quantity mentioned in the bill of lading, therefore the 'transaction value' of the said goods would only be as per the payment made of the amounts stated in the bill of lading and not the quantity received ultimately in the shore tanks at ports in India.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee argued that it makes no difference as to whether the basis for customs duty is at a specific rate or is ad valorem, quantity of goods at the time of import alone is to be looked at.

Taxable event is only when goods are imported, and that therefore valuation at the time of import alone has to be looked at.

HELD: The levy of customs duty under section 12 is only on goods imported into India. Goods are said to be imported into India when they are brought into India from a place outside India. Unless such goods are brought into India, the act of importation which triggers the levy does not take place. If the goods are pilferred after they are unloaded or lost or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, the importer is not liable to pay the duty leviable on such goods. This is for the reason that the import of goods does not take place until they become part of the land mass of India and until the act of importation is complete which under sections 13 and 23 happens only after an order for clearance for home consumption is made and/or an order permitting the deposit of goods in a warehouse is made.

Section 1 of the Indian Bill of Lading Act, 1856 specified that title to goods carried by sea is vested with the consignee/endorsee of Bill of Lading. [Para 15]

Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Shipping, Inland waterways transport and air transport - General) - Assessment year 2022-23 - Assessee, UAE based company, was engaged in business of operation of ships in international traffic - During relevant year, assessee received an amount in form of freight income which included inland haulage charges - Assessing Officer denied benefit of Article 8 of India-UAE DTAA to assessee with respect to said income - It was noted that Tribunal in assessee’s own case for earlier year held that IHC were inextricably linked to shipping business in international traffic and activity of shipping a container from inland to port for further shipping in international traffic was an integral part of operation of ships which could not be disintegrated from profit derived from shipping business as envisaged under Article 8 - Whether, following aforesaid decision, ‘IHC’ was not taxable as business profit in India - Held, yes [Para 6.1] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, UAE based company, was engaged in the business of operation of ships in the international traffic. During relevant assessment year, the assessee received an amount in the form of freight income and other related charges in India. The assessee claimed that said income included freight income, terminal handling charges, inland haulage charges and detention charges and was exempt under Article 8 of the India-UAE DTAA as the assessee was in the business of operation of ships in the international traffic.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that said incomes were earned from multiple ports from India involving hundreds of ships voyages with ships of different names and charterers. He, thus, rejected the claim of the assessee.

■

The DRP observed that the years involved had come up for directions in assessment year 2017-18 and on the basis of those directions, it held that basis of its directions shall be directions issued for assessment year 2017-18 and earlier years to apply mutatis mutandis.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The authorities below placed their reliance on observations and findings made in preceding assessment years in assessee's own case to adjudicate the two issues. In this context, the orders of the Co-ordinate Bench in assessee's own case were perused. From the order for assessment year 2016-17 in Avana Global FZCO v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2021] 130 taxmann.com 481/191 ITD 627 (Mum-Trib.), the benefit of article 8 was extended to entire freight receipts irrespective of whether the earnings are relating to feeder vessels or by the ships in international traffic. [Para 6]

■

In respect of inland haulage charges, reference is made to the decision of the Co-ordinate Bench for assessment year 2017-18 in Avana Global FZCO v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2022] 142 taxmann.com 386 (Mum-Trib.) which held that these charges are inextricably linked to shipping business in international traffic. The activity of shipping container from inland to the port for further shipping it to international traffic is an integral part of operation of ships. Hence, ‘IHC’ cannot be disintegrated from profit derived from shipping business as envisaged under article 8 of India-UAE DTAA. Ergo, ‘IHC’ are not taxable as business profit in India. [Para 6.1]

HEADNOTE: I. Section  92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing -  Computation of Arm’s length price (Comparability factors - Operating profit margin) - Assessment year  2021-22 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading of raw cashew nuts - During year, assessee had entered into an international transaction of purchase of raw cashew nuts and sale of raw cashew nuts - Assessee had undertaken a detailed transfer pricing analysis in respect of its international transactions based on which it was concluded that its international transactions were at arm's length - However, TPO made upward adjustment on account of benchmarking of transaction made related to export - Assessee submitted that demurrage charges paid during year were due to COVID-19 lockdown and hence, same should be considered as extra ordinary costs and hence non-operating in nature - Whether demurrage charges being an extra ordinary cost shall be treated as non-operating in nature - Held, yes [Para 7.1] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was a partnership firm engaged in the business of trading of Raw Cashew Nuts. During the year under consideration, the assessee had entered into an international transaction of purchase of raw cashew nuts and sale of raw cashew nuts. The assessee had undertaken a detailed transfer pricing ('TP') analysis in respect of its aforesaid international transactions based on which it was concluded that its international transactions were at arm's length in accordance with the provisions of section 92C.

■

During the assessment proceedings, the TPO had not considered exponential increase in demurrage and detention charges as extra-ordinary cost and hence non-operating in nature and proposed upward transfer pricing adjustment.

■ The objections filed by the assessee before the Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP) were rejected.

■

Subsequently, the Assessing Officer after giving effect to the directions of the DRP, computed total income of the assessee-firm by proposing an upward adjustment.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee submitted that the TPO had not considered exponential increase in demurrage and detention charges as extraordinary cost and hence non-operating in nature. It was argued that due to Covid, owing to the lockdown, the goods which had been imported could not be cleared on timely basis which led to payment of almost 4.73 per cent of sales as demurrage charges. The demurrage charges paid in earlier years for a turnover of Rs.19 to 36 crores was Rs.1.5 lakhs to Rs.4.05 lakhs only. During the year under consideration the demurrage charges paid were to the tune of Rs.2.57 crores.Considering the demurrage charges OP/OC would be 1.35 per cent which would be within the tolerance limit of ALP of 1.78 per cent.

HELD: ■

Following the guidelines given by Co-ordinate Bench in the case of Transwitch India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy.CIT [2012] 21 taxmann.com 257/53 SOT 151 (Delhi - Trib.), it is held that the demurrage charges being an extra ordinary cost shall be treated as non-operating in nature. Appeal of the assessee on this ground is allowed. [Para 7.1]
