The Commissioner also held that the assessee had deliberately mis-classified the services under ‘Cargo handling services’ to avail of exemptions provided under the Cargo Handling Services in respect of passenger baggage and export cargo. Therefore, he confirmed the differential service tax demand with interest and also imposed penalties upon the assessee under sections 77 and 78 by invoking longer period provided under proviso to section 73(1).

On appeal : HELD: From the case records, it was found that the assessee had collected various charges from importers/exporters including passengers for keeping the cargo in transit safely, pending export or customs clearance for home consumption. In holding that keeping safe custody of cargo in transit, pending clearance by the customs would constitute an activity exigible under the above entry, the lower authorities had relied on Circulars of the CBEC which clarified that storage and warehousing service provided by, inter alia, Airport Authority is covered by the entry. The entry cargo handling service was clarified by the CBEC as not covering export cargo and passenger baggage. The clarification was not to the effect that all activities relating to export cargo and passenger baggage were also excluded from levy under other entries. The finding of the Commissioner, that the exceptions provided under cargo handling services with regard to passenger baggage and export cargo could not be claimed under storage and warehousing services, was to be agreed with. [Para 9.2]

Demurrage or wharfage charges were collected, respectively, in relation to clearance of import/export cargo beyond five days and 24 hours. As found by the original authority, these were higher charges for continued storage of cargo collected by the assessee from members of the trade. These were part of the taxable value collected towards storage and warehouse charges. [Para 9.3]

As regards the abandoned cargo, those accrued to the assessee towards storage and warehousing of cargo, which were not taken delivery of by the importer. The procedure for auctioning abandoned cargo and the sharing of the proceeds is prescribed by the Ministry of Finance. These instructions also make it clear that the assessee would receive amounts towards the service of storage and warehousing of cargo under this head. However, the services were not rendered to any person in the case of the abandoned cargo. Therefore, demand under this head was not sustainable. [Para 9.4]

As regards the destination charges, it was found that the assessee had collected the documents representing the consignments brought by Air India and Blue Dart and hand over these to the respective consignees. In cases where the assessee merely collected and handed over the documents to the respective consignees, destination charges would not form part of taxable value under storage and warehousing. [Para 9.5]

As regards the OT charges/penalties, the lower authorities had not given a finding as to the nature and purpose of these penalties but had presumed that these were collected for violations on the part of their clients in relation to storage and warehousing services. The Commissioner (Appeals) did not find this item to be taxable under storage and warehousing. In the absence of a finding as to how that amount was taxable towards any service rendered by the assessee, it was difficult to accept the stand of the revenue in this regard. The assessee had also not explained the nature and purpose of collecting these charges. This matter would be decided after hearing the party afresh. [Para 9.6]

There was considerable merit in the assessee’s submission that there was no suppression of facts, etc. to warrant invocation of larger period. From the orders impugned, one did not find a reliable finding by the authorities that the assessee, a State PSU, had resorted to suppression of the facts to evade appropriate service tax amount. Considering the nature of the activities involved, the Commissioner could not have found with certainty that the assessee had deliberately mis-classified the activities undertaken by it under the head ‘Cargo handling services’ instead of ‘Storage and warehousing services’. Therefore, the authorities could not have validly invoked extended period and imposed penalties. The penal liability of the assessee required reconsideration in the light of section 80. [Para 9.7]

In view of section 75 the assessee was liable to pay interest for delay in payment of the tax found due from it. Therefore, the order of the lower appellate authority as regards interest was to be upheld. [Para 10.1]

A ground raised for the first time before the Tribunal was based on the Circular No. 89/7/2006-ST, dated 18-12-2006. [Para 11]

The lower authorities had no occasion to examine that plea and to determine that liability of the assessee in the light of the same. The Tribunal was not in a position to decide the issue as it was not clear whether the circular applied to the assessee and if the assessee would come under the description of ‘public authority’, as envisaged in the above circular. In any case, records did not indicate that the charges collected by the assessee were deposited with the Government. The circular defines statutory authorities discharging sovereign functions, etc., to be those that deposit the ‘fees’ collected with the Government. [Para 12]

headnotes.text: Section 14, read with  section 151A, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Levy of, and exemption from, customs duties - Valuation of goods for purposes of assessment - Whether when circular issued by Central Board of Excise and Customs (Board) remains in operation, revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to terms of statute - Held, yes - Whether circular issued by Board in which it was said that demurrage did not form part of assessable value of goods imported, same was binding on revenue and department could not contend otherwise - Held, yes
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Mineral oil -Demurrage charges - paid on account of detention of vessel - not includible (Para 8)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Levy of duty - Valuation of goods - Whether ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purpose - Held, no [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were not liable to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purposes

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Demurrage charges - Paid by respondents to ship owners between 1994 and 1999 for delay in discharging goods from vessels - Not includible in assessable value of the goods in view of Board's circular dt. 14.8.1991 which was withdrawn w.e.f. 2.3.2001 only (Paras 21  23)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 9 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - SKO (in bulk) - Demurrage charges - paid to supplier/charterers - not includible prior to amendment of Rule in 2006 - appeals allowed (Para 7)

Demurrage - collection thereof by the International Airport Authority under IAA Act, 1971 - power to recover demurrages cannot be curtailed down by the detention certificates issued by the Customs Officers under the Customs Act, 1962 - IAAI being a statutory body entitled to frame its own regulations and rate schedule for charging demurrages - appeals accepted by setting aside Delhi High Court's order (per majority)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - LPG - Demurrage charges and Dispatch money - Demurrage charges paid to charterer of vessel for detention of vessel beyond lay time and dispatch money represented bank charges for remittance of demurrage charges - Board's Circular dt. 14.8.1991 clarifying that these charges did not form part of assessable value, was withdrawn on 2.3.2001 - In case of goods imported prior to 2.3.2001, the said charges are not includible - Appeals allowed (Paras 3 4)
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Demurrage charges - not includible (Para 6)

Demurrage charges - Detention certificate - Section 45 (2)(b) of the Customs Act, 1962 - expression 'otherwise dealt with' in Section 45(2)(b) does not empower the Customs Officer to direct/compel the carrier/custodian of the imported goods not to charge demurrage from the importer for the space occupied by his goods during their detention by the Customs - importer, as per bill of lading/contract with carrier/custodian, is liable to pay demurrage - detention certificate by the Customs on confiscation of the goods by the Customs having been finally set aside, will not absolve the importer from paying the demurrage charges (Para1)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Valuation of goods for customs - Freight - Demurrage charges - paid for rentention of vessel beyond free lay time - not to be added for period prior to 26.9.2006 - appeals allowed (Para 10.1)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for custom - Reference to Larger Bench - Assessable value - Demurrage charges - whether demurrage charges could be excluded from assessable value in cases of imports made after 2.3.2001 even where assessments were provisional - referred to Larger Bench in view of doubts about correctness of CESTAT's earlier judgments (Paras 8  9)

Section 141, read with section 157, of the Customs Act, 1962 and regulation  6 of the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 - Conveyances and goods in customs area - Whether where Central Board of Excise and Customs exercising its powers under sections 141(2) and 157 of Customs Act notified Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 and regualtion 6(1)(l) thereof obliged customs cargo service providers not to charge demurrage in certain cases, said regulation did not violate articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution - Held, yes [Paras 10, 11 and 12] [In favour of revenue]Excise  Customs : Where Central Board of Excise and Customs exercising its powers under sections 141(2) and 157 of Customs Act notified Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 and regualtion 6(1)(l) thereof obliged customs cargo service providers not to charge demurrage in certain cases, said regulation did not violate articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution

Section 111 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Confiscation of improperly imported goods - Limitation - Demurrage charges--Runs from date amount is ascertained. Owner--Is an inclusive definition. Includes only person mentioned; not others. Major Port Trusts Act. Demurrage--No provision to sue any particular person--Port Trust can sue owner/consignor/consignee. ITC-- Consignee--Notification does not specifically make defendant a consignee; hence demurrage cannot be claimed from them. Any financial investment made does not make them owners
Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Demurrage charges and Despatch money - not to be added prior to 2.3.2001 - Appeals allowed (Para 4)
Section 14 of Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Assessable value - Coal - Demurrage charges - not includable in assessable value - Revenue's appeal dismissed. (Para 5)

Section 141, read with sections 45 and 49, of the Customs Act, 1962 and Regulation 6 of the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 - Clearance of Imported Goods - Demurrage - Custodian demanded demurrage even for period during which goods were seized by department and could not be cleared - Department issued certificate favouring assessee that demurrage could not be levied - Assessee claimed that said certificate of department had overriding effect under Regulation 6 of Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 (HCCAR) - Custodian claimed that it was governed only by Policy for Waiver of Demurrage Charges notified by Airports Authority of India (AAI) - HELD : HCCAR Regulations themselves stipulate that they are subject to any law for time being in force and, therefore, HCCAR and directions of customs authorities thereunder do not override 'Policy for Waiver' framed by AAI - In cases where on conclusion of adjudication proceedings there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by customs authorities demurrage for period when goods were seized, detained or earlier confiscated would be waived as per Policy of Waiver - However, in any other case, demurrage would not be waived for period of seizure, etc. and provisional release order would be subject to furnishing of bond and/or security that in case any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by customs authorities, importer would pay demurrage charges [Para 50] [In favour of revenue]Customs : Customs Authorities cannot order custodian to waive demurrage for period of seizure/detention, etc.; waiver is grantable only if on conclusion of adjudication, there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by customs authorities

Demurrage charges - Liability - Carrier - entitled to demurrage charges from the importer under the terms and conditions of Bill of Lading till the goods are kept by the carrier - liability of importer to pay demurrage charges ceases if the confiscation of the goods by Customs is finally set aside (Para 4)
Section 80 of the Customs Act, 1962 Detention certificate can be denied where delay is due to the importer. Demurrage has to be paid by him at rates charged by Port authorities.

Section 14, read with section 111 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Valuation: reduction in original value of old machine can only be to the extent of depreciation; rise in general labour costs after first purchase is no justification for under-valuation. EXCHANGE RATE for old machine is the one applicable on date of import, not the date of original purchase abroad; ITC licence is to be debited with this value. Penalty high demurrage charges incurred call for compensatory reduction in penalty

Section 2 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Duty leviability of - Penalty/fine justified for deliberate fraud. Licence--non-production is violation of policy. Section 58 of the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 - Demurrage charges - to be paid by importer before the goods are removed - even where Customs Authority has to pay the charges, importer should first pay the charges to Port Trust and thereafter claim re-imbursement from the Customs Authority

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Where for importing drilling equipment goods at zero customs duty, essentiality certificate (EC) from Director General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) was required and there was delay in obtaining essentiality certificate from DGH and that delayed clearance from customs within 'demurrage free period', demurrage paid by assessee was allowable as business expenditure [In favour of assessee]

Demurrage, Warehouse rent, and Container charges - goods not released in terms of formal order dt. 16.1.91 of Asstt. Collector after payment of redemption fine as another proceedings for confiscation based on test report had commenced - charges beyond 16.1.91 to be paid by the importer as second proceedings are yet to be finalised on merits (Para 16)

Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Pilfered goods - Demurrage - BPT must remit if Customs issue certificate or Court allows it. Such certificates have binding effect--However the remission can apply only to 80%, and the maximum period allowable is 150 days

Section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962 Trade Notices or advice - no reliance can be placed on such notices--Sample tests can afford guidance only--Demurrage can be waived only for the period goods are specifically detained by Customs. Woollen rags not having been proved to be textiles, demurrage payable. ICT Item 49 (4).

Departmental Clarification - C.B.I.C. Circular No. 18/2009-Cus - Waiver of demurrage levied by ICDs/CFSs/Ports/Terminal Operators during COVID-19 lockdown - Requiring Chief and Principal Chief Commissioners to ensure ICDs and CFSs comply with Shipping Ministry's order - HELD: Circular did not have any compulsive element - As court could not issue mandamus to ICDs, CFSs and shipping lines, no such rights could inure even from CBIC circular. [Paras 39.2]

Sections 112 and 125 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Penalty  redemption fine - allegation of misdeclaration of value not established - charges of unauthorised import proved - case remanded for redetermination of redemption fine  penalty - heavy demurrage incurred during last 3 years, to be taken into consideration while computing fine  penalty (Paras 8  9)

Section 45 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Public Notice No.30/86 dated 30.4.86-Detention certificates issued by customs department-Directions to IAAI to release the goods without collecting demurrage chartes - not enforceable as Collector not entitled to impose such conditions debarring such collection (per majority)

Section 37(1) Of The Income-Tax Act, 1961-Business Expenditure-Whether Demurrage Paid To Railways Is Not In Nature Of Damage Or Penalty But Is Merely Charge Made By Railway Administration For Keeping Goods Of Assessee In Its Custody Beyond A Particular Time And Is, Therefore, Incidental To Business-Held, Yes-Whether Such Payment Of Demurrage Is Allowable As Deduction-Held, Yes
Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Demurrage charges - Refund - not refundable by the Customs as there is no provision in the Customs Act to this effect (Paras 6  7)

Section 172 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Non-resident - Shipping business of - Whether demurrage payable to non-resident owner of charterer of ship on account of delay in loading goods sold to non-resident would not be taxable - Held, yes

a foreign company for mooring job of floating dock - Having regard 
to delay, foreign company claimed additional payment for extra period 
of work - Whether only because foreign company in debit note used expression ‘demurrage’ instead of ‘fee for technical services’ benefit of section 10(6A) could be denied to assessee - Held, no

Section 125 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Redemption fine - Demurrage charges - form part of landed cost and their abatement to be allowed while determining profit margin for fixing redemption fine (Para 5 (b))

Section 40(a)(i), read with sections 172 and 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business disallowance - Interest, etc., paid to a non-resident without deduction of tax at source - Assessment year 2013-14 - Whether there is no obligation cast upon assessee to deduct tax at source under section 195 in respect of demurrage charges, paid to a non-resident shipping company, as latters income was liable to be brought to tax under section 44B and consequently under section 172 and therefore, said amount could not be disallowed under section 40(a)(i) - Held , yes [Paras 7 and 8] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX: No obligation is cast upon assessee/Indian company to deduct tax at source at time of making of payment towards demurrage charges to a non-resident shipping company, as latters income was liable to be brought to tax under section 44B and consequently under section 172

Section 47 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Clearance of imported goods for home consumption - Cannot be withheld when import lawful and correct value declared/accounted. Demurrage/Ground rent waived as goods were not being released

Section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [corresponding to section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961] - Business expenditure - Goods unauthorisedly imported by assessee-firm confiscated by customs authorities - Option to assessee to get import regularised on paying Rs. 22,000 as fine - Matter unsuccessfully agitated before higher authorities for four years - Assessee finally took delivery of goods after paying fine and substantial demurrage charges for use of port facilities beyond permissible free period - Whether tribunal was justified in law in disallowing demurrage charges as admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) - Held, on Facts, No

Section 145, read with section 145A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Valuation of closing stock (Demurrage charges) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee had not included demurrage charges paid to Port Authorities in valuation of closing stock as at year-end, in departure with its consistent past practice of valuing its closing inventory by including same as an element of cost, alluding to section 145A - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's method of valuation of its closing stock - Whether demurrage/detention charges, being toward cost for delay in removal of goods could only broadly be said to be a holding cost, and it would be more appropriate to consider it as a cost for delayed removal of goods, i.e., beyond stipulated period same was thus, only a revenue expenditure of period to which it related and, hence, not liable for inclusion in value of goods from any stand point - Held, yes - Whether therefore, revision made by assessee in method of valuation of closing stock was approved on basis of accounting principles, which would govern matter in absence of any specific provision/s in Act toward same, with section 145A being inapplicable - Held, yes - Whether thus, valuation of opening stock which would continue to be valued as per old method was invalid - Held, yes [Paras 3.1 and 4] [In favour of assessee/matter remanded]IT : Demurrage/detention charges were not liable for inclusion in valuation of closing stock

Section 125 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Redemption fine - Second hand diesel engine - reduced in view of previous orders of Collector and demurrage incurred. (Para 13)

facts.text:
The respondent imported various petroleum products and crude oil into India and had cleared the same upon payment of customs duty. The customs authorities having noted that the respondent had paid demurrage charges to the shipowners under the charter party agreements through negotiating bank issued a show-cause notice to the appellant and included the bank charges and demurrage paid in the customs value of the goods and created additional demand of customs duty against the respondent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order. On second appeal, the Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal (CEGAT) allowed the appeal of the respondent on the grounds; (i) that the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) had issued a circular on 14-8-1991 under section 151A of the Customs Act in which it was said that the demurrage did not form part of the assessable value of the goods imported and the circular was binding on the revenue and the department could not contend otherwise, (ii) that the decision of the Supreme Court in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [1999] 113 ELT 358 relied upon by the revenue was not an authority for the proposition that demurrage payable on account of delay in discharging goods from a vessel was includible in the value of goods while assessing the customs duty payable thereon, and (iii) that under section 14 the assessable value of the imported goods must be the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold and the payment of demurrage was not an incident of an ordinary sale and an extraordinary expenditure, like demurrage, could not be included in the assessable value of the imported goods.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The question involved in the instant appeal is as to whether ship demurrage charges paid by the assessee-importer on the import of the goods were to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for purpose of levy of customs duty.

The petitioner imported 71 cartons and the Bill of Entries were presented on February 27, 1988 and the Customs Authorities issued a show cause notice on December 15, 1988, which was discharged by the Assistant Collector of Customs. The petitioner stated that since the show cause notice had been discharged, the petitioner had no liability to pay demurrage charges and/or ground rent charges and that after issuance of the Detention Certificate, the Inland Container Depot being custodian for Customs was under obligation to release the goods without payment of demurrage and ground rent charges.

The petitioners entered into an agreement to sell ore to foreign buyer. The agreement was in the nature of FOB contract. The ships were chartered by the foreign buyer of ore for the purpose of conveying the ores purchased from the seller. The seller was paid price at the rate specified in the agreement and the quantity of the ore was quantified with reference to their loading into the ship. In case there was delay in loading, the seller had to pay demurrage and similarly in case time was saved in loading, the seller was entitled to receive dispatch money. The ITO held that this demurrage was essentially an extended freight payable towards the carriage of the goods and was taxable in the same manner, as the receipt towards freight was taxed.

On writ, the Single Judge held that the demurrage was not an extended freight at all; that section 172 covered the field of taxing a non-resident owner or charterer of a ship who was not engaged in the business of operation of shipping and section 5 was inapplicable to the facts of the instant case.

On writ appeal :

Pursuant to the provisions of section 12A of the Airports Authority of India Act (AAI Act), the Airports Authority of India (AAI) and the Delhi International Airport (P) Ltd. (DIAL), i.e., the petitioner here entered into an agreement on 4-4-2006, whereby the latter was granted exclusive right and authority for performing the functions of operating, maintaining, developing, designing, constructing, upgrading, modernizing, financing and managing of the Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi [IGI Airport]. Thereupon DIAL took over the operations of the IGI Airport from AAI and was empowered under the provisions of the agreement to exercise powers under section 12A(4) of the AAI Act and was also empowered to exercise AAI's statutory powers under the Regulations framed in 2003, with regard to levy of demurrage charges at the IGI Airport.

On 17-3-2009, the Central Board of Excise and Customs [CBEC], i.e., the second respondent exercising its powers under section 141(2) read with section 157 of the Customs Act notified the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 (Cargo Regulations) and regulation 6(1)(l) thereof obliged the customs cargo service providers not to charge demurrage in certain cases if directed not to do so.

Further DIAL executed a Concession Agreement dated 24-8-2009 with Celibi Delhi Cargo Terminal Management India (P.) Ltd. [proforma fourth respondent, hereafter Celibi], which enabled it to upgrade, modernize, finance, operate, maintain and manage the cargo terminal at IGI Airport.

Thereafter the Commissioner of Customs (third respondent) started issuing directions to DIAL and Celibi to waive demurrage charges in accordance with the impugned regulation 6(1)(l). These directions were not complied with. Consequently the third respondent issued show cause notices to the petitioner and Celibi as to why the impugned regulation was not complied with and as to why action should not be initiated against them.

The petitioner filed a writ peetition challenging regulation 6(1)(l) of the Cargo Regulations on the plea that the CBEC exceeded the power delegated to it by the Customs Act and also contended that said regulation violated articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India.

The assessee-company remitted the demurrage amount for delayed loading, payable by the buyers of its iron ore to the ship owners as the assessee had to export goods on FOB basis. The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount under section 40(a)(i) for remittance without deduction of tax at source. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance.

Assessing Officer noted that assessee had paid demurrage to various non-resident companies with whom India did not have DTAA, without deducting tax at source.

Assessing Officer disallowed said expenditure in view of section 40(a)(i), as no tax had been deducted on said amount.

On appeal, the Commissioner(Appeals) deleted the disallowance holding that these payments are not demurrage but payments made to purchasers of iron ore and not to the owner of ships as applicable under section 172 and these payments are taxable under section 195 (1).

On appeal to Tribunal:

The petitioners were mine owners mining, among other things, manganese and iron ores, which they exported. The petitioners entered into an agreement with a foreign buyer to supply on credit basis iron and manganese ore and the foreign buyers sent their ships either owned by them or chartered by them for carriage of the goods. Contracts provided that in case of detention of a ship in the port for unforeseen reasons, petitioners had to bear the demurrage charges and pay the same to the owner or charterer of the ship. Payments for such demurrage were being paid with the approval of the RBI through the regular bank channels. In February, 1988, the first respondent - Dy. Controller of RBI - issued a Circular dated 22-2-1988 to all the exporters requiring them to obtain income-tax clearance certificate for remittance of demurrage payments. By yet another communication dated 11-10-1988, all the exporters had been informed by the first respondent that all demurrage amounts payable in respect of foreign vessels attract Indian Income-tax. Therefore, the exporters were advised to ensure that all applications for remittances towards demurrage payable to foreign vessels should be duly supported by income-tax clearance certificates or documentary evidence that tax was withheld along with a no-objection certificate from the department.

On writ, the petitioners disputed the circular instructions and prayed that these be quashed.

The assessee-firm ran a rolling mill where iron bars were manufactured out of billets and plate cuttings, etc. Certain goods imported by it were confiscated by customs authorities, by an order dated 10-02-1959, on finding that these were not covered by its import licence. The assessee, however, had the option to pay Rs. 22,000 as fine and clear the goods for home consumption subject to adjustment thereof against the licence held by him. After unsuccessfully agitating the matter before various authorities for four years, it finally cleared the goods by paying not only the fine but also a sum of Rs. 19,119 as demurrage charges for use of the port facilities beyond the permissible free period during the litigation period. The assessee claimed the deduction of these demurrage charges as business expenses under section 10(2)(xv) but the same was disallowed by the ITO. Its appeal before the AAC and the Tribunal were unsuccessful. The Tribunal held (i) that the demurrage was paid not for business reasons but for breach of the Import Control Order, and (ii) that there was no essential difference between the "fine" paid and the "demurrage" paid.

On reference :

The petitioner-company entered into an agreement with a Singapore based company in terms whereof the mooring job of the Floating Dock was entrusted to the latter. The work was to be completed within 16 days. As there was delay in the work, the said company was paid additional amount for extra period. According to the petitioner, although expression ‘demurrage’ had been used in debit note, in truth and substance, it was fee for technical services, which was supported by the Singapore based company. The IAC, however, treated such payment under the heading ‘Any other payments’ and held that the provisions of section 10(6A) were not applicable. On appeal, the Commissioner affirmed the order of the IAC.

On writ :

The assessee company filed its return claiming deduction of demurrage paid to a non-resident shipping company.

The assessee's case was that there was no obligation to deduct tax at source as the amount was paid to non-resident shipping company engaged in operation of ships and, therefore, governed by section 172.

The Assessing Officer, however, opined that assessee was required to deduct tax at source under section 195 while making payment to non-resident shipping company. In view of assessee's failure to do so, Assessing Officer disallowed payments in question.

Reliance was also placed upon the Circular No. 723 dated 19-9-1995 issued by CBDT which interalia provides that Section 172 is a self contained code for levy and recovery of taxes ship wise and journey wise in case of ships owned or chartered by non-residents. Therefore, the requirement of deducting tax at source would not be applicable in such a case thus the consequent disallowance of expenditure under Section 40(a)(i) was not warranted.

However, the CIT(A) did not accept the contention of the assessee and held section 44B would apply as it related to computation of profits and gains and from shipping business. In the above view, the appeal of the assessee was dismissed.

The Tribunal allowed assessee's appeal by following decision in DCIT v. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. [2009] 185 Taxman 131. The impugned order specifically held that section 172 was a charging as well as a machinery provision in respect of non-resident shipping companies. It provided for determination and collection of tax. Thus Chapter XVII of the Act in respect of deducting tax at source would not apply in such cases. Consequently, the disallowance of expenditure on account of section 40(a)(i) Act was deleted.

For the relevant assessment year, the assessee filed the return declaring nil income. From the computation of income, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had received certain amount as inland haulage charges (IHC), i.e., charges towards transporting the goods from the exporter's place to the port. Thereupon, the Assessing Officer issued show-cause notice to the assessee asking it as to why IHC be not taxed as per provisions of the Act. The assessee in reply submitted that the Explanation to section 44B included the words 'demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature' and, hence, these were wide enough to include IHC. It was further pleaded that Article 8 of the DTAA included the clause relating to the income derived from operation of ships as also the income from other activity directly connected with such transportation and the income derived from the use, maintenance or rental of containers (including trailers and related equipment for the transportation of containers). The Assessing Officer did not accept the assessee's explanation and came to hold that the revenue earned on account of receipt of IHC in India was taxable as business profit, since it was covered neither under section 44B nor under Article 8 of the DTAA.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that Article 8 of the DTAA was applicable on IHC and, accordingly, overturned the action of the Assessing Officer.

Facts

The trial court allowed the petitioner to re-export the goods being six consignments of furnace oil/fuel oil claimed to have been imported by petitioner.

The assessee challenged the direction of the Trial Court to pay port charges on ground that issue whether delay occurred due to latches on part of the Customs Authority was not considered by Trial Court.

Whether order of Trial Court was bad in law ?

The assessee, a foreign company, engaged in business of operation of ships returned income on account of inland haulage charges. It claimed that activity of inland transportation being directly connected with international traffic, was exempt under article 8 of DTAA.

The Assessing Officer held that only loading, unloading and demurrages were activities connected to shipping and, thus, income from inland haulage charges was chargeable to tax in India and made addition to assessee's income.

The court acknowledges that section 151A of the Customs Act places an obligation upon the officers of customs to follow the orders, instructions and directions of the Central Board of Excise and Customs, as far as they relate to any prohibition, restriction or procedure for import or export of goods. DIAL's further argument was that in the event of directions under the regulations, compliance would result in commercial unviability, because its autonomy to charge fully or in part might eventually result in losses. [Para 16]

In the event DIAL is of the view that customs authorities' directions to it to not charge demurrage are unwarranted, it can seek guidance and directions in that regard, from the Central Government. In these circumstances, the grievance that regulation 6(1)(l) can potentially render DIAL's functioning unviable and result in losses to it has to fail. [Para 18]

In the light of the aforesaid, the challenge to the impugned regulation 6(1)(l) fails. Consequently, the writ petition was liable to be dismissed. [Para 19]

Regulation 6 of the Cargo Regulations fixes the responsibilities of a customs cargo service provider, defined under regulation 2(1)(b). The proforma fourth respondent, by virtue of the concession agreement, comes within the purview of customs cargo service provider and is, therefore, bound by such responsibilities. The Cargo Regulations, which contain the impugned regulation 6(1)(l), derives its existence from section 141(2) read with section 157 of the Customs Act. Those provisions show that the Central Board of Excise and Customs is empowered to prescribe the responsibilities of persons engaged in the activities of receiving, storing, delivering, dispatching or otherwise handling of imported or export goods in a customs area. [Para 10]

Undoubtedly DIAL's functions in relation to operating, maintaining, developing, designing, constructing, upgrading, modernizing, financing and managing of the IGI Airport as conferred by the agreement dated 4-4-2006, except those functions pertaining to the cargo terminal which have been sub-contracted to the proforma fourth respondent by virtue of the concession agreement, are governed by the AAI Act. Nevertheless, the obligations of the customs cargo service provider/proforma fourth respondent is governed by the Cargo Regulations. The court is aware that the Supreme Court in the cases of International & Airports Authority of India v. Grand Slam International 1995 taxmann.com 344 (SC) and Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd. v. C.L. Jain Woolen Mills 2001 (129) ELT 561 (SC) has observed that there was no provision in the Customs Act empowering the customs authorities to direct the custodian of goods to waive the demurrage charges on the goods. However, these decisions were pronounced before introduction of sub-section (2) to section 141 of the Customs Act, which later gave way to the notification of the Cargo Regulations. Therefore, the petitioner's argument that the second respondent exceeded the power delegated to it by the Customs Act must fail. [Para 11]

The contention of the petitioner that the impugned regulation 6(1)(l) violates article 14 of the Constitution of India, as it has no nexus with the object sought to be achieved, is insubstantial because the Cargo Regulations were enacted for the purpose of prescribing the responsibilities of persons engaged in the activities of receiving, storing, delivering, dispatching or otherwise handling of imported or export goods in a customs area and the impugned regulation is as such an obligation cast upon the persons involved in the said activities. DIAL also urged that the regulation contravene article 19(1)(g) inasmuch as it places a blanket ban on the charge of demurrage by the custodian of goods in case of detention, confiscation or seizure of goods by customs. However, such restriction is covered under the premise of article 19(6), by which reasonable restrictions in the interest of general public may be imposed on the right under article 19(1)(g). Investigation being an integral part of working of the Customs Department, the consignments detained by the customs authorities or other investigating agencies cannot be cleared during investigation particularly if such cases involve trade policy, human safety and security, security of State, etc. It is with these considerations that the impugned regulation was included in the Cargo Regulations and it should be viewed in the light of the object with which it has been framed. Therefore, the allegation that the impugned regulation violates article 19(1)(g) does not survive. [Para 12]

The Supreme Court in the case of Maharashtra State Board of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education v. Paritosh Bhupesh Kumar [1984] 4 SCC 27 has upheld the validity of a regulation made to carry out the provisions of the Act. It was held in that case that the regulations had to be judged on a threefold tests namely: (1) whether the provisions of the regulations fall within the scope and ambit of the power conferred on the delegate, (2) whether the regulations made are to any extent inconsistent with the provisions of the enabling Act, and (3) whether they infringe any of the fundamental rights or other restrictions or limitations imposed by the Constitution. In the instant case, the first test is answered in the affirmative and the second and third tests are answered in the negative, which would imply that the Cargo Regulations is well within the scope and ambit of its parent Act, i.e., the Customs Act and is also consistent with the same and does not, in any way, violate constitutional provisions. [Para 13]

Demurrage charges--ICD being custodian for customs is bound to release the goods to the petitioner after issuance of Detention Certificate and the Customs Department is liable to pay demurrage and ground rent charges after Bills of Entries were submitted till the goods were released. ".......in the present case, the Container Corporation of India through the Inland Container Depot is the custodian of goods under section 45 of the Customs Act. . Analysis of law :

Section 45 : Section 45 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that all imported goods unloaded in the customs area shall remain in the custody of a person approved by the Commissioner of Customs till the time they are cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped in accordance with chapter VIII which deals with goods in transit. The person to whom the custody of such goods is handed over by the Commissioner of Customs is liable to keep record of the same and keep the same in the customs area and not to permit removal of the same except with prior permission and in case of any pilferage etc. the said person is liable to pay duty on the said goods. [Para 24]

Sections 49 and 57 to 73 : Under section 49, the Customs Authorities on an application of the importer, if satisfied, that the goods entered for home consumption cannot be cleared within a reasonable time, permit the importer to deposit the goods in a public area or a private warehouse for a specified period. The period may be extended from time to time by the Commissioner of Customs. Section 49 further stipulates that goods so warehoused on an application by the importer shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods for the purposes of this Act and provisions of chapter IX shall not apply. Section 57 lays down that the Assistant Commissioner/Deputy Commissioner of Customs may appoint public warehouses wherein dutiable goods may be deposited. Section 58 empowers the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs to licence private warehouses wherein dutiable goods imported may be deposited where the facilities for deposit in a public warehouse are not available. Sections 59 to 73 of chapter IX deal with the general provisions under which an importer may warehouse the imported goods and stipulates the period for which the goods may be warehoused and general conditions for removal/clearance of the goods. [Para 27]

Section 141 : Section 141 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that the conveyances and goods in a customs area are subjected to the control of the officers of customs and are to be handled in a customs area in such a manner as may be prescribed and responsibilities of a person engaged in the receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and otherwise handling import or export goods in customs area shall be such as may be prescribed by the customs authorities. [Para 29]

Goods are within control of customs authorities : The above noted sections of the Customs Act postulate a scheme or a procedure whereby goods which are imported into a customs area immediately come into the control and power of the officers of the customs. The customs authorities are empowered under the Act to appoint persons or officers who are responsible for receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and handling goods in the customs areas. Under certain circumstances, the customs authorities may permit storage of imported goods in a warehouse pending clearance on a application by the importer, where goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time (section 49) or warehoused in a public or private warehouse (sections 60, 61). [Para 30]

AAI : The Airports Authority of India, is an authority established under the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 in terms of the said Act, all rights, powers, authorities, privileges and ownership in respect of all property movable or immovable airports of India. The functions and powers of AAI include establishment of warehouses and cargo complex at the airports for storage and processing of the goods at the terminals. [Para 32]

AAI Act : Under the provision of the AAI Act, AAI is empowered to make lease of premises of Airport to carry out some of functions under the Act. AAI, for overall public interest granted some of its functions, being the functions of operating, maintaining, developing, designing, construction, upgradation, modernisation, finances and managing the airport to the Delhi International Airport Private Limited, (DIAL for short) under the operation, management and developing agreements (OMDA) dated 4.4.2006 which agreement further empowers DIAL to sub-contract any activity covered by OMDA. [Para 33]

AERA : The Government of India formulated Airports Economic Regulatory Authority of India (AERA for short) under the Airport Economic Regulatory Authority of India Act, 2008. The AERA was given the responsibility of providing and fixing demurrage charges in respect of storage, processing and handling of Cargo at the terminal. [Para 34]

Receipt from detention/demurrage, in the present case, was nonetheless during the course of the business of operation of ships and, therefore, even if it was treated as income of the assessee, for argument sake, it could not be assessed under sections 28 to 43A. The provisions of sections 30 to 43C are not attracted for computation of income in respect of these receipts. The assessing officer, therefore, committed an error in treating the receipts from demurrage as income independent of carriage charges and further committed an error in estimating the expenses at 5 per cent. At the best, he could have treated those receipts as amount on account of carriage.

However, as laid down in CIT v. Pestonji Bhicajee [1977] 107 ITR 837 (Guj.), dead freight is an agreed sum to be paid in respect of space not filled according to charter or damages provided for by a charter, in the event of the freighter not loading a full cargo. It has been held by the High Court that 'dead freight' cannot be treated as payment made on account of carriage of goods in a ship. That was considered with reference to section 172, a provision analogous to section 44B. In context with the same, i.e., section 172 the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Gosalia Shipping (P.) Ltd. [1978] 113 ITR 307 held that the amount which the time charterers were required to pay to the owners of the ship was not payable on account of the carriage of goods but was payable on account of the use and hire of the ship. In this view of the matter, the detention/demurrage charges received for retention of the containers beyond the agreed period could not be treated as on account of the carriage of goods.

Accordingly, no part of the impugned receipts could be included in the total income of the assessee.

According to Explanation to section 44B(2) inserted retrospectively, the demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature should be taxed in the same way as the amount in clause (i ) or clause (ii) of section 44B(2). Accordingly, demurrage charges or freight charges should be taxed in the same way as freight taxable under section 44B.

Section 44B provides how the income from shipping business can be taxed in the case of non-residents and the section starts with a non-obstant clause, i.e. ‘Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A of the Act’. Thus, whatever is provided in the provisions contained in sections 28 to 43A, that will not come in the way of the provisions contained in section 44B as to how the income from shipping business in the case of non-residents will be computed, whether the income will be computed or not or what will be the rate of that income. However, the question was where an income of a non-resident had accrued outside India by way of demurrage charges, could that be taxed in India? There was no specific finding by the Tribunal as to what part of the demurrage income accrued to the assessee in India or outside India. Therefore, it was necessary to have the finding whether the demurrage income accrued in India or outside India and if not the entire income of demurrages, as to what part of the income of demurrages accrued in India or outside India.

Hence, the matter was remitted back to the Tribunal to give a finding on the above issue and decide the issue afresh.

The demurrage charges are admittedly incurred after the goods reached at Indian ports and, therefore, it is a post-importation event. Such charges, therefore, cannot form part of the transaction value. [Para 5]

In view of the aforesaid, the appeal filed by the revenue was liable to be dismissed.

Section 172(1) identifies the subject of taxation. That subject is to be taxed only as provided under section 172(2) to (7). There is no question of any residuary income attributable to that subject being taxed elsewhere. That will be amending section 172(1) by reading into it a supposed intention of the law-maker; such a course is impermissible.

Section 172(1) is not attracted to the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of operation of ships. A non-resident owner of charterer of a ship which carries passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India only, is covered by section 172.

Since section 172 is a complete code by itself, the levy and collection of tax in respect of the subject on which the tax is levied thereunder has to be only as provided therein. For whatever reason, the concept of total income of a non-resident person coming within section 172(1) is confined to the specified income under section 172(2). There is no scope at all to travel outside section 172 to impose tax on such a person's income derived in the manner stated in section 172(2).

Thus, if the payment is to be made not on account of carriage of goods, etc., then section 172(2) is not attracted and, therefore, such a receipt or payment is not taxable under section 172.

A perusal of the agreements showed that that demurrage payable was to prevent delay in loading the goods. In other words, the payment was to speed up the activity of delivering the goods to the purchaser in whom the title vested on delivery into the ship. If the seller expedited the delivery and loading, then he gets "dispatch money". While dispatch money was receivable by the seller, i.e., the petitioners, the demurrage was receivable by the purchaser. The carriage of goods by the ship commenced on completion of the loading work till then the goods were in the process of delivery on board the ship. The demurrage payable in the instant case at the most was on account of deley in the delivery of the goods on board the ship. If so, certainly section 172(2) was inapplicable.

The demurrage paid or payable under the said two agreements could not be taxed in the manner pleaded by the revenue.

Exemption: Customs Authorities cannot rely upon trade advice and levy duty on the ground that the content was not according to the advice. Trade advice is not statutory and as such reliance cannot be placed on it. "The Exemption Notification dated April 20, 1966 totally exempted woollen wastes and woollen rags from the whole of the duty of customs leviable thereon. The Exemption Notification does not restrict the advantage only to those woollen wastes and woollen rags containing wool of more than 50%. In absence of any such provision in the Notification, it is not permissible for the Customs Authorities to levy duty on the imported woollen rags on the ground that the wool content was found less than 50 per cent. It is now well settled that the trade advice issued by the Government of India has no statutory force and it is not permissible for the Authorities exercising quasi judicial function to place reliance upon such trade advice to hold that the petitioners are liable for payment of duty."

2. Exemption: Physical and Chemical tests offer guidance and assistance only. "Merely because the different analysis show different conclusions it is not permissible to select that conclusion which suits the authorities to levy the duty. .........The procedure adopted by the Customs Authorities was entirely misconceived and cannot be sustained either in law or by principles of natural justice. It is the Explanation which refers to the demurrage and for the purpose of sub-section (2) of section 44B. It clarifies that the amount paid or payable or received or deemed to be received, as the case may be, by way of demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature shall for the purposes of sub-section (1) deemed to be the profits and gains of the business, namely, shipping business chargeable to tax under that head. The amounts which are paid or payable whether in or out of India to the assessee or to any person on his behalf on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India and the amount received was deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port outside India shall be deemed to be the profits and gains. On that the tax is payable by virtue of sub-section (1) of section 172. That has to be levied and recovered in terms of the sub-sections of section 172.

Once section 172 falls in Chapter XV titled as Liability in Special Cases - Profits of Non-residents, then section 172 is referable to section 44B. Both provisions open with a non obstante clause and whereas section 44B enacts special provisions for computing profits and gains of shipping business in case of non-residents, section 172 dealing with shipping business of non-residents is enacted for the purpose of levy and recovery of tax in the case of any ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident operated from India.

These sections and particularly section 172 devise a scheme for levy and recovery of tax. The sub-sections of section 44B denote as to how the amounts paid to or payable would include demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature. The sub-sections of section 172 read together and harmoniously would reveal as to how the tax should be levied, computed, assessed and recovered. Therefore, there is no warrant in applying the provisions in Chapter XVII of Act for collection and recovery of the tax and its deduction at source vide section 195. [Para 46]

It is the recipient's position and the perspective in which the recipient's income would be taxed will have to be borne in mind. The non-resident shipping company in respect of its income would be in a position to rely upon section 44B and consequently section 172. However, one does not see how there is an obligation to deduct tax at source on the resident assessee/Indian company in the instant case. While computing the income of the non-resident Indian / foreign company, assistance can be derived by such non-residents from section 44B if they are in shipping business. It would also be in a position to rely upon section 172 but the responsibility of the person making payment to a non-resident in sub-section (1) of section 195 cannot be avoided in the manner set out in other cases. The scheme as above operates only to cases covered by section 172 and none else. [Para 48]

Having regard to the terms and conditions set out between the foreign buyer who had chartered the ship and the agreement with the petitioners, payment of demurrage clearly fell outside the amount mentioned in section 44B and section 172(2). Therefore, it could not be said to be an 'income'. Demurrage, though a receipt as compensation for detention, would not for the purpose of section 172 of the Act, be an income. Therefore, the contention of the petitioners must be upheld that the impugned circulars could not prescribe a mode of recovery and payment in respect of demurrage paid by exporters from India when the ship in question clearly fell within the ambit of section 172 of the Act. The petitioners, however, were not entitled to the relief they had prayed for but only to a declaration of the law in relation to section 172. In that view of the matter, the procedure required to be adopted as indicated in the circular dated 11-10-1988 was clearly without the authority of law but the court could not prevent the Central Board of Direct Taxes in forming a legal opinion as indicated in that circular. The Circular dated 22-2-1988 referred to Indian (resident) charterer and, therefore, the petitioners, not being the charterers, were not affected by the same. The petitions were disposed of as above.

Storage cost is neither a cost of purchase nor of conversion nor can it be considered as toward bringing the inventory held in stock to its present location or condition. It is in the nature of a holding cost, which could be considered as an element of cost only where the goods have to be necessarily held in a particular manner, entailing cost, for a defined period, prior to their further processing, i.e., itself represents a process integral to their conversion, so that it represents a process and, thus, conversion cost. There is accordingly no question of the same being added to its value. A simple question would clarify the issue, i.e., whether rent, were the goods, instead of lying at the port, removed expeditiously to a rented premises, saving demurrage, or the cost of the staff attending thereto (godown) or otherwise supervising the storage, etc. be said to form part of the acquisition or conversion cost of the goods or otherwise incurred in bringing the same to their present location and condition, so as to be included in their valuation? Surely not. The third element of cost, i.e., other than toward acquisition and conversion, it would be noted, is broadly worded, so that it could in fact be said to include the cost of acquisition and conversion as well. It is only the direct cost incurred toward so bringing that could be included in as much as it adds value. In fact, the demurrage/detention charges, being toward the cost for the delay in removal of the goods, can only loosely/broadly be said to be a holding cost, and it would be more appropriate to consider it as a cost for the delayed removal of goods, i.e., beyond the stipulated period. The same thus is only a revenue expenditure of the period to which it relates and no more and, thus, not liable for inclusion in the value of the goods from any stand point.

As regards the objection by the revenue with reference to section 145A, the same deserves to fail. This is as even if the detention/demurrage charge is considered as not arising on account of a contractual obligation, but a statutory one, i.e., as in the nature of a levy or impost (which would though need to be established), it would stand to be included under section 145A only where it represents a qualifying cost - which have found as not, and not otherwise. [Para 3.1]

The opening stock for the year under reference would include demurrage charges, while the closing stock would not, and which would itself become a source of distortion. Though normally both the opening and the closing stock are to be valued on the same basis, it cannot also be denied that the valuation of the opening stock has to agree with that of the closing stock for the immediately preceding year. It is not in dispute that the value of opening stock, as assumed by the assessee, is the same as adopted in respect of the closing stock for the immediately preceding year. Any change would lead to a distortion - to the extent of the change - in the year the same is effected, so that the same is incidental thereto, and the fundamental question that would need to be addressed and answered is if the change is valid. It is found as so. Further, altering the value of the opening stock would amount to effectively modifying the closing stock and, thus, the income for the immediately preceding year, which stands assessed. The change thus gets effectively shifted to that year. The argument qua uniformity in the valuation of opening and closing stock would then stand to be assumed for that year, leading to a modification in the value of the opening stock for that year, and so on, thus causing a ripple effect. The argument is, thus, to no moment, and inasmuch as a change has been validated for the current year, an exception to the principle of uniformity in the valuation of the closing and opening stock for that year would have to be drawn. These and the like arguments would thus suggest non-disturbance of the value of the (opening) stock as carried forward from the preceding year, even though the same may not be valid, subject of course to the change in the method of valuation being bona fide. [Para 3.3]

Power of customs is to control storage, removal and handling : Section 156 of the Customs Act lays down the general rule making power of the central government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act and section 157 lays down the power of the board to make regulations to carry out the purposes of the Act. Customs not concerned with finance of custodian : The customs authorities are concerned with the receiving, storing, delivering and handling of cargo in a customs area. Customs authorities are issuing certificate of waiver on regular basis : The customs authorities it appears issues certificate for waiver in every type of case irrespective of the fact whether the importer is at fault or not. The customs authorities have issued certificate for waiver of the demurrage charges in both the cases at hand. In one case the release of the goods are on provisional basis pending adjudication and in the other there is imposition of both fine and penalty. These are not cases where the importer has been held to be not at fault. In one case the Importer has been found to be at fault and penalty and fine imposed. The importer has accepted the said order. In the other case adjudication proceedings are pending and are yet to be finalised. [Para 42]
Since the fact was that the demurrage income had accrued in India and was also received in India, the Tribunal had committed an error by allowing the claim of the assessee.

The assessee has paid the demurrage charges to the non-resident in respect of delay in loading the ship. The sum was reimbursed by the assessee to the foreign buyer to compensate the foreign buyer for paying demurrage to the ship owner when ship came to Indian port and the assessee could not load the goods on to the ship within the limited time period. The export sales were made to the foreign Pakistani buyer on FOB basis. In view of the contract with the Pakistani buyer the assessee was bound to compensate the Pakistani buyer in respect of demurrage paid by the Pakistani buyer to the ship owner. This payment can be regarded to be the expenditure incurred by the assessee for the sale of the goods and was not akin to price deduction due to fault in product/service and was equivalent to discount/rebate which can be adjusted against the sale price. [Para 31]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of the goods in India for the purpose of export. The non-resident buyer got the compensation towards the demurrage incurred through the operation which was confined to the purchase of the goods, i.e. in relation to the ship which it had arranged for taking the delivery of the goods from the assessee/seller from India. Therefore, this income cannot be deemed to accrue or arise in India in the hands of the foreign buyer, and therefore, it cannot be taxable in India and is not liable to tax deduction at source. On this basis, no disallowance can be made under section 40(a)(ia), and accordingly, the disallowance is deleted. [Para 32]

From a perusal of the Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995, it is apparently clear that the provisions of sections 194C and 195 relating to tax deduction at source are not applicable where the provisions of section 172, relating to shipping business are applicable. The circular issued by the CBDT is binding on the department. In view of the circular, the assessee was not obliged to deduct TDS on the payment made as demurrage charges and the demurrage charges are also liable to be taxed under section 172. The assessee, since, is not liable to deduct tax at source, no question arises for making any disallowance under section 40(a)(i). [Para 33]

Regarding the other disallowance, it is not a case where the assessee had deducted tax at source, but the assessee had assisted the shipping owner in discharging their legal obligation by making payment of their income tax to the revenue for which they were liable under section 172. This is not a case where assessee has deducted TDS, as the assessee was not liable to deduct any TDS in respect of payment made to the ship owner for the demurrage. There is no dispute that the income of the foreign shipping companies were chargeable to tax under section 172. The demurrage paid to these shipping companies were also to be treated as freight in view of specific provision of section 172(8). In view of Circular Number 723, dt. 19-9-1995, the provision of sections 194C and 195 relating to tax deduction at source are not applicable to the income which is chargeable to tax under section 172. In view of this circular, the assessee was not obliged to deduct tax at source on the demurrage paid to the ship owners during the year. Since the provision of TDS were not applicable, therefore no disallowance can be sustained under section 40(a)(ia). Therefore, the order of the CIT(A) on these issues is set aside and the disallowance is deleted. [Para 33.1]

[Para 42] Apparent overlapping but harmonious construction : There is an overlap in the Policy for Waiver framed by AAI and the HCCAR. Though initially there appears to be a conflict between the policy and the regulations but on closer scrutiny it is apparent that they can both be harmoniously construed and coexist. [Para 43]

AAI Policy of Waiver distinguishes between innocent and culprit importers - Said policy overrides : The policy makes a distinction between the cases where the importer is innocent but his imported goods are seized and detained pending an enquiry and adjudication and the cases where the importers have indulged in mis-declaration, mis-description, under valuation or concealment and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities. Importers who are innocent cannot be equated with the importers who violate the law and be given the same treatment. The AAI policy makes a distinction between the two. [Para 44]

HCCAR subject to policy of waiver : The regulations framed in 2009 themselves stipulate that they are subject to any law for the time being in force and as such the regulations would be applicable in terms of the Policy for Waiver framed by the AAI in 2003. [Para 45]

Faulty importers cannot get benefit of waiver : In case the HCCAR were to be made applicable in all cases then the result would be that in no case where there is a fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning imposed by the customs authorities CELEBI would be able to charge demurrage charges. Customs authorities are issuing waiver directions even in cases where the importers are clearly at fault and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning has been imposed by the customs authorities. Even in cases of mis-declaration, undervaluation and concealment, the certificates are being issued. This is clearly giving premium to dishonesty. The waiver should be granted in genuine cases where the importers are ultimately found not at fault. It cannot be that all importers honest and dishonest are treated equally. [Para 46]

Innocent importer - Demurrage may be waived : In cases where the importer is found innocent and there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by the customs authorities, the policy for waiver would be applicable and the importer would be entitled to be considered for its benefit provided a certificate entitling him to be so considered is issued by the customs authorities. The importer would not be automatically exempt but would be covered under the policy for waiver and eligible for waiver which would be granted subject to other compliances. [Para 47]

Policy of waiver not overridden by superdginama of CELEBI : The execution of the superdginama by CELEBI that it would not claim any storage charges for the safe custody of the goods charge would also not be in conflict with the policy for waiver. The policy has been framed by the Airports Authority of India and the execution of the Superdginama by an employee would not override the policy. It would be applicable in cases where no fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities. In cases where the importer is found eligible for the benefit of the Policy, the Superdginama would automatically become applicable. [Para 48]

No waiver if importer is at fault - HCCAR not overrides : Where the importer is clearly at fault and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities, making the regulations applicable and granting the benefits of waiver would be clearly unreasonable and would grant benefit of waiver, with the person who has provided space suffering. This was and is not the intention and purpose behind HCCAR. Regulation recognises and accepts that any other law in force is not abrogated or repealed . The existing provision applicable stands protected. [Para 49]

III. Conclusion :

Conclusion as to principle of law :

(1)

In cases where on conclusion of the adjudication proceedings there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by the customs authorities :

(i)

the Policy for Waiver would be applicable; and

(ii)

the importer would be entitled to be considered for its benefit when the goods were seized, detained or earlier confiscated; and

(iii)

waiver would be granted subject to other compliances.

(2)

In cases where pending the adjudication proceedings, provisional release order is issued and a certificate is issued by the customs authorities, the goods would be released subject to furnishing of bond and/or security as may be prescribed that in case any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities, the Importer would pay the demurrage charges. [Para 50]
