incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition have to be included in the cost of inventories. It does not matter whether such costs were incurred before production or after production. [Expert Advisory Committee's Opinion - Dec. 2003 Issue of the Chartered Accountant].

The test for determining whether or not the cost of carrying out a particular activity should be included in the cost of inventories is "whether the activity contributes to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition". Where the liability for royalty arises for the company at the time of production and is payable to the Central/State Government at the rate and time specified in the Act and the Rules, the royalty charge is a necessary operational expense which must be incurred to bring the inventories to their present location and condition. Accordingly, actual royalty incurred and accounted in the books by the company should be included in the cost of finished crude oil stock. - [Expert Advisory Committee Opinion response to Query No. 36 - ICAI's website]

4.15-1 Inclusion of other costs of tank farm and pipeline, viz., depreciation/depletion, operation and maintenance cost and insurance charges of tank farm and pipeline in the cost of finished crude oil stock

The crude oil which still contains formation water is despatched from the storage tanks to tank farms, where it is processed for further separation of formation water by gravity separation process or are routed through dehydration facilities like Electrostatic Emulsion Treater and that in gravity separation process, the crude once received in the tanks is allowed to settle for a retention time of ideally 10-12 hours for free water and sludge to settle. Thus, the crude oil lying in the tank farm is subjected to certain operations and that some production process is carried out in tank farm. Accordingly, the other costs of tank farm, viz., depreciation/depletion, operation and maintenance cost and insurance charges related to tank farm are the costs necessary in the production process and that these costs are necessary for changing the condition of the inventory from unprocessed to processed. Accordingly, these costs should be included in the valuation of crude oil lying in the tank farm and pipelines. [Expert Advisory Committee Opinion response to Query No. 36 - ICAI's website]

The pipelines are used to transmit the crude oil to the custody transfer point at the refinery gate and that the sale takes place at the refinery gate with the passing of risks and rewards to the refineries. Thus, considering the refinery gate as point of sale, the pipelines are used to transmit the oil to the point of sale. Therefore, the abovementioned expenditure is incurred in changing the location of the inventories, i.e., bringing the inventories to the intended point of sale. Accordingly, depreciation/depletion, operation and maintenance cost and insurance charges of pipelines should be considered in arriving at the costs of inventories lying in the pipelines. [Expert Advisory Committee Opinion response to Query No. 36 - ICAI's website]

4.16 Exclusions from the cost of inventories

In determining the cost of inventories, the following costs shall be excluded and recognised as expenses of the period in which they are incurred, namely:—

(a)

Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;

(b)

Storage costs, unless those costs are necessary in the production process prior to a further production stage;

(c)

Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition;

(d)

Selling costs. [para 12 of ICDS-II (New)]

4.16-1 Administrative overheads

It may be noted that :

General administrative overheads (e.g. general manager's salary, rent of general administration building, printing and stationery expenses of general administrative offices etc.) generally do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition and are not treated as part of inventory costs.

Cost of factory management and administration (factory manager's salary, printing and stationery consumed at factory etc.) are clearly costs related to production activities and are treated as factory overheads and included in cost of inventory. [Expert Advisory Committee, Compendium of Opinions, Vol. XIII - page 83]

4.16-2 Demurrage - Whether includible in cost of inventories?

According to the Expert Advisory Committee, demurrage would generally be treated as abnormal loss and excluded from cost of inventories. However, if it can be demonstrated that demurrage is a normal cost in the facts and circumstances of the case, it should be included in the cost of inventories-i.e. where incurrence of demurrage is directly linked to savings in costs that are includible inventory. For example, an enterprise may, on a consideration of costs and benefits, decide to pay demurrage rather than hire additional storage space. In such a case, demurrage is includible in the cost of inventories. [Compendium of Opinions, Vol. XX - page 23]

4.17 Cost formulae

ICDS II (New) prescribes only three cost formulae for determination of costs of inventories:

Specific identification

First-in-first-out (FIFO)

Weighted average cost

The cost of inventories of the following items should be assigned by specific identification of their individual costs:

Items that are not ordinarily interchangeable; and

Goods or services produced and segregated for specific projects (whether purchased or produced).

HEADNOTE: Section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [corresponding to section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961] - Business expenditure - Goods unauthorisedly imported by assessee-firm confiscated by customs authorities - Option to assessee to get import regularised on paying Rs. 22,000 as fine - Matter unsuccessfully agitated before higher authorities for four years - Assessee finally took delivery of goods after paying fine and substantial demurrage charges for use of port facilities beyond permissible free period - Whether tribunal was justified in law in disallowing demurrage charges as admissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) - Held, on Facts, No

FACT: The assessee-firm ran a rolling mill where iron bars were manufactured out of billets and plate cuttings, etc. Certain goods imported by it were confiscated by customs authorities, by an order dated 10-02-1959, on finding that these were not covered by its import licence. The assessee, however, had the option to pay Rs. 22,000 as fine and clear the goods for home consumption subject to adjustment thereof against the licence held by him. After unsuccessfully agitating the matter before various authorities for four years, it finally cleared the goods by paying not only the fine but also a sum of Rs. 19,119 as demurrage charges for use of the port facilities beyond the permissible free period during the litigation period. The assessee claimed the deduction of these demurrage charges as business expenses under section 10(2)(xv) but the same was disallowed by the ITO. Its appeal before the AAC and the Tribunal were unsuccessful. The Tribunal held (i) that the demurrage was paid not for business reasons but for breach of the Import Control Order, and (ii) that there was no essential difference between the "fine" paid and the "demurrage" paid.

On reference :

HELD: 1. Demurrage charged by port authorities is in the nature of compensation for delay in clearing the goods from the godowns of the port authorities. It includes amount chargeable for storage and safe custody of the goods by the port authorities beyond the free period allowed under port rules. In the instant case, the demurrage paid by the assessee was not a fine paid for any criminal act but compensation for use of the port facilities beyond the permissible free period.

2. Once the unauthorized import of goods had been regularized on payment of fine, commercial expediency dictated the assessee to take delivery of the goods after paying the demurrage failing which its stock-in-trade would have been auctioned by the port authorities to realise their dues. The payment was, thus, made by the assessee to preserve its stock-in-trade and to utilise it for its manufacturing business.

3. The impugned expenditure was, therefore, held to be a permissible revenue deduction under section 70(2)(xv).

The petitioner-firm utilised woollen rags for manufacturing shoddy woollen yarn and blankets. The GOI permitted import of woollen rags and garment rags (rags from woven woollen fabrics and rags from knitted woollen material) and exempted woollen waste and rags from levy of customs duty by a notification dt. 20.4.1966. The importers have to claim the said exemption under Item 49(4) of Indian Customs Tariff read with the notification before clearing and consignment of woollen rags from the customs. Since 1966, the STC has been given monopoly in licences for importing woollen rags, which are not granted individually but allotted a quota on recommendation of the Textile Commissioner. The petitioners were allotted a quota of 37 bales of woollen hosiery rags which were imported from foreign suppliers by STC. The Customs Authorities carried out a visual inspection by taking samples, and later decided to have a chemical test. In spite of these two tests the Authorities decided to resort to the core-drilling test. On the basis of this the department held that the wool content of these bales was less than 50 per cent and therefore not eligible for exemption under the notification dt. 20.4.1966 and though clearance of goods was allowed they were charged to appropriate duty. The goods were kept in the sheds of the Port Trust of Bombay and it was not permitting clearance without payment of demurrage charges.

It is clear from provisions of section 172 that in case of shipping of goods at a port in India, seven and a half per cent of the carriage charges shall be deemed to be income accruing in India on account of such carriage; that unless and until the tax assessable under section 172 is paid or arranged for and the Collector of Customs is satisfied to that effect, the ship shall not be granted port clearance; that the carriage charges, as and envisaged by section 172(2) shall be included in the amount of demurrage charge or handling charge or any other amount of similar nature. [Para 15]

In this regard, as per CBDT Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995, where payments are made to shipping agents of non-resident ship-owners or charterers for carriage of passengers, etc., shipped at a port in India, since the agent acted on behalf of the non-resident ship-owner or charterer, he steps into the shoes of the principal and, accordingly, the provisions of section 172 shall apply and those of sections 194C and 195 will not apply. [Para 16]

Further, in ITO v. Freight Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. [2006] 6 SOT 473 (Delhi), it has been held that payment of ocean freight and Inland haulage charges cannot be subjected to TDS by virtue of the provisions of section 172, which position is clarified by CBDT Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995. No decision contrary to Freight Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) has been cited on behalf of the department. Thus, in view of the clear provisions of section 172(8), as supplemented by CBDT Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995, both of which have been duly considered in Freight Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), the grievance of the assessee is found to be justified and is accepted as such. Accordingly, the demand raised under section 201(1) and under section 201(1A) for non-deduction of TDS on payment of shipping expenses is cancelled. [Para 17]

During the period November 1991 to January 1992, 78 shipments of zinc ingots and copper iron bars were imported by 5 different consignees from one MDL. These consignments were landed at the Bombay Port. The consignees filed bills of entry for 37 out of the 78 consignments, but, subsequently, failed to lift the consignments and, thus, they came to be stored at by the Port of Bombay. Facing a grave loss MDL requested the present appellant, if they were interested in purchasing the goods.

The appellant applied to the Customs Authorities to have the Bills of Entry substituted in their name for the 37 consignments for which the original consignees had filed Bills of Entry, and also applied to file Bills of Entry for the remaining 41 consignments lying unclaimed.

The clearing agent of the petitioner wrote to the Customs Authorities seeking an amendment of the Import General Manifest so that the goods could be cleared. The appellant was granted a detention certificate by the Customs Authority for the 41 consignments.

Government of India vide Statement of Guidelines for Remission of Demurrage Charges', notified that goods/consignments detained by Customs for 'ITC Facilities' were to be considered for grant of remission from payment of demurrage for the period the goods were being so processed by Customs Authorities. However, in the meantime, the Respondent levied a total of Rs. 2.81 crore as demurrage charges, the total remission granted by the Port of Bombay was Rs. 90 crore and, therefore, demanded a balance of Rs. 1.91 crore for the period of 23-3-1992 till 9-9-1992, on the ground that no remission could be granted prior to date of noting.

Aggrieved by the order of the respondent, the appellant, filed writ petition. The appellant, however, cleared the goods after making payment of the amount under protest.

By the judgment under appeal, the High Court dismissed the writ petition.

On appeal:

The case of the Department is that the Assessee has remitted/ paid the amount for design and drawing contracts. It is in such situation and the facts peculiar to the present case, firstly, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer was in error in applying both Section 44B and Section 195. The facts as set out are not found to be so by both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal. In fact the question of law arises out of payment of demurrage. That is reimbursed to the supplier of crude oil. It is in the nature of reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal found that this reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee cannot be brought within sub-section (1) of Section 44B. That is special provision for computing the profits and gains of shipping business in the case of a non-resident. That envisages the profits and gains of business of operation of ships. The sum to be covered by this provision should be of the nature referred to therein. In the present case, what has been paid is the sum for reimbursing the expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee by a non-resident. The amount referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 44B and which are deemed to be profits and gains of the business of operation of ships chargeable to tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" shall be the amount firstly, paid or payable, whether in or out of India, to the Assessee or to any person on his behalf on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port in India and secondly, received or deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the Assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port outside India. [Para 4]

In the present case, the finding of fact is that both conditions envisaged by sub-section (1) of Section 44B are not fulfilled. The provision has been invoked in case of reimbursement of demurrage charges paid or reimbursed by Assessee for import of crude oil. It is such a finding of fact which is recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) and which has been confirmed by the Tribunal in the impugned order. The reasons assigned in Tribunal's order would, therefore, go to show that the view taken is in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case at hand. The view taken, therefore, is possible one. It cannot be termed, by any stretch of imagination, as perverse or vitiated by error of law apparent on the face of the record. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 49 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Storage of imported goods in warehouse pending clearance - Detained goods - Plea for storage of goods in warehouse--Assistant Collector is empowered under Section 49 to order storage of goods in a warehouse pending determination of dispute regarding duty liability of goods--Petitioner accordingly directed to file application to Assistant Collector

FACT: Release of a consignment of goods from the Inland Container Depot (Railways) at New Delhi was requested by the petitioners who pleaded that detention of goods was causing them great loss and that if the goods could not be released, they should be stored or deposited in a public or private warehouse. The respondents urged that a proper application should be filed by the owner before the Assistant Collector who had the power and authority under Section 49 to order the storage of goods in a public or private warehouse pending a decision on whether the goods had been legally imported or whether they were leviable to duty.

HELD: Jurisdiction: Application for storage or deposit of goods in a public or private warehouse should be filed before the Assistant Collector who is empowered under Section 49 to order storage pending determination of whether goods have been legally imported or are liable to duty, as clearly provided for in Section 49. "In view of the clear language of Section 49, it is imperative for the petitioner to seek his relief under Section 49 from the Assistant Collector concerned by making a proper application. I hope and trust that if an application under Section 49 is made by the applicant, the same shall be disposed of without any delay or loss of any time keeping in view of the huge losses which are being suffered by the petitioner in the form of payment of demurrage."

IT : Where there was nothing in export agreement that only balance after adjusting demurrage and dead freight charges alone would be sale consideration, sale consideration for purpose of claiming deduction under section 80HHC would be whole amount without deduction of demurrage charges

ITC-Confiscation--Redemption fine--fine cannot be imposed when goods are simultaneously ordered to be re-exported. The appellant is therefore entitled to refund of redemption fine paid.

"When the goods are confiscated because of any ITC prohibition in terms of section 111(d) of the Act and an option to pay fine in lieu of such confiscation is given, the effect of such option is to lift the prohibition. In other words, the importer/appellant is entitled to import the goods and consume them within the country on payment of such redemption fine. Therefore, the simultaneous imposition of two conditions namely (i) imposition of fine in lieu of confiscation and (ii) directing re-export, cannot co-exist together. In view of this legal position the appellant is entitled to refund of Rs. 71,250/- on account of redemption fine paid by him if the goods have already been re-exported."

2. ITC--Penalty-- As the appellant had offered another licence for clearing the imported goods, the order regarding imposition of penalty is therefore set aside. "As regards the plea of the appellant regarding imposition of penalty, we find sufficient force in this respect because of non-entertainment of the offer of second licence produced by the importer/appellant for clearance of the goods. The penalty of Rs. 50,000/- imposed on the importer/appellant is also set aside."

3. Refund--Demurrage charges--Tribunal has no authority to pass such orders even though it feels it should be paid. Interest on amounts paid not acceptable as there is no such provision in the Customs Act To and fro freight not refundable as appellant not exercise option of stay. "Appellant's plea for ordering refund of Rs. 1,58,106/- on account of demurrage paid should be considered favourably and sympathetically by the Customs authorities in view of the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case as narrated above. The Tribunal, however, does not have the authority to order refund of demurrage. ...Appellant's plea for awarding interest at the rate of 18% per annum on all amounts paid by him is not accepted in view of the fact that there is no provision for it in the Customs Act. The Tribunal being a creature of the Act cannot be beyond the provisions of the Act. Hence this plea is also not tenable and is rejected. ..Regarding refund of to and fro fright of Rs. 4,026/-, no relief can be given at this stage. The appellant was also given an option. It was for him not to exercise the option and come up for staying the operation of the impugned order."

The assessee-company claimed deduction of certain amount on account of demurrage payable to a non-resident company 'M'. As no tax had been deducted on that amount, the Assessing Officer considered said amount as non-deductible claim in view of section 40(a)( i). On appeal, the Commis-sioner (Appeals) observed that demurrages debited by the assessee in the hands of the recipient were in the nature of profits of non-resident from occasional shipping business under section 44B, read with section 172. "Having heard Ld. Counsel for the Collector of Customs, Bombay and M/s. So far as the detention certificate for a period exceeding six months is concerned, it can be issued only with the approval of and under the signature of the Collector. Para 4 of the public notice deals with issue of detention certificates to the parties succeeding in appeals and read as follows:

"Detention Certificate, as a rule, will be issued by the concerned competent Customs Authority to the Appellants succeeding in Appeals on receipt of the copies of such Orders which the latter making formal application for issue of Detention Certificates. However, in cases where the Customs House decides to go in second Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, the issue of Detention Certificate will be considered only after such second appeal is finally disposed of in favour of the parties."

The Apex Court held as follows:

"6. According to the above mentioned para 4, the goods will not be released even where the party succeeds in cases where the Customs Authorities decide to go in Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court. The Counsel for the assessee characterised the direction as arbitrary and contrary to law. We see the force in his submission. If the authorities are of the opinion that the goods ought not to be released pending the Appeal, the straight forward course for them is to obtain an Order of Stay or other appropriate direction from the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. Section 44B is a special provision enshrined for computing the profits and gains of shipping business in the case of non-residents. Sub-section (1) provides that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A, an assessee, being a non-resident, engaged in the business of operation of ships, a sum equal to 7½ per cent of the aggregate amount specified in sub-section (2) shall be deemed to be the 'business income'. Sub-section (2) further provides that the amount paid or payable to the assessee on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from any port of India and the amount received or deemed to be received by the assessee on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from any port outside India shall be deemed as the business income. The case of the Assessing Officer was that the IHC was not covered under section 44B. The assessee had placed reliance on the Explanation to section 44B to contend that IHC would be covered within its Explanation. [Para 6]

A plain reading of the Explanation to section 44B reveals that the demurrage charges or handling charges or other amounts of similar nature have been brought within the ambit of 'business income' for applying the rate of 7½ per cent. The very nature of items prescribed in the Explanation being demurrage charges or handling charges, which precede 'any other amount of similar nature', show that the latter category has to draw a colour from the items referred to in the earlier part. The expression 'any other amount of similar nature' cannot be read in isolation by disregarding the nature of items preceding it. The meaning of the succeeding expression has to be understood in the context of the preceding words. Since the demurrage charges or handling charges have been mentioned in the Explanation prior to 'any other amount of similar nature', 'any other amount' has to be considered, which is similar to or closely resembles with the nature of demurrage or handling charges. Handling charges are the charges paid for loading/unloading/stacking, etc., of the containers and the demurrage charges are in nature of penalty for non-removal of the cargo in time. On the contrary, the IHC are towards transport of the goods from the exporter's place to the port. The very nature of inland transportation charges clearly differentiates it from handling or demurrage charges, which are of a different genus. Therefore, there was no substance in the submission of the assessee that inland haulage charges were covered under section 44B, as these were equal to or part and parcel of the amount on account of carriage of goods shipped at any port in or outside India, and, hence, were automatically covered under Article 8. [Paras 7 and 8]

Answer: In the instant case, demurrage is incurred on account of a nationwide transporters strike, which represents abnormal cost. Therefore, the demurrage should not be capitalised as per AS 10 and Ind AS 16. However, unlike AS 10 and Ind AS 16, ICDS-V(Revised) does not provide that abnormal costs should not be capitalised as part of actual cost of a TFA. As per ICDS-V(Revised), directly attributable costs should be capitalised, whether normal costs or abnormal costs. Therefore, demurrage is to be capitalised as part of cost of the now imported plant and machinary for income-tax purposes though it would not be capitalised for accounting purposes. Under the Scheme of Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), Government of India, all service providers (other than hotels and restaurants) shall be entitled to duty credit equivalent to 10% of the foreign exchange earned by them in the preceding financial year. The salient features of the 'duty credit certificates' are as under:

(a)

These certificates are valid for 2 years from the date of issue.

(b)

Duty credit entitlements may be used for import of any capital goods including spares, office equipment and professional equipment, office furniture and consumables; that are otherwise freely importable under ITC (HS) classification of export and import items, provided it is part of the main line of business.

(c)

The entitlements and the goods imported shall be non-transferable (except within group company and managed hotels) and be subject to actual user condition.

As per the Foreign Trade Policy, the duty credit entitlement under SFIS is granted to exporters with the objective to accelerate growth in export of services. Thus, the grant is awarded with reference to exports made by the company, and not with reference to total investment in an undertaking or by way of contribution towards its capital outlay. The duty credit entitlement under SFIS cannot be considered as a grant related to a specific tangible fixed asset, as no specific asset has been identified for its utilisation. Such duty credit entitlement under SFIS can be utilised not only for payment of duty on import of capital goods but also for their spare parts or consumables which can be revenue in nature. Moreover, it is not necessary under the Scheme that its recipient should utilise the scrips for importing goods only. The recipient may transfer them to another company within the same group or managed hotels as per the conditions of the Scheme resulting into an income for it. Thus, the award of duty credit entitlement under SFIS should be considered to be generating income to the recipient. The duty credit entitlement under SFIS should be treated as a grant related to revenue in terms of ICDS-VII (Revised) and is taxable as income. The SFIS scrip should not be deducted from value of capital goods imported duty-free. [Based on ICAI's Expert Advisory Committee Opinion in the context of AS 9 & AS 12].

Taxation of demurrage income in computing profits and gains of shipping business in the case of non-residents

5.7 Section 44B deals with computation of profits and gains of shipping business in the case of non-residents. It provides for presumptive taxation @7.5% of the amount paid or payable on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, etc. Similarly, section 172 provides for levy and recovery of income-tax @7.5% on such receipts. Courts have held that demurrage is the compensation provided for in a contract of affreightment for the detention of a vessel beyond the time agreed on for loading or unloading; it is not 'amount paid or payable on account of carriage' for the purposes of section 44B and section 172 and accordingly, it is not income eligible to tax under section 44B or section 172' [V.M. Salgaocar & Bros. Ltd. v. Dy. Controller [1991] 187 ITR 381 (Kar.)and; CBDT v. Chowgule & Co. Ltd. [1991] 192 ITR 40(Kar.)].

Section 44B has been amended with retrospective effect from assessment year 1976-77 to clarify that the expression 'the amount paid or payable on account of carriage' includes any of demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature.' A corresponding amendment has also been made in section 172.

Petroleum Coke - Whether declared goods?

The language of clause (i) of Section 14 is clearly wide and coal has been stated to include coke in all its forms. It is not denied that petroleum coke is one of the forms of coke. Therefore, on a plain reading of the above clause it is incomprehensible how petroleum coke can be excluded from its ambit. It may be that the clause mentions coal only and then declares that the word shall include coke in all its forms. That shows that the object of the words that follow coal is to extend the meaning. Coke is the refuse left after destructive distillation of coal, shale oil and is called petroleum coke, metallurgical coke or pitch coke, to indicate its source of origin; but all these are carbonaceous materials used for the same purpose and having same properties, more or less, main being – mixed carbon, volatile matters, ash and moisture. At any rate, the language employed is so wide, viz, "coke in all its forms", that petroleum coke which is a form of coke cannot possibly be excluded merely by reference to the word "coal". Section 40 deals with amounts not deductible. The amounts which cannot be deducted in computing the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession' in the case of an assessee are set out in clause (a) and sub-clause (i) refers to any interest, royalty, fees for technical services or other sum chargeable under the Act which is payable outside India or in India to a non-resident, not being a company, or to a foreign company on which tax is deductible at source under Chapter XVII-B and such tax has not been deducted or after deduction has not been paid.

Section 172 has application to shipping business of non-residents and the provisions of that section have application notwithstanding anything contained in the other provisions of the Act for the purpose of levy and recovery of tax in the case of any ship, belonging to or chartered by a non-resident which carries passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India.

Section 195 falling under Chapter XVII-B 'Collection and Recovery - Deduction at Source' by sub-section (1) deals with any person responsible for paying to a non-resident, not being a company, or to a foreign company, any interest or any other sum chargeable under the provisions of the Act, not being income chargeable under the head 'Salaries' and obliges him to deduct tax thereon at the rates in force. It is evident, therefore, that the responsibility is on any person making payment to a non-resident. It is that person's obligation to deduct the tax at source. If the tax is deductible at source and any assessee declares his income chargeable under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession', while computing the income chargeable under this head, the amounts mentioned in section 40 (a) (i) should not be deducted in the event there is a failure to deduct the tax at source in terms of Chapter XVII-B.

Therefore, a sum ought to be of the nature payable under sub-clause (i) outside India or in India to a non-resident, not being a company, or to a foreign company, but which invites the obligation to deduct the tax at source on the payment thereof. The assessee is a resident in India. It is the assessee's income under the above heads from which certain deduction has been disallowed. That is for failure to discharge the obligation to deduct the tax at source. The assessee contends that the payment is made to a non-resident/foreign company and, therefore, there may be an obligation to deduct the tax at source in terms of sub-section (1) of section 195 but the overriding provision in section 172 will come to its assistance. [Para 44]

The shipping business of non-residents is an aspect dealt with by section 172. While considering the levy and recovery of tax in case of such business which is carried on with the aid of any ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident which carries passengers etc. shipped at a port in India, then, it is to compute the tax and recover it in relation to such business of a non-resident that section 172 is incorporated in the Statute Book. There are special provisions for computing profits and gains for shipping business in the case of a non-resident and enacted by section 44B which falls in Chapter IV - 'Computation of Business Income'. [Para 45]

A bare perusal of section 44B would indicate as to how this provision covers the case of an assessee who is a non-resident and engaged in the business of operation of ships. That stipulates a sum equal to 7½ per cent of the aggregate of the amount specified in sub-section (2) of section 44B as deemed to be profits and gains of such business chargeable to tax under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession'. It is the Explanation which refers to the demurrage and for the purpose of sub-section (2) of section 44B. It clarifies that the amount paid or payable or received or deemed to be received, as the case may be, by way of demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature shall for the purposes of sub-section (1) deemed to be the profits and gains of the business, namely, shipping business chargeable to tax under that head.

HELD: Section 172 comes under sub-title 'H - Profits of non-residents from occasional shipping business'. Title of section 172 is 'Shipping business of non-residents'. Storage in public warehouse pending clearance

Normally, imported goods are either cleared for home consumption on payment of customs duty or kept in customs bonded warehouse after goods are assessed to duty.

However, occasionally, it may happen that assessment of customs duty may take time for want of some clarification/reports etc. In such cases, goods lying in docks incur heavy demurrage.

Hence, if assessment is likely to be delayed, section 49 of Customs Act allows that goods can be stored in public warehouse for period upto 30 days. This period can be extended for 30 days at a time by Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs - second proviso to section 49 of Customs Act as amended w.e.f. 31-3-2017.

The goods may or may not be dutiable if these are to be cleared for home consumption. However, if these are to be cleared for warehousing, then only dutiable can be kept in public warehouse pending clearance - section 49 of Customs Act as amended w.e.f. 31-3-2017.

Such goods are not to be treated as 'warehoused goods' for purposes of Chapter IX Customs Act (which makes provisions for warehousing of goods), as the goods are not assessed - first proviso to section 49 of Customs Act as amended w.e.f. 31-3-2017.

Hence, such warehousing can be called 'storage without warehousing' or 'warehousing without warehousing'. The goods are cleared from the public warehouse after duty is assessed and paid.

FACT: The assessee company filed its return claiming deduction of demurrage paid to a non-resident shipping company.

The assessee's case was that there was no obligation to deduct tax at source as the amount was paid to non-resident shipping company engaged in operation of ships and, therefore, governed by section 172.

The Assessing Officer, however, opined that assessee was required to deduct tax at source under section 195 while making payment to non-resident shipping company. In view of assessee's failure to do so, Assessing Officer disallowed payments in question.

Reliance was also placed upon the Circular No. 723 dated 19-9-1995 issued by CBDT which interalia provides that Section 172 is a self contained code for levy and recovery of taxes ship wise and journey wise in case of ships owned or chartered by non-residents. Therefore, the requirement of deducting tax at source would not be applicable in such a case thus the consequent disallowance of expenditure under Section 40(a)(i) was not warranted.

However, the CIT(A) did not accept the contention of the assessee and held section 44B would apply as it related to computation of profits and gains and from shipping business. In the above view, the appeal of the assessee was dismissed.

The Tribunal allowed assessee's appeal by following decision in DCIT v. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. [2009] 185 Taxman 131. The impugned order specifically held that section 172 was a charging as well as a machinery provision in respect of non-resident shipping companies. It provided for determination and collection of tax. Thus Chapter XVII of the Act in respect of deducting tax at source would not apply in such cases. Consequently, the disallowance of expenditure on account of section 40(a)(i) Act was deleted.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: This Court in CIT v. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. [2010] 325 ITR 554/[2009] 185 Taxman 131 held that section 172 is applicable only in respect of non-resident carrying on shipping business while assessee i.e. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. was admittedly a resident and therefore section 172 could not be applied. Thus the expenditure of demurrage charges could not be allowed in the absence of tax being deducted at source. [Para 10]

The above view of this Court in Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. (supra) cannot be accepted. This is for the reason that the assessee placed reliance upon section 172 in respect of payments made by it to a non-resident shipping company by way of demurrage charges. The tax which is deducted at source by the assessee company is on behalf of the recipient of the charges. The issue before the Court was whether demurrage charges which are paid by the assessee to a non-resident company would be allowed as an expenditure in the absence of deduction of tax at source in view of section 40(a)(i) of the Act.

Although the Court was concerned with the issue in an appeal concerning a resident company. The introduction of section 172 by the assessee was to determine whether in view thereof, was there any obligation to deduct tax at source by the payer-assessee. Section 172 has to be examined through the prism of the non-resident shipping company in respect of its income. It is in the above view that section 172 and Circular No. 723 issued by the CBDT was relied upon by the assessee to point out that as section 172 provides a complete code itself for recovery of tax ship wise and journey wise. Thus there is no occasion to deduct tax under Chapter XVII of the Act. [Para 11]

Stores supplies to foreign going vessel/used in foreign going vessel - Stores supplied to foreign going vessel are 'export' as per section 89 of Customs Act. Hence, duty drawback will be available on supply of such stores. As per section 87 of Customs Act, imported stores may be consumed on foreign going vessel without payment of customs duty. As per section 86(2) of Customs Act, stores can be transferred from one foreign going vessel to another with permission of customs officer.

Sea going/ocean going vessel - In CCE v. Vipul Shipyard - 1996 (88) ELT 640 (SC), it was held that vessels built and equipped for traversing the ocean are 'ocean going vessels', even if the goods (barges and vessels) were used for inland navigation. Its actual use is of no consequence. In Bharati Shipyard v. CCE 1998 (101) ELT 33 (CEGAT), it was held that dredgers, barges and tugs are 'ocean going vessels'. In CC v. Vipul Shipyard 2000 (117) ELT 616 (CEGAT), it was held that barges are 'ocean going vessels'.

In UOI v. V M Salgaoncar AIR 1998 SC 1367 = (1998) 4 SCC 263 = 99 ELT 3 (SC 3 member bench), it was held that transshippers, which are vessels fitted with equipment for transshipping and topping operations and used for carrying cargo from harbour and unloading it into large vessels afloat in high seas, are 'ocean going vessels'. It was held that there is no qualitative difference between the terms 'ocean going vessel', and 'sea going vessel'.

In CC v. Mustan Taharbhai 1998 (102) ELT 367 (CEGAT), it was held that a vessel will continue be an 'ocean going vessel', even if it is imported in India for breaking up.

Barges and tugs are 'ocean going vessels' - AFL P Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 295 ELT 211 (CESTAT).

In Aban Lloyd Chiles Offshore v. CC 2003 (156) ELT 490 (CESTAT), it was held that when oil rig enters into India for purpose of repairs, it loses its character of 'foreign going vessel'. However, if it is brought in India for repairs and taken out after repairs, goods are not intended to be used in India. It is not import for home consumption. Hence, no duty will be payable on such oil rigs. This view has been confirmed in CCE v. Aban Lloyd Chiles Offshore (2017) 346 ELT 513 (SC).

In Aban Loyd Chiles v. UOI 2002 (139) ELT 273 (Bom HC DB), relying on Pride Foramer v. UOI AIR 2001 Bom HC DB 332 = 148 ELT 19 (Bom HC DB), it was held that oil rigs proceeding to designated areas or operating therein would be deemed to be part of Indian territory. Hence, the oil rig proceeding to such area will not be 'foreign going vessel' - view confirmed in Aban Loyd Chiles v. UOI (2008) 11 SCC 439 = 227 ELT 24 (SC).

Other provisions of Baggage

Other provisions regarding baggage are explained below.

Indian Government officers posted abroad - Baggage Rules, 1994 are fully applicable to Indian diplomatic officers and their families as well as Government of India officers posted abroad, when they return to India. Some concessions were granted to them vide instructions dated 16-4-1951. These concessions have now been withdrawn. In specific cases, ad hoc exemption on merits may be granted - CBE & C Circular No. 4/95-Cus dated 12-1-1995.

Export of Baggage - There are very few restrictions in taking out personal baggage. Prohibited goods cannot be taken out as baggage. Foreign and Indian currency can be taken out within the limits prescribed by RBI under FEMA.

Goods even in commercial quantities can be taken out as accompanied or un-accompanied baggage, if the passenger is able to establish source of funds for buying these goods as foreign exchange brought by him on his arrival in India. - CBI&C circular No. 17/95-Cus dated 1-3-1995.

If a tourist purchases goods in free foreign currency and takes it out as tourist baggage, duty drawback and other export benefits are available. The exporter must submit relevant encashment document of foreign currency, shipping bill etc. - CBI&C circular No. 36/98-Cus dated 20-5-1998.

14.5-1 Detention and Transshipment of baggage

It may happen that goods brought by a tourist may be prohibited in India. In such case, if he makes true declaration in respect of those goods, the goods can be temporarily detained by customs authorities. These will be returned to him when he leaves India. If he is not able to personally take the goods, he can authorise any other passenger leaving India to collect the goods. Alternately, the goods can also be returned as cargo consigned in his name - [section 80 of Customs Act].

Transshipment of baggage - It may happen that the un-accompanied baggage lands at once customs station but the passenger may like to clear the goods from another customs station. In such cases, such baggage may be permitted to be transported by air or passenger train, under Baggage (Transit to Customs Stations) Regulations, 1967. The baggage will be under supervision of officer of customs. The passenger will have make all arrangements for transport and pay for supervision charges. This facility is available only at Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Trivandrum, Hyderabad, Cochin, Ahmedabad, Goa, Calicut, Coimbatore, Lucknow or Amritsar. The baggage can come by air, passenger train or trucks.

Levy of fees on detained or seized baggage - If customs authorities decide to detain the baggage for inspection/payment of duty/clarification etc.; the same will be kept in store in custody of customs. In such cases, the passenger will have to pay fees as prescribed by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs. The fees will be prescribed depending on nature of articles contained in baggage and expenses for transportation of goods from landing place to storage place and other expenditure incurred.

Clearance of passenger's baggage for export - Baggage for export also should be allowed after clearance from Customs Officer. The passenger should pay export duty, where leviable and produce export license, if applicable.

No demurrage on baggage - In International Airport Authority of India v. Ashok Dhawan 1999(106) ELT 16 (SC), it has been held that 'baggage' is not 'cargo' and hence no demurrage can be levied upon baggage. Same principle applies in case of transshipment also.

14.5-2 Samples in baggage or through port or by a courier

India is signatory to 1952 Geneva Convention to facilitate importation of commercial samples and advertisement material. Samples can be brought in as baggage or through port or by a courier.

No Authorisation shall be required for Import of bona fide technical and trade samples of items "restricted" in ITC(HS) except defence/security items, seeds, bees and new drugs. Import of samples shall be further governed by Para 2.62 of Handbook of Procedures - Para 2.25 of FTP 2023.

Legal provisions in respect of import of samples are summarised in Chapter 18 of CBIC's Customs Manual, 2023.

Prohibited goods cannot be imported as samples.

19.1-1 Difference between sections 13 and 23(1)

Difference in sections 13 and 23(1) of Customs Act can be summarised as follows : 19.1-2 Loss after order of clearance but before actual clearance

Section 13 of Customs Act provides that duty on pilfered goods is not payable if the imported goods are pilfered before order of clearance is made. This section is on basis of principle that goods are not in control of importer when they are in port and he should not be penalised if these are pilfered. As the sections 13 and 23(1) stand today, there is no remedy if goods are pilfered after the order for clearance is made but before the goods are actually cleared.

In Zenith Bearing Enterprises v. Collector of Customs (ACC), Bombay - 1995 (75) ELT 801 (CEGAT 2 v 1 decision), held that once 'out of charge' order is given by customs authorities, no remission of customs duty can be granted for any shortage or loss found later. - same view in CC v. Relaxo Rubber 2001(134) ELT 797 (CEGAT) * NTI Materials v. CC (2021) 378 ELT 435 (CESTAT).

[Legally, these decisions seem to be correct, though really unfair to the importer.].

In Bharat Earth Movers v. CC 2001(129) ELT 580 (Mad HC DB), it was held that in case of pilferage, only section 13 applies and claim of refund u/s 23(1) of Customs Act is not permissible.

Remission if goods lost after order of clearance but before physical clearance - In CC v. Saw Pipes 2001(137) ELT 244 (CEGAT), it was (indeed rightly) held that 'clearance for home consumption' cannot be equated with order of clearance for home consumption. Physical removal of goods which is the 'clearance for home consumption' can take place only after such an order is passed. Such clearance therefore is an event distinct and separate from the order permitting clearance. [This decision is relevant for purpose of section 23(1) and not for section 13, as wording used in section 13 is different].

In CC v. Avenue Impex (2012) 285 ELT 90 (CESTAT), out of charge was given on 7-10-2008 and fire took place on 9-10-2008, before goods were physically cleared from customs. It was held that remission is available - relying on Mount Shivalik Breweries v. UOI 2003 (157) ELT 9 (Del HC DB) - view confirmed in Avenue Impex v. CC (2017) 345 ELT 173 (Mad HC).

19.1-3 Duty on pilfered goods is payable by port authorities?

If goods are pilfered after they are unloaded but before they are cleared from the port, the customs duty is payable by person having custody pursuant to any law or person approved by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of customs until they are cleared from customs [section 45(3)].

Once goods are unloaded from ship/aircraft, they are in custody of port trust authorities or airport authorities till the goods are cleared. They are in position of 'bailee'.

Thus, though importer does not have to pay duty on pilfered goods, the same is payable by authorities who were custodians of the goods so that Government does not lose any revenue on account of pilferage.

It was thought that port trust is liable for customs duty in case of pilfered goods. However, in Board of Trustees v. UOI (2009) 241 ELT 513 (Bom HC DB), it was held that port trust is not 'approved person' by Commissioner but possession of goods by Port Trust is by virtue of powers conferred under Port Trust Act. Hence, port trust is not liable for customs duty on pilfered goods. Section 45 applies only to private persons if pilferage takes place from private warehouse or customs warehouse.

In Board of Trustees of Port of Mumbai v. CC (2008) 223 ELT 635 (CESTAT SMB), if no police complaint is lodged, port trust authorities cannot be held responsible for pilferage.

In Gujarat Adani Port v. CC (2014) 46 GST 584 = 47 taxmann.com 154 = 309 ELT 120 (CESTAT), goods were received short by custodian (It is case of private port). Custodian informed the same to customs authorities immediately. It was held that custodian cannot be held liable for pilferage (as he never received the entire quantity of goods after unloading).

Woollen rags not having been proved to be textiles, demurrage payable. ICT Item 49 (4).

FACT: The petitioner-firm utilised woollen rags for manufacturing shoddy woollen yarn and blankets. The GOI permitted import of woollen rags and garment rags (rags from woven woollen fabrics and rags from knitted woollen material) and exempted woollen waste and rags from levy of customs duty by a notification dt. 20.4.1966. The importers have to claim the said exemption under Item 49(4) of Indian Customs Tariff read with the notification before clearing and consignment of woollen rags from the customs. Since 1966, the STC has been given monopoly in licences for importing woollen rags, which are not granted individually but allotted a quota on recommendation of the Textile Commissioner. The petitioners were allotted a quota of 37 bales of woollen hosiery rags which were imported from foreign suppliers by STC. The Customs Authorities carried out a visual inspection by taking samples, and later decided to have a chemical test. In spite of these two tests the Authorities decided to resort to the core-drilling test. On the basis of this the department held that the wool content of these bales was less than 50 per cent and therefore not eligible for exemption under the notification dt. 20.4.1966 and though clearance of goods was allowed they were charged to appropriate duty. The goods were kept in the sheds of the Port Trust of Bombay and it was not permitting clearance without payment of demurrage charges.

HELD: Exemption: Customs Authorities cannot rely upon trade advice and levy duty on the ground that the content was not according to the advice. Trade advice is not statutory and as such reliance cannot be placed on it. "The Exemption Notification dated April 20, 1966 totally exempted woollen wastes and woollen rags from the whole of the duty of customs leviable thereon. The Exemption Notification does not restrict the advantage only to those woollen wastes and woollen rags containing wool of more than 50%. In absence of any such provision in the Notification, it is not permissible for the Customs Authorities to levy duty on the imported woollen rags on the ground that the wool content was found less than 50 per cent. It is now well settled that the trade advice issued by the Government of India has no statutory force and it is not permissible for the Authorities exercising quasi judicial function to place reliance upon such trade advice to hold that the petitioners are liable for payment of duty."

2. Exemption: Physical and Chemical tests offer guidance and assistance only. "Merely because the different analysis show different conclusions it is not permissible to select that conclusion which suits the authorities to levy the duty. .........The procedure adopted by the Customs Authorities was entirely misconceived and cannot be sustained either in law or by principles of natural justice. In my judgment, the finding of the Customs Authorities that the import of woollen rags by the petitioners is not eligible for duty exemption is totally incorrect and deserves to be set aside. The petitioners ore entitled to the clearance without payment of any duty."

3. Detention Certificate: Demurrage charges to be paid to the Port Trust Authorities cannot be questioned even though the goods are not be cleared because of the insistence of the Customs Authorities for the payment of duty. Waiver available only during special examination of goods and a detention certificate issued accordingly. "......... exemption from payment of demurrage charges is available only during such period when the goods are detained for special examination. In the present case, the facts establish that the goods were detained by the Customs Authorities till end of May 1975 for special examination and it is abvious that the petitioners would not be liable to pay the demurrage charges to the Port Trust authorities till end of May 1975."

4. Classification: Woollen rags not being textiles demurrage, charges are to be paid accordingly, "In the present case, the question which arises is whether the expression 'textile' in Item No. 85 of the Scales of Rates would cover the woollen rags. In my judgment, it would not be possible to hold so. What was contemplated by Item No. 85 was textile or fabrics in its fuse form and not the woollen rags. ...the petitioners are liable to pay the demurrage charges computed by the Port Trust authorities according to the rates provided by Item No. 92 of the Scale of Rates."

This shall he the final order in these appeals."

3. Natural Justice: High Court's order not imposing any condition for safeguarding of interests of the Port Trust is erroneous since the Port Trust was not a party to the Writ Petition and since in the absence of a notice, would not have been able to recover full demurrage charges after the goods were cleared under Detention Certificates. "It is, however, to be observed that before compelling the Customs authorities to issue a Detention Certificate, the High Court should have issued notice as regards the demurrage charges recoverable by it under law. This was necessary because on the production of the Detention Certificate issued by the Customs authorities the Port Trust was under an obligation to permit the clearance of the goods without payment of full demurrage charges. If ultimately the party concerned is found to be at fault and becomes liable to pay the full demurrage charges the Port Trust may no: he in a position to recover such full demurrage charges from the party concerned, since it would have no longer any lien as provided by section 59 of the Act on the goods which are already cleared. The Port Trust being a body corporate constituted under the Act is entitled to be heard by the Court before any order which affects its interests prejudicially is passed. ......The orders passed by the High Court in the proceedings to which the Port Trust was not a party which had the effect of prejudicially affecting the interests of the Port Trust would. not be binding on it in view of the violation of the principles of natural justice. The High Court erred in not imposing any condition on the 1st Respondent for protecting the interests of the Port Trust even in the Writ Petition to which it was a party. The impugned orders are contrary to the public notice issued by the Customs authorities as well as the rules of the Port Trust."

As per the required procedures, these imported raw materials are kept in customs warehouses and are then cleared from warehouses after payment of duty. As per the current practice, the company is not creating any provision of custom duty for the goods lying at customs warehouse. Is the company's treatment in accordance with AS-2/ICDS-II(Revised)/section 145A?

Answer: No. As required by para 6 of AS-2/Para 4 of ICDS-II, the cost of inventories should comprise of all costs incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition. As per the present laws and regulations and as per the present facts and circumstances, the customs duty is a cost which has to be incurred by the entity to bring the inventory in India. Further as per section 12 of Customs Act 1962, custom duty shall be levied when the goods are imported into India. Further section 2(27) of the Customs Act 1962 provides that India includes territorial waters of India. Accordingly custom duty liability is incurred once the goods enter territorial waters of India. However, the payment of custom duty is done afterwards. Accordingly, the company should have created a provision for the custom duty for the goods lying at customs warehouse and included customs duty in the cost of the inventory of imported raw materials lying at bonded warehouses. [The Chartered Accountant Journal, Volume 58, No. 11, May, 2010]

Case Study 2.17.4 : A company is in the business of manufacturing of general products. It makes certain percentage of its total sales as export sales. As per the current regime regarding export incentives, the company can import certain quantity of inputs (without any duty) provided the inputs are used to manufacture finished goods to be exported. The company gets licenses for importing inputs without any duty. The company is not able to use its licenses against import of inputs because there is shortage in the international market. The price of the inputs is costlier in the domestic market.

The company managed to get a domestic supplier for the required inputs and entered into an agreement with the domestic supplier. As per the agreement, the company will transfer certain quantum of its licenses to the domestic supplier and shall receive similar quantum of inputs at a price ('Deemed export price') which is lower than had the company imported inputs from international market without paying any duty. As at the year end, the company decided to account for the unutilized licenses as follows:-

- Recognise the difference between domestic input price and deemed export price as the value of unutilized licenses (import entitlements).

Whether the company's treatment for year-end unused import licenses is correct ?

Answer: The treatment followed is not correct. No value should be ascribed to the year-end unused import licenses. Cost of purchases should be recorded based on actual purchase price. A portion of the deductions from purchase price of inventory cannot be carved out and shown as other income. This is not permitted as per AS-2. Providing a value for import licenses just because a license is transferred to domestic supplier (for reducing input prices) does not result in creating a value for the unused license. [EAC opinion Query 29 Volume 27 Opinion finalised on 30 Jan 2008]

Case Study 2.17.5: A company is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of iron and steel products. It stores the products at its stockyards. The handling of stock at stockyards is done through handling agents. The company also uses services of consignment agents for the places it does not have its own stockyards. The stockyards are far from manufacturing facilities and, hence, goods are first loaded, then unloaded at stockyards and then are stacked at the stockyards. These activities lead to transportation, loading and unloading expenses, stacking and segregating expenses at stockyards. For the purpose of valuing finished goods at stockyard, transportation costs, loading & unloading expenses, stacking and segregating expenses are added to the cost of production. The company terms the transportation costs as 'freight outwards' and loading and unloading, stacking and segregating expenses as 'selling and distribution' expenses. Another viewpoint is that these expenses should not be included while valuing stock at stockyards because these expenses are freight outwards and selling and distribution expenses. Whether the company's accounting treatment is correct ?

Answer : In the present case the company should firstly use the nomenclatures of the costs correctly. The nomenclatures 'freight outwards' and 'selling and distribution expenses' are not correct considering the elements of the costs highlighted above.

Section 10(48A) has been introduced with retrospective effect from assessment year 2016-17 to provide that the following income shall be exempt from tax:

The buyer is a person resident in India;

The rationale behind the amendment is explained in the Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2016 as follows:

"The Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL) is in the process of setting up underground storage facility for storage of crude oil as part of strategic reserves. The maintenance of strategic reserves is in India's national interest and ensures price stability for Indian oil companies. The filling cost of such facility entails huge financial burden. The Government has explored the possibility of meeting a substantial part of the financial burden through participation of private players including foreign national oil companies (NOCs) and multinational companies (MNCs) storing and selling crude oil from outside India. However, the storage of crude oil by NOCs/MNCs and its sale in India would create tax liability for these entities.

In order to achieve neutrality in terms of taxation to encourage the NOCs MNCs to store their crude oil in India and to build up strategic oil reserves, it is proposed to amend the provisions of section 10 of the Act to provide that any income accruing or arising to a foreign company on account of storage of crude oil in a facility in India and sale of crude oil therefrom to any person resident in India shall not be included in the total income,

… Since the storage of oil is expected to begin in the current financial year, this exemption would be available from the previous year 2015-16, i.e. assessment year 2016-17."

19.1-1 Difference between sections 13 and 23(1)

Difference in sections 13 and 23(1) of Customs Act can be summarised as follows :

| Section 13 | Section 23(1) |
| --- | --- |
| Section 13 deals with pilferage. | Section 23(1) deals with loss or destruction of goods, except pilferage. |
| No duty is payable at all under section 13, but liability revives of duty if goods are restored. | Duty is payable under section 23(1), but it is remitted by Assistant Commissioner of Cus- toms. Thus, unless remitted, duty has to be paid under section 23(1). |
| Importer does not have to prove pilferage. | Burden of proof is on importer to prove loss or destruction. |
| Pilferage should be before order for clear- ance is made. | Loss or destruction can be any time before clearance. |
| Loss must be only due to pilferage. | Loss or destruction may be due to fire, accident etc. but not pilferage. e.g. loss by leakage is covered under section 23. |
| Under section 13, normally duty is not paid. However, if duty is paid before examination of goods, refund can be claimed if goods are found to be pilfered during examination but before order for clearance is made. | Under section 23(1), if duty is paid, then refund can be obtained only if remission is granted by Customs Authorities. Thus, remis- sion under section 23(1) is at the discretion of Custom Authorities. [Of course, the discretion has to be exercised judiciously]. |
| Section 13 is not applicable for warehoused goods. | Section 23(1) is applicable for warehoused goods also. [as goods transferred to warehouse are not 'cleared for home consumption']. |

HEADNOTE: Section 44B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Profits And Gains of Shipping Business in Case of Non-Residents Computation Of - Assessment year 1986-87 - Assessee, a non-resident company, was engaged in business of operation of ships - Whether detention/demurrage charges received by assessee for retention of containers beyond agreed period could be treated as on account of carriage of goods so as to be includible in total income of assessee- Held, no

FACT: The assessee, a non-resident company, was engaged in the business of operation of ships. For the assessment year 1986-87 the assessing officer held that the entire receipts from detention/demurrage were the income of the assessee and therefrom allowed deduction of 5 per cent as expenses on estimate basis. On appeal, the assessee contended before the Commissioner (Appeals) that the detention/demurrage charges were part and parcel of the carriage of goods within the meaning of section 44B. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee's claim and directed the assessing officer that like freight only 7.5 per cent of the detention/demurrage charges should be treated as profits of the business of operation of ships.

On further appeal by the revenue:

HELD: Receipt from detention/demurrage, in the present case, was nonetheless during the course of the business of operation of ships and, therefore, even if it was treated as income of the assessee, for argument sake, it could not be assessed under sections 28 to 43A. The provisions of sections 30 to 43C are not attracted for computation of income in respect of these receipts. The assessing officer, therefore, committed an error in treating the receipts from demurrage as income independent of carriage charges and further committed an error in estimating the expenses at 5 per cent. At the best, he could have treated those receipts as amount on account of carriage.

However, as laid down in CIT v. Pestonji Bhicajee [1977] 107 ITR 837 (Guj.), dead freight is an agreed sum to be paid in respect of space not filled according to charter or damages provided for by a charter, in the event of the freighter not loading a full cargo. It has been held by the High Court that 'dead freight' cannot be treated as payment made on account of carriage of goods in a ship. That was considered with reference to section 172, a provision analogous to section 44B. In context with the same, i.e., section 172 the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Gosalia Shipping (P.) Ltd. [1978] 113 ITR 307 held that the amount which the time charterers were required to pay to the owners of the ship was not payable on account of the carriage of goods but was payable on account of the use and hire of the ship. In this view of the matter, the detention/demurrage charges received for retention of the containers beyond the agreed period could not be treated as on account of the carriage of goods.

Accordingly, no part of the impugned receipts could be included in the total income of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation of imported goods - Duty rate - Relevant date is date of entry inwards of the vessel, even if Bill of Entry has been presented before that date - Ultra vires--Section 15 is not ultra vires, as it lays down a procedure, and following that procedure cannot be termed arbitrary. Discrimination--Different rates of duty for different categories of importers are not violative of fundamental rights. Constitution or India: Art. 14

FACT: The petitioners imported a consignment of edible oils. The vessel carrying the goods approached Bombay and made its "prior entry" on July 4, 1981. It actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay on July 11, 1981, at which time the rate of duty applicable to the petitioners' goods was 12.5%. As there was no berth available and the vessel was under heavy pressure from the parties whose goods she was carrying, she left Bombay for Karachi for unloading other cargo intended for that port. The vessel returned after discharging the Karachi cargo, arrived in the Port of Bombay on July 23, 1981 and waited for a berth. On August 4, 1981 she was allowed to berth and the Customs Authorities made the "final entry" on that date. The petitioners contend that when the vessel made its original journey to Bombay and was waiting in the waters of the Port they presented the Bill of Entry to the Customs authorities on July 9, 1981, and that the Bill of Entry was accepted by the Import Department and an order was passed by the Customs Officer on the Bill of Entry on July 18, 1981 directing the examination of the consignment. The Customs authorities imposed duty on the edible oils at the rate of 150% on the footing that the import was made on July 31, 1981, the date of "Inward Entry". The case of the petitioners is that the rate of duty leviable on the import should be that ruling on July 11, 1981, when the vessel actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay, and that but for the fact that a berth was not available the vessel would have discharged its cargo at Bombay, and would not have left that Port and proceeded to Karachi to return to Bombay towards the end of July, 1981. Alternatively, the case of the petitioners is that even if the rate of customs duty found leviable on their goods is 150 per cent, such levy is unconstitutional and void as it violates of Article 14 of the Constitution, inasmuch as customs duty at 5 per cent only was levied on the STC for similar imports. The petitioners have also challenged the validity of section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 under which the rate of duty and tariff valuation are determined.

HELD: Duty rate--Relevant date is date of entry inwards of the vessel, even if Bill of Entry has been presented before that date. "It is urged......that the import of goods must be deemed to have taken place on 11 July, 1981, when the ship originally arrived in Bombay Port and registered itself. The rate of customs duty prevailing on that date was 12.5 per cent..............The provisions of section 15 are clear in themselves. The date on which a Bill of Entry is presented under section 46 is, in the case of goods entered for home consumption, the relevant date for determining the rate of duty and tariff valuation. Where the Bill of Entry is presented before the date of Entry Inwards of the vessel, the Bill of Entry is deemed to have been presented on the date of such Entry Inwards. .............In the present case, "the date of inwards entry" is mentioned as 31 July, 1981. In the absence of anything else, we may take it that the entry was recorded on that date itself. Accordingly, the rate of import duty and the tariff valuation shall be that in force on 31 July, 1981. The contention of the petitioners that the rate of import duty and tariff valuation will be that ruling on 11 July, 1981 cannot be sustained and is rejected."

HEADNOTE: Section 57 read with section 58 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Appointing public warehouse - Baggage - Demurrage--Airport authorities not entitled to claim any demurrage in view of public notice 29/86 specifying that demurrage charges will not be recovered for warehousing baggage detained by the Customs Authorities

FACT: The petitioners are citizens of Nepal. Some of their goods which were being transhipped from Singapore arrived as unaccompanied baggage at the IGI Airport for onward shipment to Kathmandu. Being under the impression that this importation was improper, the Customs Authorities confiscated these goods under section 117 of the Customs Act. The confiscated goods were stored in the customs warehouse of IGI Airport. After the completion of adjudication proceedings, the Deputy Collector of Customs permitted transshipment of the seized goods. The petitioners have filed these appeals being aggrieved by the refusal of the Airport Authorities to release the goods unless the demurrage charges were paid. It is their contention that this claim was illegal as the goods had been stored in the warehouse upon the insistence of the Customs Authorities and not the petitioners. Moreover, in view of the detention certificate issued by the Assistant Collector of Customs, the respondents were bound to waive the demurrage charges.

HELD: Airport Authorities are not entitled to claim any demurrage charges from the petitioners--respondents bound by Public Notice 29/86 which specifies that demurrage charges will not be recovered for warehousing baggage detained by the Customs Authorities. "For the purpose of waiver or remission of the warehouse charges customs authorities have to certify that goods were not cleared up to a certain period for them to make enquiries under the Act. This certification is the detention certificate. The Public Notice 29/86 and the Regulations and guidelines of the Airports Authority, the first respondent, talk of detention certificate to be issued by the customs authorities. Reference may well be made to section 63 of the Act falling under Chapter IX dealing with warehousing. Under sub-section (1) of section 63, the owner of any warehoused goods shall pay to the warehouse-keeper rent and warehouse charges at the rates fixed under any law for the time being in force or where no rates are so fixed, at such rates as may be fixed by the Collector of Customs. We have seen above, rates for warehousing baggage have not been fixed by the first respondent and Public Notice 29/86 in effect specifies under clause (vii) that charges for warehousing baggage for the period it is detained will not be charged by the Airports Authority, the first respondent. ........We are, therefore, of the opinion that the first respondent is not entitled to charge any demurrage in all these cases and the petitioners are entitled to have their goods transhipped to Nepal without payment of any ground rent/demurrage charges."
