Per P. Venkatarama Reddi, J. : 23. I am in agreement with my learned sister that without entering into the merits of the contentions advanced, the Revenue's appeal is liable to be dismissed in the light of the Circular dated 14-8-1991 issued by Central Board of Excise and Customs which is traceable to the power conferred on the Board by Section 151-A of the Customs Act. The purpose of this separate opinion is only to highlight certain doubts I have entertained as to the correctness of the proposition laid down in the two Dhiren Chemical Industries cases - one decided by the Constitution Bench and the other by a three Judge Bench. The absence of reasoning in both these decisions has aggravated my doubts and made me ponder over the possible implications of the said judgments. Hence I felt impelled to express the thoughts passing in may mind and my prima facie views, hoping that the legal position will perspicuously be laid down by a Constitution Bench sooner or later. For the time being, I have refrained from persuading my learned Sister to refer the matter to a larger Bench as the decision in the instant case need not rest on the principle enunciated in the said two decisions.

24. I have no reservations in accepting the principle that the circulars issued by the Board under Section 151(A) of the Customs Act or Section 37(B) of the Central Excise Act are generally binding on the Revenue. Normally, the Instructions issued by the superior authorities on administrative side cannot fetter the exercise of quasi judicial power and the statutory authority invested with such power has to act independently in arriving at a decision under the Act vide : Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Hyderabad [(1970) 1 SCC 795]. However, when there is a statutory mandate to observe and follow the orders and instructions of the Board in regard to specified matters, that mandate has to be complied with. It is not open to the adjudicating authority to deviate from those orders or instructions which the statute enjoins that it should follow. If any order is passed contrary to those instructions the order is liable to be struck down on that very ground. That is what has been held in some of the cases referred to by my learned sister. Extending this principle which flows from the statutory provision contained in Section 151(A) of the Customs Act or a pari-materia provision in other fiscal enactments, this Court also held that it is not open to the department to file an appeal against the order passed in conformity with the circular. To this extent I have no difficulty in understanding the rationale of the decisions of this Court leaving apart for the time being the decisions in which a somewhat different note was struck. However, I am unable to reconcile myself to the view that even after the highest Court settles the law on the subject, the view expressed by the Central Board on the same point of law should still hold the field until and unless it is revoked.

25. As is evident from Section 151-A the Board is empowered to issue orders or instructions in order to ensure uniformity in the classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty. The need to issue such instructions arises when there is a doubt or ambiguity in relation to those matters. The possibility of varying views being taken by the customs officials while administering the Act may bring about uncertainty and confusion. In order to avoid this situation, Section 151A has been enacted on the same lines as Section 37(A) (sic-37B) of the Central Excise Act. The apparent need to issue such circulars is felt when there is no authoritative pronouncement of the Court on the subject. Once the relevant issue is decided by the Court at the highest level, the very basis and substratum of the circular disappears. The law laid down by this Court will ensure uniformity in the decisions at all levels. By an express constitutional provision, the law declared by the Supreme Court is made binding on all the Courts within the territory of India (vide Article 141). Proprio vigore the law is binding on all the tribunals and authorities. Can it be said that even after the law is declared by the Supreme Court the adjudicating authority should still give effect to the circular issued by the Board ignoring the legal position laid down by this Court? Even after the legal position is settled by the highest Court of the land, should be customs authority continue to give primacy to the circular of the Board? Should Section 151 (A) be taken to such extremities? Was it enacted for such purpose? Does it not amount to transgression of constitutional mandate while adhering to a statutory mandate? Even after the reason and rationale underlying the circular disappears, is it obligatory to continue to follow the circular? These are the questions which puzzle me and these are the conclusions which follows if the observations of this Court in the two cases of Dhiren Chemical Industries are taken to their logical conclusion.

IAAI/Port Trustees/CWC are acting as custodians on behalf of Customs Department. However, they can charge demurrage from consignees as per their own regulations, even when goods are detained for customs assessment purposes and customs issues detention certificate.

2. The appellants are M/s. Shine Petroleum Pvt. Ltd., Chennai and M/s. Elf Gas India Ltd., Bangalore. The first appellant imported Superior Kerosene Oil known as SKO and the second appellant imported Commercial Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG). The issue in both the appeals is one and the same and therefore, we are taking up the matter for issue of a common order.

3. The appellants have a CIF Contract with the foreign supplier. The goods are loaded in vessels and thereafter they reach the port for unloading. A minimum time is given for unloading before which the goods have to be unloaded and this time is known as lay time. If there is a delay in discharge of cargo, due to various reasons, demurrage is charged by the carrier to the supplier of the goods. In turn the supplier collects this demurrage charges from the importers who are the appellants. The point at issue is whether the demurrage charges are to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for customs duty purposes.

4. Revenue proceeded against the appellants in both the cases by way of issue of show cause notice for inclusion of the demurrage charges in the assessable value of the goods imported. In the case of the first appellant, the Adjudicating Authority confirmed a demand of Rs. 79,73,330/-. Interest to the tune of Rs. 28,98,945/- was demanded. Further, a penalty of Rs. 1,08,72,275/- was imposed. The period involved in the case of first appellant is from May 2003 to November 2003. As regards the second appellant, the Commissioner confirmed the duty demand of Rs. 20,38,610/- and imposed equal penalty under Section 114A of the Customs Act. The period involved in the case of second appellant is from October 1999 to November 2004. The appellants strongly challenge the impugned orders of the Commissioner. Therefore, they have come before this Tribunal for relief.

5. Shri G. Shiva Dass, learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the appellants and Smt. Sudha Koka, learned Departmental representative for the Revenue.

6. We heard both sides. The learned advocate took us through the relevant statutory provisions and made the point that the issue of includability of demurrage charges to the assessable value of the imported goods has been exhaustively dealt with in the Tribunal's decision in the case of IOC Ltd. and Others Vs. CC, Calcutta - 2000 (41) RLT 251 (CEGAT-LB)=2000 (122) ELT 615, which was affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2004 (61) RLT 2 (SC)=2004 (165) ELT 257 (SC). The department went in against the above decision by Review Petition which was also dismissed by Apex Court in 2005 (186) ELT A199. The learned advocate pointed out that once there is a CIF contract which includes the freight, no further addition can be made to the freight in respect of the CIF contract. He relied on the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Ispat Industries Ltd. Vs. CC - 2006 (77) RLT 1 (SC)=2006-TIOL-127-SC-Cus. Further, he relied on the Board's Circular dated 14.8.1991, according to which demurrage is not to be included in the assessable value of the imported goods. The idea in all these circulars and decisions is that the demurrage cannot be considered as cost of transportation. It is completely different from the cost of transportation. The learned advocate took us through the decision in the case of IOC and said that the assessable value is value of the goods which are ordinarily sold. He emphasized the word ordinary and said that the demurrage is paid only when there is delay in unloading of the goods and the situation in which there is delay in unloading of goods is not an ordinary situation but in fact it is an extra ordinary situation. In view of this, he submitted that the Tribunal held that demurrage is not includable in the assessable value and this decision has been upheld by the Supreme Court.

Regulation 6 of the Cargo Regulations fixes the responsibilities of a customs cargo service provider, defined under regulation 2(1)(b). The proforma fourth respondent, by virtue of the concession agreement, comes within the purview of customs cargo service provider and is, therefore, bound by such responsibilities. The Cargo Regulations, which contain the impugned regulation 6(1)(l), derives its existence from section 141(2) read with section 157 of the Customs Act. Those provisions show that the Central Board of Excise and Customs is empowered to prescribe the responsibilities of persons engaged in the activities of receiving, storing, delivering, dispatching or otherwise handling of imported or export goods in a customs area. [Para 10]

Undoubtedly DIAL's functions in relation to operating, maintaining, developing, designing, constructing, upgrading, modernizing, financing and managing of the IGI Airport as conferred by the agreement dated 4-4-2006, except those functions pertaining to the cargo terminal which have been sub-contracted to the proforma fourth respondent by virtue of the concession agreement, are governed by the AAI Act. Nevertheless, the obligations of the customs cargo service provider/proforma fourth respondent is governed by the Cargo Regulations. The court is aware that the Supreme Court in the cases of International & Airports Authority of India v. Grand Slam International 1995 taxmann.com 344 (SC) and Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd. v. C.L. Jain Woolen Mills 2001 (129) ELT 561 (SC) has observed that there was no provision in the Customs Act empowering the customs authorities to direct the custodian of goods to waive the demurrage charges on the goods. However, these decisions were pronounced before introduction of sub-section (2) to section 141 of the Customs Act, which later gave way to the notification of the Cargo Regulations. Therefore, the petitioner's argument that the second respondent exceeded the power delegated to it by the Customs Act must fail. [Para 11]

The contention of the petitioner that the impugned regulation 6(1)(l) violates article 14 of the Constitution of India, as it has no nexus with the object sought to be achieved, is insubstantial because the Cargo Regulations were enacted for the purpose of prescribing the responsibilities of persons engaged in the activities of receiving, storing, delivering, dispatching or otherwise handling of imported or export goods in a customs area and the impugned regulation is as such an obligation cast upon the persons involved in the said activities. DIAL also urged that the regulation contravene article 19(1)(g) inasmuch as it places a blanket ban on the charge of demurrage by the custodian of goods in case of detention, confiscation or seizure of goods by customs. However, such restriction is covered under the premise of article 19(6), by which reasonable restrictions in the interest of general public may be imposed on the right under article 19(1)(g). Investigation being an integral part of working of the Customs Department, the consignments detained by the customs authorities or other investigating agencies cannot be cleared during investigation particularly if such cases involve trade policy, human safety and security, security of State, etc. It is with these considerations that the impugned regulation was included in the Cargo Regulations and it should be viewed in the light of the object with which it has been framed. Therefore, the allegation that the impugned regulation violates article 19(1)(g) does not survive. [Para 12]

The Supreme Court in the case of Maharashtra State Board of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education v. Paritosh Bhupesh Kumar [1984] 4 SCC 27 has upheld the validity of a regulation made to carry out the provisions of the Act. It was held in that case that the regulations had to be judged on a threefold tests namely: (1) whether the provisions of the regulations fall within the scope and ambit of the power conferred on the delegate, (2) whether the regulations made are to any extent inconsistent with the provisions of the enabling Act, and (3) whether they infringe any of the fundamental rights or other restrictions or limitations imposed by the Constitution. In the instant case, the first test is answered in the affirmative and the second and third tests are answered in the negative, which would imply that the Cargo Regulations is well within the scope and ambit of its parent Act, i.e., the Customs Act and is also consistent with the same and does not, in any way, violate constitutional provisions. [Para 13]

The court acknowledges that section 151A of the Customs Act places an obligation upon the officers of customs to follow the orders, instructions and directions of the Central Board of Excise and Customs, as far as they relate to any prohibition, restriction or procedure for import or export of goods. [Para 14]

The circular dated 14-8-1999 in no uncertain terms excludes demurrage from the assessable value. In the light of the judicial principles enunciated earlier, it was not open to the appellant to either issue the show-cause notice or contend otherwise. The demand based on an assessable value inclusive of demurrage could not be sustained as long as the circular remained operative and as long as the decisions on the issue remain good law. [Para 13] The submission of the appellant that the respondent had not acted on the basis of the circular and, therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel did not apply is misconceived. The circulars issued by the CBDT under the Income-tax Act and the CBEC under section 37B of the Central Excise Act have been held to be binding primarily on the basis of the language of the statutory provisions buttressed by the need of the adjudicating officers to maintain uniformity in the levy of tax/duty throughout the country. [Para 14]

The stand of the appellant that the Supreme Court had taken the view that demurrage was includible in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) both in the adjudication order and before the Tribunal appears to have been abandoned in the written notes of submission. Apart from the decision of the Constitution Bench in Collector of Central Excise v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 143 ELT 19 on the binding nature of the circulars, in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) the decision was on landing charges. It did not construe the 1988 Rules. The circular on the other hand was issued on a re-examination of the issue in the light of the GATT Valuation principles as incorporated in the 1988 Rules. [Para 17]

Therefore, demurrage was wrongly included by the adjudicating officer in the assessable value contrary to the directive of the CBEC at a time when the circular had not been withdrawn. [Para 18]

PER P. VENKATARAMA REDDI, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW) : The revenue's appeal is liable to be dismissed in the light of the circular dated 14-8-1991 issued by the CBEC which is traceable to the power conferred on the Board by section 151A of the Customs Act. The purpose of this separate opinion is only to highlight certain doubts as to the correctness of the proposition laid down in the two Dhiren Chemical Industries' cases (supra) - one decided by the Constitution Bench and the other by a three Judge Bench. [Para 20]

The circulars issued by the Board under section 151A of the Customs Act or section 37B of the Central Excise Act are generally binding on the revenue. However, when there is a statutory mandate to observe and follow the orders and instructions of the Board in regard to specified matters, that mandate has to be complied with. It is not open to the adjudicating authority to deviate from those orders or instructions which the statute enjoins that it should follow. If any order is passed contrary to those instructions the order is liable to be struck down on that very ground. Extending this principle which flows from the statutory provision contained in section 151A of the Customs Act or a pari materia provision in other fiscal enactments, the Supreme Court also held that it is not open to the department to file an appeal against the order passed in conformity with the circular. To this extent one has no difficulty in understanding the rationale of the decisions of the Supreme Court leaving apart for the time being the decisions in which a somewhat different note was struck. However, one is unable to reconcile to the view that even after the highest Court settles the law on the subject, the view expressed by the Central Board on the same point of law should still hold the field until and unless it is revoked. [Para 21]

As is evident from section 151A the Board is empowered to issue orders or instructions in order to ensure uniformity in the classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty. The need to issue such instructions arises when there is a doubt or ambiguity in relation to those matters. The possibility of varying views being taken by the customs officials while administering the Act may bring about uncertainty and confusion. In order to avoid this situation, section 151A has been enacted on the same lines as section 37A of the Central Excise Act. The apparent need to issue such circulars is left when there is no authoritative pronouncement of the Court on the subject. Once the relevant issue is decided by the Court at the highest level, the very basis and substratum of the circular disappears. The law laid down by the Supreme Court will ensure uniformity in the decisions at all levels. By an express constitutional provision, the law declared by the Supreme Court is made binding on all the Courts within the territory of India (vide Article 141), Proprio vigore the law is binding on all the Tribunals and authorities. [Para 22]

HEADNOTE: Section 44B, read with section 172, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Shipping business in case of non-residents - Petitioners were mine owners and exporters of iron and manganese ore, who entered into export agreements with foreign buyers who sent their ships either owned by them or chartered by them - It was provided in contract that for detention of ships for unforeseen circumstance petitioners had to bear demurrage charges and pay same to owner or charterer of ships - Whether payments of such demurrage could fall under section 44B or 172(2) - Held, no

FACT: The petitioners were mine owners mining, among other things, manganese and iron ores, which they exported. The petitioners entered into an agreement with a foreign buyer to supply on credit basis iron and manganese ore and the foreign buyers sent their ships either owned by them or chartered by them for carriage of the goods. Contracts provided that in case of detention of a ship in the port for unforeseen reasons, petitioners had to bear the demurrage charges and pay the same to the owner or charterer of the ship. Payments for such demurrage were being paid with the approval of the RBI through the regular bank channels. In February, 1988, the first respondent - Dy. Controller of RBI - issued a Circular dated 22-2-1988 to all the exporters requiring them to obtain income-tax clearance certificate for remittance of demurrage payments. By yet another communication dated 11-10-1988, all the exporters had been informed by the first respondent that all demurrage amounts payable in respect of foreign vessels attract Indian Income-tax. Therefore, the exporters were advised to ensure that all applications for remittances towards demurrage payable to foreign vessels should be duly supported by income-tax clearance certificates or documentary evidence that tax was withheld along with a no-objection certificate from the department.

On writ, the petitioners disputed the circular instructions and prayed that these be quashed.

HELD: There is this difference between section 44B and section 172. In section 44B no procedure for assessment and collection of tax is provided. The use of non obstante clause refers only to sections 28 to 43A and not to the other provisions of the Act as contemplated under sub-section (1) of section 172. Section 28 and the following sub-sections up to 43A are to be found under the heading - D - 'Profits and gains of business or profession' in Chapter IV of the Act. In other words, income from shipping accrued or deemed to have accrued to a non-resident shipowner or charterer falls outside the scope of trade and business normally so understood. The incidence of tax under section 44B is on a non-resident engaged in the business of operation of ships owned or chartered by him or it, and if such income constituted the amounts earned on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from any port in India and the amount so received or deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods etc.

In contrast section 172 does not refer to a non-resident assessee. It only refers to levy and recovery of tax in case of any ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident which carries passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from a port in India. If this difference is borne in mind, then the want of special procedure for levy and collection under section 44B becomes patent and obvious. In the result, a non-resident engaged in shipping business subject to the qualification of carrying goods, passengers, livestock, mail or goods etc., being an assessee shall be assessed in accordance with section 143 and not in accordance with the procedure prescribed for a non-resident shipowner or charterer covered by section 172(1) and (2) of the Act. Therefore, the inevitable conclusion is that the shipowner or charterer in section 172(1) is not an assessee as defined in clause (7) of section 2 of the Act.

A person who is required to be covered and controlled by the provisions contained in section 172 is, therefore, not an assessee. He is a mere shipowner who is a non-resident or a charterer of a ship, also a non-resident. In other words, the heading under H in Chapter XV assumes some significance in interpreting section 172 of the Act. The Court is bound to take notice of it. That heading is as follows:

"H — Profits of non-residents from occasional shipping business." [Emphasis supplied]

Section 141, read with sections 45 and 49, of the Customs Act, 1962 and Regulation 6 of the Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 - Clearance of Imported Goods - Demurrage - Custodian demanded demurrage even for period during which goods were seized by department and could not be cleared - Department issued certificate favouring assessee that demurrage could not be levied - Assessee claimed that said certificate of department had overriding effect under Regulation 6 of Handling of Cargo in Customs Areas Regulations, 2009 (HCCAR) - Custodian claimed that it was governed only by Policy for Waiver of Demurrage Charges notified by Airports Authority of India (AAI) - HELD : HCCAR Regulations themselves stipulate that they are subject to any law for time being in force and, therefore, HCCAR and directions of customs authorities thereunder do not override 'Policy for Waiver' framed by AAI - In cases where on conclusion of adjudication proceedings there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by customs authorities demurrage for period when goods were seized, detained or earlier confiscated would be waived as per Policy of Waiver - However, in any other case, demurrage would not be waived for period of seizure, etc. and provisional release order would be subject to furnishing of bond and/or security that in case any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by customs authorities, importer would pay demurrage charges [Para 50] [In favour of revenue]Customs : Customs Authorities cannot order custodian to waive demurrage for period of seizure/detention, etc.; waiver is grantable only if on conclusion of adjudication, there is no imposition of any fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning by customs authorities

HEADNOTE: II. Section 9, read with sections 40(a)(ia), 172, 194C and 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India [Business connection] - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee-company reimbursed demurrage charges for delayed loading, payable by foreign buyers to shipowners, as assessee had to export goods on FOB basis, which was disallowed under section 40(a)(ia) for non-deduction of tax at source - Whether, such payment was in nature of expenditure incurred for sales in view of contract with foreign buyer - Held, yes - Whether, since Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) provides that no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to a non-resident, through or from operations confined to purchase of goods in India for export, amount of demurrage could not be deemed as income in hands of foreign buyer, and no disallowance could be made under section 40(a)(ia) - Held, yes [Para 33.1] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company remitted the demurrage amount for delayed loading, payable by the buyers of its iron ore to the ship owners as the assessee had to export goods on FOB basis. The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount under section 40(a)(i) for remittance without deduction of tax at source. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the disallowance.

HELD: The assessee has paid the demurrage charges to the non-resident in respect of delay in loading the ship. The sum was reimbursed by the assessee to the foreign buyer to compensate the foreign buyer for paying demurrage to the ship owner when ship came to Indian port and the assessee could not load the goods on to the ship within the limited time period. The export sales were made to the foreign Pakistani buyer on FOB basis. In view of the contract with the Pakistani buyer the assessee was bound to compensate the Pakistani buyer in respect of demurrage paid by the Pakistani buyer to the ship owner. This payment can be regarded to be the expenditure incurred by the assessee for the sale of the goods and was not akin to price deduction due to fault in product/service and was equivalent to discount/rebate which can be adjusted against the sale price. [Para 31]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of the goods in India for the purpose of export. The non-resident buyer got the compensation towards the demurrage incurred through the operation which was confined to the purchase of the goods, i.e. in relation to the ship which it had arranged for taking the delivery of the goods from the assessee/seller from India. Therefore, this income cannot be deemed to accrue or arise in India in the hands of the foreign buyer, and therefore, it cannot be taxable in India and is not liable to tax deduction at source. On this basis, no disallowance can be made under section 40(a)(ia), and accordingly, the disallowance is deleted. [Para 32]

From a perusal of the Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995, it is apparently clear that the provisions of sections 194C and 195 relating to tax deduction at source are not applicable where the provisions of section 172, relating to shipping business are applicable. The circular issued by the CBDT is binding on the department. In view of the circular, the assessee was not obliged to deduct TDS on the payment made as demurrage charges and the demurrage charges are also liable to be taxed under section 172. The assessee, since, is not liable to deduct tax at source, no question arises for making any disallowance under section 40(a)(i). [Para 33]

HEADNOTE: Section 44B of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 8 of Model OECD Convention - Non-resident - Shipping business of (Reimbursement of expenses) - Assessee engaged in business of refining crude oil, entered into contracts with non-resident for supply of equipment, designs and drawings and project management and supervision contract - Demurrage charges incurred by non-resident on behalf of assessee were reimbursed - Said charges were brought to tax under section 44B - Whether in present case, both conditions envisaged by sub-section (1) of section 44B were not fulfilled and, thus, section 44B was not applicable - Held, yes [Paras 4  5] [In favour of assessee]IT: Section 44B could not be invoked in case of demurrage charges reimbursed by assessee to non-resident for import of crude oil

FACT: Assessee engaged in business of refining crude oil, entered into contracts with non-resident for supply of equipment, designs and drawings and project management and supervision contract. Demurrage charges incurred by non-resident on behalf of assessee were reimbursed.

Said charges were brought to tax under section 44B.

HELD: The case of the Department is that the Assessee has remitted/ paid the amount for design and drawing contracts. It is in such situation and the facts peculiar to the present case, firstly, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer was in error in applying both Section 44B and Section 195. The facts as set out are not found to be so by both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal. In fact the question of law arises out of payment of demurrage. That is reimbursed to the supplier of crude oil. It is in the nature of reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal found that this reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee cannot be brought within sub-section (1) of Section 44B. That is special provision for computing the profits and gains of shipping business in the case of a non-resident. That envisages the profits and gains of business of operation of ships. The sum to be covered by this provision should be of the nature referred to therein. In the present case, what has been paid is the sum for reimbursing the expenses incurred on behalf of the Assessee by a non-resident. The amount referred to in sub-section (1) of Section 44B and which are deemed to be profits and gains of the business of operation of ships chargeable to tax under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" shall be the amount firstly, paid or payable, whether in or out of India, to the Assessee or to any person on his behalf on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port in India and secondly, received or deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the Assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port outside India. [Para 4]

In the present case, the finding of fact is that both conditions envisaged by sub-section (1) of Section 44B are not fulfilled. The provision has been invoked in case of reimbursement of demurrage charges paid or reimbursed by Assessee for import of crude oil. It is such a finding of fact which is recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) and which has been confirmed by the Tribunal in the impugned order. The reasons assigned in Tribunal's order would, therefore, go to show that the view taken is in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case at hand. The view taken, therefore, is possible one. It cannot be termed, by any stretch of imagination, as perverse or vitiated by error of law apparent on the face of the record. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 172 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Non-resident - Shipping business of - Whether demurrage payable to non-resident owner of charterer of ship on account of delay in loading goods sold to non-resident would not be taxable - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioners entered into an agreement to sell ore to foreign buyer. The agreement was in the nature of FOB contract. The ships were chartered by the foreign buyer of ore for the purpose of conveying the ores purchased from the seller. The seller was paid price at the rate specified in the agreement and the quantity of the ore was quantified with reference to their loading into the ship. In case there was delay in loading, the seller had to pay demurrage and similarly in case time was saved in loading, the seller was entitled to receive dispatch money. The ITO held that this demurrage was essentially an extended freight payable towards the carriage of the goods and was taxable in the same manner, as the receipt towards freight was taxed.

On writ, the Single Judge held that the demurrage was not an extended freight at all; that section 172 covered the field of taxing a non-resident owner or charterer of a ship who was not engaged in the business of operation of shipping and section 5 was inapplicable to the facts of the instant case.

On writ appeal :

HELD: Section 172(1) identifies the subject of taxation. That subject is to be taxed only as provided under section 172(2) to (7). There is no question of any residuary income attributable to that subject being taxed elsewhere. That will be amending section 172(1) by reading into it a supposed intention of the law-maker; such a course is impermissible.

Section 172(1) is not attracted to the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of operation of ships. A non-resident owner of charterer of a ship which carries passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India only, is covered by section 172.

Since section 172 is a complete code by itself, the levy and collection of tax in respect of the subject on which the tax is levied thereunder has to be only as provided therein. For whatever reason, the concept of total income of a non-resident person coming within section 172(1) is confined to the specified income under section 172(2). There is no scope at all to travel outside section 172 to impose tax on such a person's income derived in the manner stated in section 172(2).

Thus, if the payment is to be made not on account of carriage of goods, etc., then section 172(2) is not attracted and, therefore, such a receipt or payment is not taxable under section 172.

A perusal of the agreements showed that that demurrage payable was to prevent delay in loading the goods. In other words, the payment was to speed up the activity of delivering the goods to the purchaser in whom the title vested on delivery into the ship. If the seller expedited the delivery and loading, then he gets "dispatch money". While dispatch money was receivable by the seller, i.e., the petitioners, the demurrage was receivable by the purchaser. The carriage of goods by the ship commenced on completion of the loading work till then the goods were in the process of delivery on board the ship. The demurrage payable in the instant case at the most was on account of deley in the delivery of the goods on board the ship. If so, certainly section 172(2) was inapplicable.

The demurrage paid or payable under the said two agreements could not be taxed in the manner pleaded by the revenue.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 13 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Pilfered goods - Demurrage - BPT must remit if Customs issue certificate or Court allows it. Such certificates have binding effect--However the remission can apply only to 80%, and the maximum period allowable is 150 days

FACT: Goods imported by the petitioners were detained at the Bombay port on the ground that the licences produced did not adequately cover the goods. Petitioners' appeal was allowed, and the Customs authorities were instructed to clear the goods forthwith and to issue a detention certificate for waiving of port trust charges. Bombay Port Trust, however, refused to release the goods without payment of demurrage charges which petitioners paid under protest. After clearance of the goods the Petitioners applied for remission and/or refund of demurrage charges, which was rejected. Their contention in this petition is that goods were detained by mistake by Customs authorities for which the petitioners cannot be made to suffer, and that they should be allowed remission of 80% of demurrage charges for the full period of 225 days. It is also argued that the order passed by the B.P.T. authorities was invalid and bad in law for having been passed without a personal hearing.

HELD: Remission of demurrage charges--rule of law is binding on executive authorities. Action of B.P.T. in rejecting remission of demurrage charges, in spite of the High Court order, held to be wrong and arbitrary and it was passed without assigning any valid reasons. "As I have pointed out heretofore in the order of the Secretary of the B.P.T. Authorities dated 27.8.1986, no reasons at all have been assigned for rejecting the claim for remission made by the Petitioners. I have dealt with the reasons given in the affidavit-in-reply, and I have come to the conclusion that the reasons given are such that no reasonable person would arrive at the conclusion arrived at by the Secretary. The order of the Bombay Port Trust authorities, therefore, is certainly not one which is informed by reason and hence the same is perverse. On that ground the order needs to be struck down".

2. Demurrage charges--remission of demurrage charges is allowable only up to the limit of 80% of charges and for a maximum period of 150 days, the remaining 20% of which is to be detained as handling and storage charges. B.P.T. policy statement, paragraphs 4, 10 & 4.11. "I am afraid it is not possible to accept this submission of Shri Mehta in view of the Policy Statement of the B.P.T. Authorities, Respondent No. 4, stated heretofore in paragraphs 4.10 and 4.11, which ultimately became part of Resolution No. 635 of 1975. Under those rules, the B.P.T. Authorities decided that the remission of the demurrage charges would be only to the tune of 80%, keeping the 20% towards service charges including handling costs and storage charges. Paragraph 4.11 laid down that the concession of remission would be applicable only to the extent of 150 days. The Remission Committee was empowered to decide each case on merits. The petitioners, therefore, under the policy decision of the B.P.T. Authorities, Respondent No. 4, would be entitled only to 80% of the demurrage charges for a period of 150 days."

3. Natural justice is not isolated if the aggrieved party has not asked for a personal hearing, consequent to which no personal hearing is given by the Remission Committee. "In the instant case also, I find that the Petitioners at no stage had asked the Remission Committee to give a personal hearing. This being the case, I do not think that Shri Mehta's contention can be accepted that in the absence of a personal hearing the order passed by the B.P.T. Authorities dated 28.7.1986 was bad."

DEMURRAGE CHARGED BY AIRLINES NOT TAXABLE IN HANDS OF CHA :

1. We are Custom House Agents and doing clearances on behalf of our clients from the Airport, ICD Tughlakabad and ICD CFS Patparganj. We are providing hereinbelow an amendment made to the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rule, 2006 in Rule 6. Rule 6(1) provides that, subject to the provisions of Section 67, the value of Taxable Services shall include :

(x) the amount realised as demurrage or by any other name whatever called for the provision of a service beyond the period originally contracted for or in any other manner relatable to the provision of a service.

The definition of "Demurrage", as found on the internet, is given below:

(i)

Penalty for exceeding free time (usually 72 hours) allowed for taking delivery of a shipment from the shipping or transporting company's warehouse.

(ii)

Penalty assessed against a consignor, consignee or such other party responsible for delay in loading or unloading of a shipping vessel or for undue detention (usually over 48 hours) of the transportation equipment, also called as detention charge.

(iii)

In international transportation there is a charge for the failure to remove cargo from a terminal within the free time allowed. Also, a charge for failure to load or unload a ship within the allowed period.

We are doing the clearances from the Airport, ICD Tughlakabad and ICD CFS Patparganj. For clearance of goods from all these places, we are paying some amount as "demurrage" on behalf of our clients and are realising the same from our clients in the capacity of a "Pure Agent". The receipt from the Airport Authority mentions it as "demurrage"; the receipt from the Container Corporation of India (ICD Tughlakabad) mentions it as "Storage and Warehousing charges" and the receipt from ICD Patparganj also mentions it as "Storage Charges".

The above mentioned authorities charge the demurrage in case the goods are not cleared within the free time (without demurrage) allowed for Customs Clearance. In 95% of cases the clearances cannot be done within the free time due to one of the following reasons:—

Delay in providing documents by the Importer, i.e., our client.

Delay due to the lengthy procedure of custom clearance.

Delay due to clarifications given by the client on the objections raised by the customs department.

Delay due to systems failure at the Airport/ICD, Tughlakabad/ICD CFS Patparganj.

In view of above reasons, the fact remains that a specific amount of "demurrage" is charged by the above mentioned authorities and that amount of "demurrage" is paid by us on behalf of our clients and is presently being reimbursed (realised) by us from the clients in the capacity of a "Pure Agent".

Our queries are:-

(1)

Does the amendment, for including "demurrage realised" in the value of Taxable Service, refer to the demurrage mentioned above which is realised by us from our clients?

(2)

Should the value of demurrage realised by us from the clients in the capacity of a "Pure Agent" be included in the value of taxable services w.e.f. 1-7-2012?

(3)

The amendment mentions "beyond the period originally contracted or in any other manner relatable to the provision of service". Generally, in our trade there is no "period originally contacted" for the activity of customs clearance. However, every client expects us to release the goods within the free period allowed (demurrage free) by the authorities. Therefore, it is not practically possible to work out the "Originally contracted period" in the services provided by us. Therefore, can the demurrage realised by us be covered under "or in any other manner relatable to the provision of service" as per the amendment.

(4)

The Airport or ICD Tughlakabad or ICD CFS Patparganj authorities do not provide any separate receipt for only "demurrage" amount. However, their receipt does provide separate value charged by them as demurrage in their receipt, thereby indicating the amount of "Demurrage" or "Storage & Warehousing Charges" or "Storage Charges" clearly in their receipt. A copy of the receipt issued by each authority is attached for your ready reference. We have highlighted "demurrage" charged in each receipt for your ready reference.

We would request you to let us have your views as to whether this amendment is actually applicable to the type of demurrage realised by us from our clients.

In view of aforesaid decision, validity of following decisions is doubtful.

11.12-1 Demurrage due to Custom's mistake should be paid by Customs

Often demurrage is charged because goods are detained by Customs. It has been held that if the detention and consequent confiscation has been held illegal by competent court/authority, demurrage should be paid by the customs department. The carrier/port authorities have right to recover demurrage and innocent importer is not liable to pay. - Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. v. CL Jain Woollen Mills 2001 AIR SCW 1547 = (2001) 5 SCC 345 = AIR 2001 SC 1806 = 129 ELT 561 (SC 3 member bench) [In UOI v. R C Fabrics (2002) 1 SCC 718 = 139 ELT 12 = 2001 AIR SCW 4805 (SC 3 member bench), it was held that the importer is liable to pay the demurrage and not the customs authorities. It appears from the order that the fact that the detention was due to fault (rather high handedness) of customs authorities was not placed before the Court].

In Patiala Castings v. UOI 2003 (156) ELT 458 (P&H HC DB), goods of assessee were detained for mis-declaration. Importer offered to mutilate goods, but department continued seizure of goods. It was held that this is harassment. Importer is not required to pay any demurrage. Demurrage charges should be paid by Government. Notice was issued to departmental officer for harassment of assessee.

In Sonia Overseas v. ACC (2009) 244 ELT 30 (Del HC DB), it was held that customs authorities are not liable if the detention is in good faith. Presumption of bona fide is in favour of customs authorities. Burden of proving mala fide is on person alleging the same. Every delay cannot be attributed to customs department.

However, in Jundal Drugs Ltd. v. UOI (2018) 361 ELT 369 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that if detention was bona fide, customs cannot be asked to pay demurrage, even if ultimately goods were released by customs.

In Modern Rubber Industries v. UOI 2003 (154) ELT 571 (Bom HC DB), it was held that u/s 155 of Customs Act, all actions of Government officers done in good faith are protected. Customs department cannot be saddled with warehousing charges, if their actions were not mala fide. In such case, assessee will have to pay warehousing charges, even if ultimately customs authorities accepted the contentions of assessee.

11.12-2 Department's instructions to avoid demurrage

Department has given detailed guidelines for expeditious clearance of goods in Chapter 15 Para 2 of CBIC's Customs Manual, 2023, which are briefly as follows.

Import/export goods should not be detained unless prohibited as per FTP or other laws. If these are required to be detained, importer will be advised in writing that he may shift the goods to warehouse u/s 49. If importer is willing, he can be allowed to clear goods on furnishing of bank guarantee which shall not exceed twice the amount of duty. Provisional clearance should be allows as a rule and not as exception.

FACT: The assessee, a non-resident shipping company, received detention/demurrage charges on containers. The Assessing Officer took the receipt as income in the hands of the assessee-company, and after deducting some estimated expenses, made addition. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the amount received against detention/demurrage charges should be treated at par with freight and, therefore, only 7.5 per cent thereof be treated as profit of business from operation of ships. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that nothing could be taxed as no income accrued in India.

On reference :

HELD: According to Explanation to section 44B(2) inserted retrospectively, the demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature should be taxed in the same way as the amount in clause (i ) or clause (ii) of section 44B(2). Accordingly, demurrage charges or freight charges should be taxed in the same way as freight taxable under section 44B.

Section 44B provides how the income from shipping business can be taxed in the case of non-residents and the section starts with a non-obstant clause, i.e. ‘Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A of the Act’. Thus, whatever is provided in the provisions contained in sections 28 to 43A, that will not come in the way of the provisions contained in section 44B as to how the income from shipping business in the case of non-residents will be computed, whether the income will be computed or not or what will be the rate of that income. However, the question was where an income of a non-resident had accrued outside India by way of demurrage charges, could that be taxed in India? There was no specific finding by the Tribunal as to what part of the demurrage income accrued to the assessee in India or outside India. Therefore, it was necessary to have the finding whether the demurrage income accrued in India or outside India and if not the entire income of demurrages, as to what part of the income of demurrages accrued in India or outside India.

Hence, the matter was remitted back to the Tribunal to give a finding on the above issue and decide the issue afresh.

HEADNOTE: Section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962 Trade Notices or advice - no reliance can be placed on such notices--Sample tests can afford guidance only--Demurrage can be waived only for the period goods are specifically detained by Customs. Woollen rags not having been proved to be textiles, demurrage payable. ICT Item 49 (4).

FACT: The petitioner-firm utilised woollen rags for manufacturing shoddy woollen yarn and blankets. The GOI permitted import of woollen rags and garment rags (rags from woven woollen fabrics and rags from knitted woollen material) and exempted woollen waste and rags from levy of customs duty by a notification dt. 20.4.1966. The importers have to claim the said exemption under Item 49(4) of Indian Customs Tariff read with the notification before clearing and consignment of woollen rags from the customs. Since 1966, the STC has been given monopoly in licences for importing woollen rags, which are not granted individually but allotted a quota on recommendation of the Textile Commissioner. The petitioners were allotted a quota of 37 bales of woollen hosiery rags which were imported from foreign suppliers by STC. The Customs Authorities carried out a visual inspection by taking samples, and later decided to have a chemical test. In spite of these two tests the Authorities decided to resort to the core-drilling test. On the basis of this the department held that the wool content of these bales was less than 50 per cent and therefore not eligible for exemption under the notification dt. 20.4.1966 and though clearance of goods was allowed they were charged to appropriate duty. The goods were kept in the sheds of the Port Trust of Bombay and it was not permitting clearance without payment of demurrage charges.

HELD: Exemption: Customs Authorities cannot rely upon trade advice and levy duty on the ground that the content was not according to the advice. Trade advice is not statutory and as such reliance cannot be placed on it. "The Exemption Notification dated April 20, 1966 totally exempted woollen wastes and woollen rags from the whole of the duty of customs leviable thereon. The Exemption Notification does not restrict the advantage only to those woollen wastes and woollen rags containing wool of more than 50%. In absence of any such provision in the Notification, it is not permissible for the Customs Authorities to levy duty on the imported woollen rags on the ground that the wool content was found less than 50 per cent. It is now well settled that the trade advice issued by the Government of India has no statutory force and it is not permissible for the Authorities exercising quasi judicial function to place reliance upon such trade advice to hold that the petitioners are liable for payment of duty."

2. Exemption: Physical and Chemical tests offer guidance and assistance only. "Merely because the different analysis show different conclusions it is not permissible to select that conclusion which suits the authorities to levy the duty. .........The procedure adopted by the Customs Authorities was entirely misconceived and cannot be sustained either in law or by principles of natural justice. In my judgment, the finding of the Customs Authorities that the import of woollen rags by the petitioners is not eligible for duty exemption is totally incorrect and deserves to be set aside. The petitioners ore entitled to the clearance without payment of any duty."

3. Detention Certificate: Demurrage charges to be paid to the Port Trust Authorities cannot be questioned even though the goods are not be cleared because of the insistence of the Customs Authorities for the payment of duty. Waiver available only during special examination of goods and a detention certificate issued accordingly. "......... exemption from payment of demurrage charges is available only during such period when the goods are detained for special examination. In the present case, the facts establish that the goods were detained by the Customs Authorities till end of May 1975 for special examination and it is abvious that the petitioners would not be liable to pay the demurrage charges to the Port Trust authorities till end of May 1975."

4. Classification: Woollen rags not being textiles demurrage, charges are to be paid accordingly, "In the present case, the question which arises is whether the expression 'textile' in Item No. 85 of the Scales of Rates would cover the woollen rags. In my judgment, it would not be possible to hold so. What was contemplated by Item No. 85 was textile or fabrics in its fuse form and not the woollen rags. ...the petitioners are liable to pay the demurrage charges computed by the Port Trust authorities according to the rates provided by Item No. 92 of the Scale of Rates."

HEADNOTE: Section 57 read with section 58 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Appointing public warehouse - Baggage - Demurrage--Airport authorities not entitled to claim any demurrage in view of public notice 29/86 specifying that demurrage charges will not be recovered for warehousing baggage detained by the Customs Authorities

FACT: The petitioners are citizens of Nepal. Some of their goods which were being transhipped from Singapore arrived as unaccompanied baggage at the IGI Airport for onward shipment to Kathmandu. Being under the impression that this importation was improper, the Customs Authorities confiscated these goods under section 117 of the Customs Act. The confiscated goods were stored in the customs warehouse of IGI Airport. After the completion of adjudication proceedings, the Deputy Collector of Customs permitted transshipment of the seized goods. The petitioners have filed these appeals being aggrieved by the refusal of the Airport Authorities to release the goods unless the demurrage charges were paid. It is their contention that this claim was illegal as the goods had been stored in the warehouse upon the insistence of the Customs Authorities and not the petitioners. Moreover, in view of the detention certificate issued by the Assistant Collector of Customs, the respondents were bound to waive the demurrage charges.

HELD: Airport Authorities are not entitled to claim any demurrage charges from the petitioners--respondents bound by Public Notice 29/86 which specifies that demurrage charges will not be recovered for warehousing baggage detained by the Customs Authorities. "For the purpose of waiver or remission of the warehouse charges customs authorities have to certify that goods were not cleared up to a certain period for them to make enquiries under the Act. This certification is the detention certificate. The Public Notice 29/86 and the Regulations and guidelines of the Airports Authority, the first respondent, talk of detention certificate to be issued by the customs authorities. Reference may well be made to section 63 of the Act falling under Chapter IX dealing with warehousing. Under sub-section (1) of section 63, the owner of any warehoused goods shall pay to the warehouse-keeper rent and warehouse charges at the rates fixed under any law for the time being in force or where no rates are so fixed, at such rates as may be fixed by the Collector of Customs. We have seen above, rates for warehousing baggage have not been fixed by the first respondent and Public Notice 29/86 in effect specifies under clause (vii) that charges for warehousing baggage for the period it is detained will not be charged by the Airports Authority, the first respondent. ........We are, therefore, of the opinion that the first respondent is not entitled to charge any demurrage in all these cases and the petitioners are entitled to have their goods transhipped to Nepal without payment of any ground rent/demurrage charges."
Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Demurrage charges - Refund - not refundable by the Customs as there is no provision in the Customs Act to this effect (Paras 6  7)

The petitioners entered into an agreement to sell ore to foreign buyer. The agreement was in the nature of FOB contract. The ships were chartered by the foreign buyer of ore for the purpose of conveying the ores purchased from the seller. The seller was paid price at the rate specified in the agreement and the quantity of the ore was quantified with reference to their loading into the ship. In case there was delay in loading, the seller had to pay demurrage and similarly in case time was saved in loading, the seller was entitled to receive dispatch money. The ITO held that this demurrage was essentially an extended freight payable towards the carriage of the goods and was taxable in the same manner, as the receipt towards freight was taxed.

HELD: The dispute in this case centres around demurrage. The expression "demurrage" is not defined under the Act. The expression demurrage in the world of shipping meant a sum agreed by the charterer to be paid as liquidated damages for delay beyond a stipulated or reasonable time for loading or unloading, generally referred to as the laydays or laytime. Where the sum is only to be paid for a fixed number of days, and a further delay takes place, the shipowner's remedy is to recover unliquidated "damages for detention" for the period of the delay. The phrase "demurrage" is sometimes loosely used to cover both these meanings.' [Para 24]

In Trustees of the Port of Madras v. Aminchand Pyarelal [1976] 3 SCC 167, it was opined that the "Board has used the expression "demurrage" not in the strict mercantile sense but merely to signify a charge which may be levied on goods after the expiration of free days".[Para 25]

Regulation 2(g) of the International Airports Authority (Storage and Processing of Goods) Regulation, 1980 made under the provisions of the International Airports Authority Act, 1971, defined the expression 'demurrage' to mean, the rate or amount payable to the airport by a shipper or consignee or carrier, for not removing the cargo within the time allowed. [Para 26]

8. This Court has, in a series of decisions, held that circulars issued under section 119 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and 37B of Central Excise Act are binding on the Revenue. 9. The somewhat different approach in Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 5 SCC 365 by two learned Judges of this Court, apart from being contrary to the stream of authority cannot be taken to have laid down good law in view of the subsequent decision of the Constitution Bench in Collector of Central Excise v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 139 ELT 3. After this Court had construed an exemption notification in a particular manner, it said :

"We need to made it clear that, regardless of the interpretation that we have placed on the said phrase, if there are circulars which have been issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs which place a different interpretation upon the said phrase, that interpretation will be binding upon the Revenue". (p. 5)

Despite the categorical language of the clarification by the Constitution Bench, the issue was again sought to be raised before a Bench of three Judges in Collector of Central Excise v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 143 ELT 19 where the view of the Constitution Bench regarding the binding nature of circulars issued under section 37B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 was reiterated after it was drawn to the attention of the Court by the Revenue that there were in fact circulars issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs which gave a different interpretation to the phrase as interpreted by the Constitution Bench. The same view has also been taken in Simplex Castings Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs [2003] 5 SCC 528.

10. The principles laid down by all these decisions are :

(1)

Although a circular is not binding on a Court or an assessee, it is not open to the Revenue to raise the contention that is contrary to a binding circular by the Board. When a circular remains in operation, the Revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to the terms of the statute.

(2)

Despite the decision of this Court, the Department cannot be permitted to take a stand contrary to the instructions issued by the Board.

(3)

A show-cause notice and demand contrary to existing circulars of the Board are ab initio bad.

(4)

It is not open to the Revenue to advance an argument or file an appeal contrary to the circulars.

11. As we have noted the provisions of section 151A are in pari materia with the provisions of section 119 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and section 37B of the Central Excise Act. Parliament introduced section 151A by an amendment to the Customs Act, 1962 in 1995 but with effect from 27th December, 1985 (Act 80 of 1995), when this Court had already construed identical language in the manner indicated. It may be assumed that Parliament had legislatively approved the construction by using the exact words so construed again in the Customs Act. There is, therefore, no reason why the principles enunciated by this Court under the two earlier Acts should not also be determinative of the construction put on the later in respect of a materially similar statutory provision. This was also not argued by the appellant.

"Subject : Demurrage charges and dispatch money not to form part of the assessable value - Regarding.

Pursuant to the decision taken in the Tariff Conference of Collector held in August 1981, the issue was further discussed in the Tariff Conference of February 1989. The Conference had desired that the matter may be re-examined in its totality especially in the context of current valuation principles based on the GATT Valuation at Goa on 4th and 5th April, 1991 examined the problem posed in entirety. The issue dealt with by their Lordships in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. case was whether the customs authorities can add or include landing charges in arriving at the value of the goods while assessing customs duty payable in respect of the imported goods. Their Lordships were not concerned with the demurrage payable on account of the delay in discharging the goods from the vessel or from removing the same out of the port's area. It is further noticed that their Lordships in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. case were not concerned with the amendment brought out to the Act in 1988 and the framing of the Rules, and the impact of Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 (hereinafter referred to as the Rules) in finding out the value of the goods. This aspect has been made clear by their Lordships by observing:

"Post 1988, therefore the value of the imported goods has to be determined in accordance with the rules which, according to the respondents, are based on the GATT Valuation Code (also called Article VII of the General Agreement on Tariff and Trade) which was adopted in 1979. With these Rules, however, we are not concerned in the present case because all the goods were imported prior to the incorporation of sub-section 1A of Section 14 of the Act."

12. Scheme of the Act shows that Customs authorities will have to determine the value of the imported goods for the purpose of imposing Customs duty. In determining the deemed price as per Section 14(1), the element of port charges, which have to be borne by the importer in addition to the CIF value, must necessarily form a part. So, the value or cost of the imported article at the time of importation, i.e. at the time when it reached the Customs barrier is to be assessed by the authorities. In making this assessment, the Customs authorities must keep in mind the price at which such or like goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale. Imported goods are ordinarily sold in situations where demurrage is not paid or becomes payable. Situation where demurrage is paid or becomes payable is not an ordinary situation. Costs incurred on such extraordinary situations cannot be taken into consideration for fixing the value of the imported goods for the purpose of levying Customs duty.

13. On behalf of the Revenue it was contended that Rule 9(2)(a) of the Rules requires addition of cost of transport of the imported goods to the place of importation. So, the cost paid or payable by the importer to bring the goods up to the Customs barrier must form part of the value. That cost should necessarily take within it demurrage as well. Therefore, according to counsel, the Garden Silk Mills Ltd. case is authority for the proposition that the entire cost incurred for bringing the imported goods up to the Customs barrier should form the assessable value. We find it difficult to agree with this argument. Fist of all, the apex Court was not concerned with the demurrage paid or payable by the importer on account of the delayed clearance of the goods from the ship. Demurrage becomes payable only on extraordinary situations. The provisions contained in the Rules were not adverted to by the Apex Court in the said decision. Their Lordships have categorically held that the price at which the imported goods are ordinarily sold should be the basis for valuation under Section 14(1) of the Act. Ordinarily demurrage is not payable. Only in extraordinary circumstances where delay in discharging the goods from the ship occurs, demurrage becomes payable. Such extraordinary circumstances are not falling within the purview of Section 14(1) of the Act. This aspect can be illustrated by the following example:-

According to Explanation to section 44B(2) inserted retrospectively, the demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature should be taxed in the same way as the amount in clause (i ) or clause (ii) of section 44B(2). Thus, whatever is provided in the provisions contained in sections 28 to 43A, that will not come in the way of the provisions contained in section 44B as to how the income from shipping business in the case of non-residents will be computed, whether the income will be computed or not or what will be the rate of that income. However, the question was where an income of a non-resident had accrued outside India by way of demurrage charges, could that be taxed in India? There was no specific finding by the Tribunal as to what part of the demurrage income accrued to the assessee in India or outside India. HELD: Section 172 comes under sub-title 'H - Profits of non-residents from occasional shipping business'. Title of section 172 is 'Shipping business of non-residents'. 'Non-resident' is defined under section 2(30 ), as a person who is not a 'resident' and for the purpose of sections 92, 93 and 168, includes a person who is not ordinarily resident within the meaning of clause (6) of section 6. The assessee, being a company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956, could not be said to be non-resident. The assessee could not lay fingers on section 172, since profits of non-residents were not to be dealt with. The other aspect is that such profits of non-residents should be from occasional shipping business. It was not the case that the assessee had earned some profits from occasional shipping business and was a non-resident. The tax liability of the foreign company, i.e., 'M', Japan which was recipient of demurrages was not being examined. Section 172 did not apply to the facts of the instant case wherein the assessee was an Indian company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. The Tribunal had recorded a perverse observation/finding regarding application of sections 44B and 172. [Para 8]

The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal had wrongly interpreted the circular dated 19-9-1995 issued by the CBDT. That circular could not be considered in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, in aid of the assessee. The Assessing Officer, in fact, had passed a legal, proper and reasoned order, holding that the provisions laid down under section 40(a )(i) applied to the case in hand. [Para 10]

In the instant case, there were no pleadings or material brought on record to show that the case was governed by occasional shipping within the meaning of section 172 and said section applied. [Para 11]

The facts of the instant case were governed by section 40(a)(i ). The order passed by the Assessing Officer was legal, proper and in accordance with the scheme of the Act. Therefore, the appeal deserved to be allowed by quashing and setting aside the orders passed by the Commissioner(Appeals) and the Tribunal. [Para 12]

In certain situations (of FOB shipment to a country applying the CIF system) ships may have to wait for days or weeks or months until the goods can be loaded or unloaded and demurrage cost may have to be borne by the buyer in addition to price and transportation cost. Storage cost is neither a cost of purchase nor of conversion nor can it be considered as toward bringing the inventory held in stock to its present location or condition. It is in the nature of a holding cost, which could be considered as an element of cost only where the goods have to be necessarily held in a particular manner, entailing cost, for a defined period, prior to their further processing, i.e., itself represents a process integral to their conversion, so that it represents a process and, thus, conversion cost. There is accordingly no question of the same being added to its value. A simple question would clarify the issue, i.e., whether rent, were the goods, instead of lying at the port, removed expeditiously to a rented premises, saving demurrage, or the cost of the staff attending thereto (godown) or otherwise supervising the storage, etc. be said to form part of the acquisition or conversion cost of the goods or otherwise incurred in bringing the same to their present location and condition, so as to be included in their valuation? Surely not. The third element of cost, i.e., other than toward acquisition and conversion, it would be noted, is broadly worded, so that it could in fact be said to include the cost of acquisition and conversion as well. It is only the direct cost incurred toward so bringing that could be included in as much as it adds value. In fact, the demurrage/detention charges, being toward the cost for the delay in removal of the goods, can only loosely/broadly be said to be a holding cost, and it would be more appropriate to consider it as a cost for the delayed removal of goods, i.e., beyond the stipulated period. The same thus is only a revenue expenditure of the period to which it relates and no more and, thus, not liable for inclusion in the value of the goods from any stand point.

The case of the Assessing Officer was that the IHC was not covered under section 44B. The assessee had placed reliance on the Explanation to section 44B to contend that IHC would be covered within its Explanation. [Para 6] A plain reading of the Explanation to section 44B reveals that the demurrage charges or handling charges or other amounts of similar nature have been brought within the ambit of 'business income' for applying the rate of 7½ per cent. The very nature of items prescribed in the Explanation being demurrage charges or handling charges, which precede 'any other amount of similar nature', show that the latter category has to draw a colour from the items referred to in the earlier part. The expression 'any other amount of similar nature' cannot be read in isolation by disregarding the nature of items preceding it. The meaning of the succeeding expression has to be understood in the context of the preceding words. Since the demurrage charges or handling charges have been mentioned in the Explanation prior to 'any other amount of similar nature', 'any other amount' has to be considered, which is similar to or closely resembles with the nature of demurrage or handling charges. Handling charges are the charges paid for loading/unloading/stacking, etc., of the containers and the demurrage charges are in nature of penalty for non-removal of the cargo in time. On the contrary, the IHC are towards transport of the goods from the exporter's place to the port. The very nature of inland transportation charges clearly differentiates it from handling or demurrage charges, which are of a different genus. Therefore, there was no substance in the submission of the assessee that inland haulage charges were covered under section 44B, as these were equal to or part and parcel of the amount on account of carriage of goods shipped at any port in or outside India, and, hence, were automatically covered under Article 8. [Paras 7 and 8]

Section 47 of the Act is the provision to obtain clearance of goods for home consumption. Section 49 provides for storage of imported goods in public warehouse, or in a private warehouse, if permitted by the Deputy Commissioner of Customs or Assistant Commissioner of Customs. Under chapter IX of the Act, the Deputy commissioner or Assistant Commissioner of Customs may appoint public warehouses wherein dutiable goods may be deposited, as provided in Section 57 of the Act. Under Section 58, the Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner may even license private warehouses wherein dutiable imported goods could be deposited. But all warehoused goods would be subject to the control of the proper officer of the customs department, as provided in Section 62 and the owner of the goods is required to pay the rent and warehouse charges to be fixed by the Commissioner of Customs, as provided in Section 63. No warehoused goods could be taken out of the warehouse except for clearance of home consumption or for removal to another warehouse, as stipulated in Section 67 of the Act. Section 68 provides the procedure which an importer would follow for clearing the warehoused goods for home consumption. The expression "warehouse" has been defined in Section 2(43) to mean a public warehouse appointed under Section 57 or a private warehouse licensed under Section 58. Trustees of the Port of Madras Vs. M/s. Aminchand Pyarelal & Ors. [(1976) 1 SCR 721] is the first of such decisions of this Court. That was a case, where imported goods of M/s. Aminchand Pyarelal - 'the importer' were not cleared from the customs area of the Port of Madras by the Customs authorities before the expiry of free days. The goods, therefore, continued to be in the custody of Trustees of the Port of Madras - "the Board", as approved custodian of such goods on behalf of the Customs authorities. However, a detention certificate was issued to the importer by the Customs authorities stating that the detention of the imported goods beyond the free days was not due to fault or negligence on the part of the importer. The Board, based on the detention certificate waived demurrage charges payable by the importer amounting to Rs. 3,20,951/-, and released the goods to the importer. Later, when the Customs authorities owned their mistake of issuing the detention certificate wrongly, the Board, filed a suit against the importer, the Union of India and the Customs authorities for recovery of the demurrage charges which had not been recovered on account of the detention certificate. But, that suit was resisted by the importer on the plea that the delay in clearing the goods was due to fault on the part of the Customs authorities and hence there was no legal obligation on its part to pay the demurrage charges. The suit was dismissed by the High Court accepting the plea of the importer. When the Board brought up the matter before this Court in appeal, the provisions of the Madras Port Trust Act and the scale of rates fixed by the Board with the approval of the Central Government pursuant to the provisions of the Act having been thoroughly examined, it was held that the High Court was in error in its conclusion that the Board had no power to charge demurrage where goods were not removed from its premises not due to the fault or negligence on the part of the importer, but due to fault of the Customs authorities.

17. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay Vs. Indian Goods Supplying Co. [(1977) 3 SCR 343] is the second of such decisions of this Court, where this Court examined the sustainability of scales of rates of demurrage of goods framed by the Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay - "the Board", the provisions of which were in pari materia with the Madras Port Trust Act. This Court held that the case it was examining being in all force with the case of M/s. Aminchand Pvare Lal (supra) it had to be concluded on the basis of the decision rendered therein. Consequently, it reversed the judgement of the High Court in appeal by holding that the High Court was in error in its view that the importer of the goods could not be held responsible for any delay not attributable to his own fault and that the demurrage under the statute could never be imposed as long as goods were detained for the purpose of Import Trade Control Regulations.

2. I have gone through reply to your Query No. 1 published in May 5 to May 19 Issue of the Service Tax Today [STT Vol. 39 Part 3]. What will be the amount liable to service tax if the restaurant doesn't collect any service charges ? Please enlighten me.

Where a restaurant doesn't recover any service charges, there is no question of any charge of service tax.

We have the Supreme Court's judgment in K. Damodarasamy Naidu & Bros. v. State of Tamil Nadu [2000] 117 STC 1 [Constitution Bench] ruling that restaurant transactions are "deemed sales", in entirety under article 366(29A)(f). When it is said that it is a deemed sale, it cannot be a service, as definition of service reads as follows : "service …includes declared service …but does not include …deemed sale of goods falling under Article 366(29A).." [Section 65B(44)(a)] Hence, to the extent of deemed sale, there is no service. Therefore, supply of goods at any price (even if it is high) is deemed sale and no part of it can be charged to service tax.

Further, the judgment of the Supreme Court in Tamil Nadu Kalyana Mandapam Assn. [2006] 4 STT 308 (2-judge Bench) dealt only with outdoor catering services and did not deal with restaurant services, though the judgment in K. Damodarasamy Naidu & Bros. (supra) was referred to in that judgment (without any observations).

Hence, till date, in view of ruling in K. Damodarasamy Naidu & Bros. (supra) no service tax can be levied on any part of the price charged for food, etc., supplied in a restaurant.
