Section 45 : Section 45 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that all imported goods unloaded in the customs area shall remain in the custody of a person approved by the Commissioner of Customs till the time they are cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped in accordance with chapter VIII which deals with goods in transit. The person to whom the custody of such goods is handed over by the Commissioner of Customs is liable to keep record of the same and keep the same in the customs area and not to permit removal of the same except with prior permission and in case of any pilferage etc. the said person is liable to pay duty on the said goods. [Para 24]

Sections 49 and 57 to 73 : Under section 49, the Customs Authorities on an application of the importer, if satisfied, that the goods entered for home consumption cannot be cleared within a reasonable time, permit the importer to deposit the goods in a public area or a private warehouse for a specified period. The period may be extended from time to time by the Commissioner of Customs. Section 49 further stipulates that goods so warehoused on an application by the importer shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods for the purposes of this Act and provisions of chapter IX shall not apply. Section 57 lays down that the Assistant Commissioner/Deputy Commissioner of Customs may appoint public warehouses wherein dutiable goods may be deposited. Section 58 empowers the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs to licence private warehouses wherein dutiable goods imported may be deposited where the facilities for deposit in a public warehouse are not available. Sections 59 to 73 of chapter IX deal with the general provisions under which an importer may warehouse the imported goods and stipulates the period for which the goods may be warehoused and general conditions for removal/clearance of the goods. [Para 27]

Section 141 : Section 141 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that the conveyances and goods in a customs area are subjected to the control of the officers of customs and are to be handled in a customs area in such a manner as may be prescribed and responsibilities of a person engaged in the receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and otherwise handling import or export goods in customs area shall be such as may be prescribed by the customs authorities. [Para 29]

Goods are within control of customs authorities : The above noted sections of the Customs Act postulate a scheme or a procedure whereby goods which are imported into a customs area immediately come into the control and power of the officers of the customs. The customs authorities are empowered under the Act to appoint persons or officers who are responsible for receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and handling goods in the customs areas. Under certain circumstances, the customs authorities may permit storage of imported goods in a warehouse pending clearance on a application by the importer, where goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time (section 49) or warehoused in a public or private warehouse (sections 60, 61). It is the Explanation which refers to the demurrage and for the purpose of sub-section (2) of section 44B. It clarifies that the amount paid or payable or received or deemed to be received, as the case may be, by way of demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature shall for the purposes of sub-section (1) deemed to be the profits and gains of the business, namely, shipping business chargeable to tax under that head. The amounts which are paid or payable whether in or out of India to the assessee or to any person on his behalf on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India and the amount received was deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port outside India shall be deemed to be the profits and gains. On that the tax is payable by virtue of sub-section (1) of section 172. That has to be levied and recovered in terms of the sub-sections of section 172.

Once section 172 falls in Chapter XV titled as Liability in Special Cases - Profits of Non-residents, then section 172 is referable to section 44B. Both provisions open with a non obstante clause and whereas section 44B enacts special provisions for computing profits and gains of shipping business in case of non-residents, section 172 dealing with shipping business of non-residents is enacted for the purpose of levy and recovery of tax in the case of any ship belonging to or chartered by a non-resident operated from India.

These sections and particularly section 172 devise a scheme for levy and recovery of tax. The sub-sections of section 44B denote as to how the amounts paid to or payable would include demurrage charges or handling charges or any other amount of similar nature. The sub-sections of section 172 read together and harmoniously would reveal as to how the tax should be levied, computed, assessed and recovered. Therefore, there is no warrant in applying the provisions in Chapter XVII of Act for collection and recovery of the tax and its deduction at source vide section 195. [Para 46]

It is the recipient's position and the perspective in which the recipient's income would be taxed will have to be borne in mind. The non-resident shipping company in respect of its income would be in a position to rely upon section 44B and consequently section 172. However, one does not see how there is an obligation to deduct tax at source on the resident assessee/Indian company in the instant case. It would also be in a position to rely upon section 172 but the responsibility of the person making payment to a non-resident in sub-section (1) of section 195 cannot be avoided in the manner set out in other cases. The scheme as above operates only to cases covered by section 172 and none else. [Para 48]

Section 172(1) identifies the subject of taxation. That subject is to be taxed only as provided under section 172(2) to (7). There is no question of any residuary income attributable to that subject being taxed elsewhere. That will be amending section 172(1) by reading into it a supposed intention of the law-maker; such a course is impermissible.

Section 172(1) is not attracted to the case of a non-resident assessee engaged in the business of operation of ships. A non-resident owner of charterer of a ship which carries passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at a port in India only, is covered by section 172.

Since section 172 is a complete code by itself, the levy and collection of tax in respect of the subject on which the tax is levied thereunder has to be only as provided therein. For whatever reason, the concept of total income of a non-resident person coming within section 172(1) is confined to the specified income under section 172(2). There is no scope at all to travel outside section 172 to impose tax on such a person's income derived in the manner stated in section 172(2).

Thus, if the payment is to be made not on account of carriage of goods, etc., then section 172(2) is not attracted and, therefore, such a receipt or payment is not taxable under section 172.

In pursuance of Regulation 6 IAAI has framed a policy of waiver of demurrage charges. It is framed on principle of 'capacity to pay'. Paragraph 2 of the Policy incorporates the general principles. It divides the cargo imported for purpose of tree period into three classes; (1) commercial, (2) unaccompanied baggage, and (3) non-commercial cargo. It allows seven calendar days from the date of landing as free period to commercial and non-commercial cargo whereas the unaccompanied baggage is allowed 14 days. Clause (d) provides that unscheduled holidays declared by Central Government would be considered as free period. And clause (e) allows as free period the period of processing application for waiver of demurrage. It further allows three days for postal communication as free period. But Paragraph 3 provides that beyond the period mentioned in Paragraph 2, the cargo may be entitled to remission of demurrage in the circumstances mentioned therein. Paragraph 3.1 provides that wherever detention certificate is submitted from the competent authority that the detention of the goods was for no fault of consignee, then the consignee shall be entitled to demurrage on the scale mentioned in sub-paragraphs (a) to (g). Clause (a) deals with detention of goods by the Customs in connection with I.T.C. formalities. It provides for 80% waiver for first 90 days, 50% thereafter for six months and full charges thereafter. Clause (b) permits 80% waiver for period under detention in transfer, 'of residents appeal where the appellate authority decides the case in favour of the consignee without imposing any penalty'. And clause (c) allows 80% waiver for full period of detention where the detention certificate shows that detention was by, 'customs for analytical purposes, such detention should be for specific Analytical Test by Customs Control Laboratory or Central Drugs Control Laboratory.' This policy was framed by the IAAI in 1979 whereas the Public Notice was issued in 1986. For purposes of detention of imported goods by the Customs Department at Indira Gandhi International Airport, therefore, Paragraph 3.1 has to be read that where detention certificate has been issued by the Customs Authorities in accordance with sub-paragraph (vii) of the Public Notice no demurrage shall be charged for the period mentioned in it.

Section 45 : Section 45 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that all imported goods unloaded in the customs area shall remain in the custody of a person approved by the Commissioner of Customs till the time they are cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped in accordance with chapter VIII which deals with goods in transit. The person to whom the custody of such goods is handed over by the Commissioner of Customs is liable to keep record of the same and keep the same in the customs area and not to permit removal of the same except with prior permission and in case of any pilferage etc. the said person is liable to pay duty on the said goods. [Para 24]

Sections 49 and 57 to 73 : Under section 49, the Customs Authorities on an application of the importer, if satisfied, that the goods entered for home consumption cannot be cleared within a reasonable time, permit the importer to deposit the goods in a public area or a private warehouse for a specified period. The period may be extended from time to time by the Commissioner of Customs. Section 49 further stipulates that goods so warehoused on an application by the importer shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods for the purposes of this Act and provisions of chapter IX shall not apply. Section 57 lays down that the Assistant Commissioner/Deputy Commissioner of Customs may appoint public warehouses wherein dutiable goods may be deposited. Section 58 empowers the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs to licence private warehouses wherein dutiable goods imported may be deposited where the facilities for deposit in a public warehouse are not available. Sections 59 to 73 of chapter IX deal with the general provisions under which an importer may warehouse the imported goods and stipulates the period for which the goods may be warehoused and general conditions for removal/clearance of the goods. [Para 27]

Section 141 : Section 141 of the Customs Act, 1962 stipulates that the conveyances and goods in a customs area are subjected to the control of the officers of customs and are to be handled in a customs area in such a manner as may be prescribed and responsibilities of a person engaged in the receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and otherwise handling import or export goods in customs area shall be such as may be prescribed by the customs authorities. [Para 29]

Goods are within control of customs authorities : The above noted sections of the Customs Act postulate a scheme or a procedure whereby goods which are imported into a customs area immediately come into the control and power of the officers of the customs. The customs authorities are empowered under the Act to appoint persons or officers who are responsible for receiving, storing, delivering, despatching and handling goods in the customs areas. Under certain circumstances, the customs authorities may permit storage of imported goods in a warehouse pending clearance on a application by the importer, where goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time (section 49) or warehoused in a public or private warehouse (sections 60, 61). [Para 30]

Thirdly, sections 13 and 23 of the Customs Act have been wholly lost sight of. Where goods which are imported are lost, pilfered or destroyed, no import duty is leviable thereon until they are out of customs and come into the hands of the importer. This is as even if the detention/demurrage charge is considered as not arising on account of a contractual obligation, but a statutory one, i.e., as in the nature of a levy or impost (which would though need to be established), it would stand to be included under section 145A only where it represents a qualifying cost - which have found as not, and not otherwise. [Para 3.1] The opening stock for the year under reference would include demurrage charges, while the closing stock would not, and which would itself become a source of distortion. Though normally both the opening and the closing stock are to be valued on the same basis, it cannot also be denied that the valuation of the opening stock has to agree with that of the closing stock for the immediately preceding year. It is not in dispute that the value of opening stock, as assumed by the assessee, is the same as adopted in respect of the closing stock for the immediately preceding year. Any change would lead to a distortion - to the extent of the change - in the year the same is effected, so that the same is incidental thereto, and the fundamental question that would need to be addressed and answered is if the change is valid. It is found as so. Further, altering the value of the opening stock would amount to effectively modifying the closing stock and, thus, the income for the immediately preceding year, which stands assessed. The change thus gets effectively shifted to that year. The argument qua uniformity in the valuation of opening and closing stock would then stand to be assumed for that year, leading to a modification in the value of the opening stock for that year, and so on, thus causing a ripple effect. The argument is, thus, to no moment, and inasmuch as a change has been validated for the current year, an exception to the principle of uniformity in the valuation of the closing and opening stock for that year would have to be drawn. These and the like arguments would thus suggest non-disturbance of the value of the (opening) stock as carried forward from the preceding year, even though the same may not be valid, subject of course to the change in the method of valuation being bona fide. [Para 3.3]

The Assessing Officer having adopted the same method of valuation for the closing stock, i.e., as for the opening stock, being in fact consistently followed, the question of validity of the revision by the assessee arose for consideration. The same, as by the first appellate authority, approved on the basis of the accounting principles, which would govern the matter in the absence of any specific provision/s in the Act toward the same, with section 145A being inapplicable, also relying on the decision in the case of CIT v. British Paints India Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 44/54 Taxman 499 (SC), wherein the same issue arose; the Apex Court therein reiterating its professed stand in the matter refer: S.N. Namasivayam Chettiar v. CIT [1960] 38 ITR 579 (SC) and CIT v. A. Krishnaswami Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 122 (SC).

However, integral thereto is the question of a corresponding change in the value of the opening stock, which would otherwise continue to be valued per the old method, since held as invalid. It is axiomatic that determination of correct profit would require proper valuation of inventories, both as at the beginning as well as the end of the relevant accounting period, as stands clarified by the Apex Court in, among others, British Paints India Ltd. (supra) and Chainrup Sampatram v. CIT [1953] 24 ITR 481 (SC). This is also in essence the rule of the non obstante provision of section 145A, since statutorily mandated. The issue is legal, and goes to the root of the matter. The same would accordingly get decided on the basis of legal precedents, including an analysis thereof. The issue arising directly out of decision validating the change by the assessee, having not been dealt with by the Commissioner (Appeals) - who in fact approved the change in the first instance, with no specific arguments in the matter. It is considered to be fit and proper to refrain from deciding the matter, and only consider it proper to restore the same back to the file of the Commissioner (Appeals), who shall decide the same in accordance with law per a speaking order after allowing reasonable opportunity of hearing to both the parties before him.

The assessee has paid the demurrage charges to the non-resident in respect of delay in loading the ship. The sum was reimbursed by the assessee to the foreign buyer to compensate the foreign buyer for paying demurrage to the ship owner when ship came to Indian port and the assessee could not load the goods on to the ship within the limited time period. The export sales were made to the foreign Pakistani buyer on FOB basis. In view of the contract with the Pakistani buyer the assessee was bound to compensate the Pakistani buyer in respect of demurrage paid by the Pakistani buyer to the ship owner. This payment can be regarded to be the expenditure incurred by the assessee for the sale of the goods and was not akin to price deduction due to fault in product/service and was equivalent to discount/rebate which can be adjusted against the sale price. [Para 31]

Explanation 1(b) to section 9(1)(i) provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of the goods in India for the purpose of export. The non-resident buyer got the compensation towards the demurrage incurred through the operation which was confined to the purchase of the goods, i.e. in relation to the ship which it had arranged for taking the delivery of the goods from the assessee/seller from India. Therefore, this income cannot be deemed to accrue or arise in India in the hands of the foreign buyer, and therefore, it cannot be taxable in India and is not liable to tax deduction at source. On this basis, no disallowance can be made under section 40(a)(ia), and accordingly, the disallowance is deleted. [Para 32]

From a perusal of the Circular No. 723, dated 19-9-1995, it is apparently clear that the provisions of sections 194C and 195 relating to tax deduction at source are not applicable where the provisions of section 172, relating to shipping business are applicable. The circular issued by the CBDT is binding on the department. In view of the circular, the assessee was not obliged to deduct TDS on the payment made as demurrage charges and the demurrage charges are also liable to be taxed under section 172. The assessee, since, is not liable to deduct tax at source, no question arises for making any disallowance under section 40(a)(i). [Para 33]

Regarding the other disallowance, it is not a case where the assessee had deducted tax at source, but the assessee had assisted the shipping owner in discharging their legal obligation by making payment of their income tax to the revenue for which they were liable under section 172. This is not a case where assessee has deducted TDS, as the assessee was not liable to deduct any TDS in respect of payment made to the ship owner for the demurrage. There is no dispute that the income of the foreign shipping companies were chargeable to tax under section 172. The demurrage paid to these shipping companies were also to be treated as freight in view of specific provision of section 172(8). In view of Circular Number 723, dt. 19-9-1995, the provision of sections 194C and 195 relating to tax deduction at source are not applicable to the income which is chargeable to tax under section 172. In view of this circular, the assessee was not obliged to deduct tax at source on the demurrage paid to the ship owners during the year. Since the provision of TDS were not applicable, therefore no disallowance can be sustained under section 40(a)(ia). Therefore, the order of the CIT(A) on these issues is set aside and the disallowance is deleted. [Para 33.1]

Relevant Date for Rate and Valuation of Import Duty

Section 15 of Customs Act prescribes that rate of duty and tariff valuation applicable to imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force at one of the following dates. (a) if the goods are entered for home consumption, the date on which bill of entry is presented (b) in case of warehoused goods, when Bill of Entry for home consumption is presented u/s 68 for clearance from warehouse and (c) in other cases, date of payment of duty.

Concept of Territorial Waters not relevant - It may be noted that concept of 'date of entering into territorial waters' is not relevant for purposes of determination of rate of customs duty.

11.6-1 Relevant Date of Bill of Entry for home consumption

As per section 46 of Customs Act, every importer of goods has to submit a 'Bill of Entry' giving details of goods being imported. The carrier of goods has to submit 'Arrival manifest or import manifest (words 'arrival manifest' inserted w.e.f. 29-3-2018)' or 'Import Report' giving details of all goods which are brought for unloading at the port. If shipping berth is available, 'Entry Inwards' is granted to the vessel.

If there is delay in submission of Bill of Entry, there will be delay in assessment and clearance of imported goods. Goods lying on docks will incur heavy demurrage. Hence, it is permitted to submit 'Bill of Entry' if the vessel or aircraft or vehicle in which goods have been shipped is expected to arrive at any time not exceeding 30 days prior to expected arrival of the aircraft or vessel if vehicle by which goods have been shipped for importation into India- second proviso to section 46(3) of Customs Act [first proviso re-numbered as second proviso w.e.f. 28-3-2021].

However, even if Bill of Entry is submitted earlier, relevant date for purpose of assessment (valuation and rate of customs duty) will be (a) date of grant of 'entry inward' to vessel or (b) date of submission of Bill of Entry whichever is later e.g. if Bill of Entry is presented on 5th January and 'Entry Inward' is granted on 10th January, relevant date will be 10th Jan., but if entry inward is on 10th January and Bill of Entry is presented on 13th January, then 13th January will be the relevant date - proviso to section 15 of the Customs Act.

In case of import by air or road, there is no procedure to grant 'Entry Inward'. Hence date of arrival of aircraft or the vehicle or submission of Bill of Entry, whichever is later, will be treated as relevant date for purpose of rate of customs duty and customs valuation - - proviso to section 15 of the Customs Act. [The words 'or the vehicle' has been inserted w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

Section 44B is a special provision enshrined for computing the profits and gains of shipping business in the case of non-residents. Sub-section (1) provides that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A, an assessee, being a non-resident, engaged in the business of operation of ships, a sum equal to 7½ per cent of the aggregate amount specified in sub-section (2) shall be deemed to be the 'business income'. Sub-section (2) further provides that the amount paid or payable to the assessee on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from any port of India and the amount received or deemed to be received by the assessee on account of carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped from any port outside India shall be deemed as the business income. The case of the Assessing Officer was that the IHC was not covered under section 44B. The assessee had placed reliance on the Explanation to section 44B to contend that IHC would be covered within its Explanation. [Para 6]

A plain reading of the Explanation to section 44B reveals that the demurrage charges or handling charges or other amounts of similar nature have been brought within the ambit of 'business income' for applying the rate of 7½ per cent. The very nature of items prescribed in the Explanation being demurrage charges or handling charges, which precede 'any other amount of similar nature', show that the latter category has to draw a colour from the items referred to in the earlier part. The expression 'any other amount of similar nature' cannot be read in isolation by disregarding the nature of items preceding it. The meaning of the succeeding expression has to be understood in the context of the preceding words. Since the demurrage charges or handling charges have been mentioned in the Explanation prior to 'any other amount of similar nature', 'any other amount' has to be considered, which is similar to or closely resembles with the nature of demurrage or handling charges. Handling charges are the charges paid for loading/unloading/stacking, etc., of the containers and the demurrage charges are in nature of penalty for non-removal of the cargo in time. On the contrary, the IHC are towards transport of the goods from the exporter's place to the port. The very nature of inland transportation charges clearly differentiates it from handling or demurrage charges, which are of a different genus. Therefore, there was no substance in the submission of the assessee that inland haulage charges were covered under section 44B, as these were equal to or part and parcel of the amount on account of carriage of goods shipped at any port in or outside India, and, hence, were automatically covered under Article 8. [Paras 7 and 8]

Section 156 of the Customs Act lays down the general rule making power of the central government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act and Section 157 lays down the power of the Board to make regulations to carry out the purposes of the Act. Under the customs Act, the custom authorities are concerned with the setting up of public or private warehouses and for storage, removal and handling of imported goods in a customs area.

39. The Handling of Cargo under Customs Area Regulations, 2009 have been framed to provide for the manner in which the imported goods/export goods shall be received, stored, delivered or otherwise handled in a customs area. The regulations also prescribe the responsibilities of the persons engaged in aforesaid activities.

40. The custom authorities are concerned with the receiving, storing, delivering and handling of cargo in a custom area. The custom authorities are not concerned with the upgradation, modernisation, finances, operation and maintenance and management and provision of services at the Cargo Terminal of the Airport, which is the function of the AAI. The custom authorities are also not concerned with the responsibility of providing and fixing demurrage charges in respect of storage, processing and handling of Cargo at the terminal, which responsibility is of the AERA.

41. The Regulations of the AAI of which the Policy for Waiver of demurrage charges is a part specifically deals with the Storage and Processing of Cargo, Courier and Express Goods and Postal Mail. The Airport Authority fixes the charges for processing of the Cargo and has thus formulated the Policy for Waiver of such demurrage charges.

42. The custom authorities it appears issues certificate for waiver in every type of case irrespective of the fact whether the importer is at fault or not. The custom authorities have issued certificate for waiver of the demurrage charges in both the cases at hand. In one case the release of the goods are on provisional basis pending adjudication and in the other there is imposition of both fine and penalty. These are not cases where the importer has been held to be not at fault. In one case the Importer has been found to be at fault and penalty and fine imposed. The importer has accepted the said order. In the other case adjudication proceedings are pending and are yet to be finalised.

43. There is an overlap in the Policy for Waiver framed by AAI and the HCCAR. Though initially there appears to be a conflict between the policy and the regulations but on closer scrutiny it is apparent that they can both be harmoniously construed and coexist.

44. The policy makes a distinction between the cases where the importer is innocent but his imported goods are seized and detained pending an enquiry and adjudication and the cases where the importers have indulged in mis-declaration, mis-description, under valuation or concealment and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning is imposed by the customs authorities. Importers who are innocent cannot be equated with the importers who violate the law and be given the same treatment. The AAI policy makes a distinction between the two and in our view rightly so.

45. The regulations frames in 2009 themselves stipulate that they are subject to any law for the time being in force and as such the regulations would be applicable in terms of the Policy for Waiver framed by the AAI in 2003.

46. In case the HCCAR were to be made applicable in all cases then the result would be that in no case where there is a fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning imposed by the customs authorities CELEBI would be able to charge demurrage charges. Custom authorities are issuing waiver directions even in cases where the importers are clearly at fault and fine, penalty, personal penalty and/or warning has been imposed by the customs authorities. Even in cases of mis-declaration, undervaluation and concealment, the certificates are being issued. This is clearly giving premium to dishonesty. The waiver should be granted in genuine cases where the importers are ultimately found not at fault. It cannot be that all importers honest and dishonest are treated equally.

Storage in public warehouse pending clearance

Normally, imported goods are either cleared for home consumption on payment of customs duty or kept in customs bonded warehouse after goods are assessed to duty.

However, occasionally, it may happen that assessment of customs duty may take time for want of some clarification/reports etc. In such cases, goods lying in docks incur heavy demurrage.

Hence, if assessment is likely to be delayed, section 49 of Customs Act allows that goods can be stored in public warehouse for period upto 30 days. This period can be extended for 30 days at a time by Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs - second proviso to section 49 of Customs Act as amended w.e.f. 31-3-2017.

The goods may or may not be dutiable if these are to be cleared for home consumption. However, if these are to be cleared for warehousing, then only dutiable can be kept in public warehouse pending clearance - section 49 of Customs Act as amended w.e.f. 31-3-2017.

Such goods are not to be treated as 'warehoused goods' for purposes of Chapter IX Customs Act (which makes provisions for warehousing of goods), as the goods are not assessed - first proviso to section 49 of Customs Act as amended w.e.f. 31-3-2017.

Hence, such warehousing can be called 'storage without warehousing' or 'warehousing without warehousing'. The goods are cleared from the public warehouse after duty is assessed and paid.

FACT: Facts

Assessee imported crude oil, which was liable to duty on ad valorem basis.

Department demanded duty on quantity of crude oil mentioned in bills of lading.

Assessee argued that since quantity actually received into shore tanks in India was lesser, quantity actually received should be basis for payment of duty.

Revenue's Arguments

The department argued that since duty was now levied on an ad valorem basis and not on a specific rate, the duty should be paid on the bill of lading quantity based on the ullage obtained when the goods were loaded on the vessel in the country of export.

Since full payment for the goods has to be made by the importer only on the basis of the quantity mentioned in the bill of lading, therefore the 'transaction value' of the said goods would only be as per the payment made of the amounts stated in the bill of lading and not the quantity received ultimately in the shore tanks at ports in India.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee argued that it makes no difference as to whether the basis for customs duty is at a specific rate or is ad valorem, quantity of goods at the time of import alone is to be looked at.

Taxable event is only when goods are imported, and that therefore valuation at the time of import alone has to be looked at.

HELD: The levy of customs duty under section 12 is only on goods imported into India. Goods are said to be imported into India when they are brought into India from a place outside India. Unless such goods are brought into India, the act of importation which triggers the levy does not take place. If the goods are pilferred after they are unloaded or lost or destroyed at any time before clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, the importer is not liable to pay the duty leviable on such goods. This is for the reason that the import of goods does not take place until they become part of the land mass of India and until the act of importation is complete which under sections 13 and 23 happens only after an order for clearance for home consumption is made and/or an order permitting the deposit of goods in a warehouse is made.

CURSOR OF CUSTOMS LAWS : THE INDIAN SCENARIO

Customs duty is imposed on goods imported into or exported out of India as per the rates specified under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. Customs duty is designed to raise revenue and to promote the economic development of the nation as well, by varying the rates of duty. This write-up is an overview of customs laws in respect of Indian Scenario.

Introduction

1. The term ‘customs’ is coined through its essence from the term ‘custom’, i.e., customary practice or course of action that is observed and repeated in the like circumstances1. The custom gradually took form of legal imposition on the imports of goods and sometimes exports2.

Customs duty3 in India4 is governed by the Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 that provide for the levy and collection of duties. The purposes of the Acts are follows : (i) regulation of imports5 and exports 6; (ii) protection of domestic industry; (iii) prevention of smuggling; (iv) conservation and augmentation of foreign exchange and so on. As there are three stages in any tax structure, viz., levy, assessment and collection, the first one is in the hands of the Legislature. The Legislature, by fulfilling the requirements of article 265, imposes the tax liability attached to its taxable event7. Under customs, the taxable events are - import of goods8 into or export of goods out of India. Section 12 is a charging section, which lays down the conditions of levy.

Conditions of levy - Customs duty

2. Customs duty is imposed on goods imported into or exported out of India as per the rates specified under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. The provisions are equally applicable to goods belonging to the Government9.

On an analysis of section 12, one derives the following points :—

(i)Customs duty is imposed on goods when such goods are imported into or exported out of India;

(ii)The levy is subject to other provisions under this Act or any other law;

(iii)The rates of duty are as specified under the Tariff Act, 1975;

(iv)Even goods belonging to the Government are subject to levy10, however, they can be exempted by some notifications11.

Taxable event

3. The basic condition for levy of customs duty is import/export of goods, i.e., goods become liable to duty when there is import12 into or export13 from India14. Though the taxable event is import/export, yet it is difficult to determine the exact time of levy. This issue has been further complicated by conflicting decisions by various High Courts. In Chetankumar & Co. v. CC15, the Madras High Court held that chargeability arises when the imported goods get mixed up with the land mass of India and the chargeability takes place at the time of unloading the goods.

Whereas in Apar (P.) Ltd. v. UOI16 . The Bombay High Court held that—

"the taxable event has to occur as soon as the goods enter the territorial waters of India and doesn’t postpone till they are actually off-loaded on the land mass or till the goods are valued17 or till the date for determining the rate at which customs duty should be levied18."

The matter was finally decided by the Supreme Court in an appeal preferred by the Apar (P.) Ltd.19. The Supreme Court in UOI v. Apar (P.) Ltd.20 overruled the full Bench decision of the Bombay High Court and held that the date of duty applicable to any imported goods is the date21 as follows :

(a)In the case of goods cleared for home consumption, the date of presentation of Bill of Entry22 or the date of grant of entry inwards to the vessel, whichever is later and

(b)In case of goods from bonded warehouse the date of actual removal from the warehouse. Date when vessel enters territorial waters is irrelevant.

The Supreme Court further clarified the position of taxable event in the case of Kiran Spg. Mills v. CC 23 wherein it is held that import is completed only when goods cross the customs barrier. The taxable event is the day of crossing the customs barrier, and not on the date when goods landed in India, or had entered territorial waters of India. In case of goods which are in the warehouse, the customs barrier would be crossed when they are sought to be taken out of the customs and brought to the mass of goods in the country.

Types of duties under Customs

4. There are various types of customs import duties which have been discussed hereinbelow.

It actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay on July 11, 1981, at which time the rate of duty applicable to the petitioners' goods was 12.5%. As there was no berth available and the vessel was under heavy pressure from the parties whose goods she was carrying, she left Bombay for Karachi for unloading other cargo intended for that port. The vessel returned after discharging the Karachi cargo, arrived in the Port of Bombay on July 23, 1981 and waited for a berth. On August 4, 1981 she was allowed to berth and the Customs Authorities made the "final entry" on that date. The petitioners contend that when the vessel made its original journey to Bombay and was waiting in the waters of the Port they presented the Bill of Entry to the Customs authorities on July 9, 1981, and that the Bill of Entry was accepted by the Import Department and an order was passed by the Customs Officer on the Bill of Entry on July 18, 1981 directing the examination of the consignment. The Customs authorities imposed duty on the edible oils at the rate of 150% on the footing that the import was made on July 31, 1981, the date of "Inward Entry". The case of the petitioners is that the rate of duty leviable on the import should be that ruling on July 11, 1981, when the vessel actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay, and that but for the fact that a berth was not available the vessel would have discharged its cargo at Bombay, and would not have left that Port and proceeded to Karachi to return to Bombay towards the end of July, 1981. Alternatively, the case of the petitioners is that even if the rate of customs duty found leviable on their goods is 150 per cent, such levy is unconstitutional and void as it violates of Article 14 of the Constitution, inasmuch as customs duty at 5 per cent only was levied on the STC for similar imports. The petitioners have also challenged the validity of section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 under which the rate of duty and tariff valuation are determined.

HELD: Duty rate--Relevant date is date of entry inwards of the vessel, even if Bill of Entry has been presented before that date. "It is urged......that the import of goods must be deemed to have taken place on 11 July, 1981, when the ship originally arrived in Bombay Port and registered itself. The rate of customs duty prevailing on that date was 12.5 per cent..............The provisions of section 15 are clear in themselves. The date on which a Bill of Entry is presented under section 46 is, in the case of goods entered for home consumption, the relevant date for determining the rate of duty and tariff valuation. Where the Bill of Entry is presented before the date of Entry Inwards of the vessel, the Bill of Entry is deemed to have been presented on the date of such Entry Inwards. .............In the present case, "the date of inwards entry" is mentioned as 31 July, 1981. In the absence of anything else, we may take it that the entry was recorded on that date itself. Accordingly, the rate of import duty and the tariff valuation shall be that in force on 31 July, 1981. The contention of the petitioners that the rate of import duty and tariff valuation will be that ruling on 11 July, 1981 cannot be sustained and is rejected."

A CASE FOR WITHDRAWAL OF SECTION 145A OF INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961

L. Venkatesan*

Accounting Standard-2 (AS-2) issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India on the subject of valuation of inventories has been made mandatory with effect from April 1, 1999. In this article, the author argues that in view of this, there is no need for retaining section 145A in the Income-tax Act, 1961 any more. The author examines the issue in detail and adduces several reasons to support the stand taken by him - EDITOR

Introduction

1. Accounting Standard-2 (AS-2), on valuation of inventories issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has been made mandatory with effect from April 1, 1999. It would, therefore, appear that there is no need for retention of section 145A in the Income-tax Act, 1961 any more. This article aims to examine this issue in some detail.

Genesis of section 145A

2. On going through various cases decided by the High Courts and the Tribunals, it is easy to infer that this provision has been introduced to plug the loopholes of the decisions which go against the Accounting Standards of the ICAI and international accounting bodies. The following two cases are important in this context:

(a) Lakhanpal National Ltd. v. ITO [1986] 162 ITR 240/ 27 Taxman 462 (Guj.).

In this case, the assessee debited loans and advances instead of debiting purchases/profit and loss account against accounting norms.

(i)Excise duty paid on stocks lying in depotsRs.29.89 lakhs

(ii)Customs duty paid on raw materials and

lying as closing stockRs.124.94 lakhs

These amounts were claimed on payment basis under section 43B.

(b)Similarly, in the case of ITO v. Food Specialities Ltd. [1994] 206 ITR 119 (AT) (Delhi) (SB), the assessee changed the method of accounting for excise duty paid on goods lying in the depot from April 1, 1984 and claimed under section 43B. Up to the previous year this was included in closing stock under the matching concept. Further, the assessee had the right to claim such duty from his buyer. These accounting principles and accounting standards were given a go-by to claim the payment by one year in advance. Thus, in order to plug these loopholes, section 145A was amended.

Section 145A

3. Section 145A requires that the valuation of purchase and sale of goods and inventory for the purpose of determining income shall be :

In accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee and further adjusted to include the amount of any tax, duty, cess or fee (by whatever name called) actually paid or incurred by the assessee to bring the goods to the place of its location and condition as on the date of valuation.

With the introduction of section 145, the assessee has to necessarily include all duties and taxes which are incurred to bring the goods to its present location and condition. In other words, excise duty paid on goods stored in depots and customs duty paid, raw materials have to be included under stock valuation and the ‘whole’ value including taxes paid will become one value. The same concept has been recognised under AS-2 except duties which are in the nature of discount.

AS-2 and international accounting standards

4. The Accounting Standard on inventory valuation (AS-2) has become mandatory from April 1, 1999. As per AS-2, valuation of inventory should comprise of all costs of purchases, cost of conversion and other costs incurred in bringing the goods to their present location and condition. The concept with regard to their present location and condition is also emphatically confirmed in the UK GAAP and the US GAAP. Thus, AS-2 is in line with international accounting standards.

AS-2, while defining costs of purchases, allows deduction of taxes recoverable subsequently and trade discount rebate, duty drawback and other similar items. In fact, this definition is also in line with the UK GAAP. Thus, it is a welcome feature that AS-2 has become mandatory and it is in line with international accounting standards.

AS-2 and section 145A

5. The main purpose of AS-2 is determination of the figure at which inventories are valued until related revenues are recognised.

When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for..........................." Parties to a contract would fix such a sum in advance at the time of making the contract, because it facilitates calculation of risks; it reduces the difficulty and expense of proving actual damage or loss and facilitates recovery of damages. Hence, liquidated damages are compensatory in nature and not in the nature of consideration and there is no provision of service involved or an act of abstaining from performing an act or tolerating of an act to be covered under section 66E(e) of the Act. It is only failure to perform an act which is distinguishable from the concept of "refraining from or tolerating an act". On the basis of the above, liquidated damages may not be subject to service tax.

5.8 Demurrage charges - The term 'demurrage' refers to the period when the charter remains in possession of the vessel after the period normally allowed to load and unload cargo has expired. Thus, by extension demurrage charges refer to the charges that the charterer pays to the owner of the ship for its extra use. Hence, demurrage charges are in the form of consideration for service and subject to service tax. Further, as per rule 6(1)(x) of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, demurrage charge is to be included in the taxable value of service.

Invoicing and payment of service tax in case of a declared service under section 66E(e) of the Act

6. Invoice is unlikely in many cases of abstinence. There may be situations when payments are agreed to be made at the end of a prescribed period for refraining from doing an act. During the interregnum, service is provided by way of abstinence, but payment may not be received. When invoice is not raised POTR takes completion of provision of service as the point for payment of tax. But in this case service is rendered on a continuous basis by refraining from performing an act and the consideration is received after an agreed period of time. It may be argued that as per section 2(d) of the IC Act, abstinence itself is a consideration and during the period of refraining from performance of an act, tax becomes payable. But for collecting tax quantification and value become relevant and, therefore, POTR comes into play to defer the same till the receipt of payment.

Conclusion

7. It is clear that clause (e) of section 66E of the Act will throw up many more interesting situations. One has to wait for authoritative judicial pronouncements to obtain clarity. Hope that the coming Budget takes cognizance of this category of declared service and limits its scope by means of specific explanations to facilitate uniform interpretation.

| Section 13 | Section 23(1) |
| --- | --- |

High Court's decision on the same point

4. Further, reference is invited to the recent decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in the case of M/s Siva Sai Constructions, Hyderabad v. Government of India, 2013-TIOL-09-HC-AP-ST. While allowing the petition filed by the assessee, the High Court clearly held that a coercive action under section 87 of the Finance Act, 1994 during the pendency of appeal is not justified. The High Court clearly directed the authorities not to initiate any coercive steps against the assessee or others who owe dues to the petitioner under section 87 or any other appropriate provision. The Court held that such coercive actions should not be taken till disposal of the petitioner's applications for condonation of delay and for grant of interim relief in the appeal preferred by the petitioner to the Tribunal.

Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1.1.2013 has completely ignored the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court and will have a devastating effect in case the tax authorities initiate the recovery proceedings. From the case records, it was found that the assessee had collected various charges from importers/exporters including passengers for keeping the cargo in transit safely, pending export or customs clearance for home consumption. In holding that keeping safe custody of cargo in transit, pending clearance by the customs would constitute an activity exigible under the above entry, the lower authorities had relied on Circulars of the CBEC which clarified that storage and warehousing service provided by, inter alia, Airport Authority is covered by the entry. The entry cargo handling service was clarified by the CBEC as not covering export cargo and passenger baggage. The clarification was not to the effect that all activities relating to export cargo and passenger baggage were also excluded from levy under other entries. The finding of the Commissioner, that the exceptions provided under cargo handling services with regard to passenger baggage and export cargo could not be claimed under storage and warehousing services, was to be agreed with. [Para 9.2]

Demurrage or wharfage charges were collected, respectively, in relation to clearance of import/export cargo beyond five days and 24 hours. As found by the original authority, these were higher charges for continued storage of cargo collected by the assessee from members of the trade. These were part of the taxable value collected towards storage and warehouse charges. [Para 9.3]

As regards the abandoned cargo, those accrued to the assessee towards storage and warehousing of cargo, which were not taken delivery of by the importer. The procedure for auctioning abandoned cargo and the sharing of the proceeds is prescribed by the Ministry of Finance. These instructions also make it clear that the assessee would receive amounts towards the service of storage and warehousing of cargo under this head. However, the services were not rendered to any person in the case of the abandoned cargo. Therefore, demand under this head was not sustainable. [Para 9.4]

As regards the destination charges, it was found that the assessee had collected the documents representing the consignments brought by Air India and Blue Dart and hand over these to the respective consignees. In cases where the assessee merely collected and handed over the documents to the respective consignees, destination charges would not form part of taxable value under storage and warehousing. [Para 9.5]

As regards the OT charges/penalties, the lower authorities had not given a finding as to the nature and purpose of these penalties but had presumed that these were collected for violations on the part of their clients in relation to storage and warehousing services. The Commissioner (Appeals) did not find this item to be taxable under storage and warehousing. In the absence of a finding as to how that amount was taxable towards any service rendered by the assessee, it was difficult to accept the stand of the revenue in this regard. The assessee had also not explained the nature and purpose of collecting these charges. This matter would be decided after hearing the party afresh. [Para 9.6]

There was considerable merit in the assessee’s submission that there was no suppression of facts, etc. to warrant invocation of larger period. From the orders impugned, one did not find a reliable finding by the authorities that the assessee, a State PSU, had resorted to suppression of the facts to evade appropriate service tax amount. Considering the nature of the activities involved, the Commissioner could not have found with certainty that the assessee had deliberately mis-classified the activities undertaken by it under the head ‘Cargo handling services’ instead of ‘Storage and warehousing services’. Therefore, the authorities could not have validly invoked extended period and imposed penalties. The penal liability of the assessee required reconsideration in the light of section 80. [Para 9.7]

In view of section 75 the assessee was liable to pay interest for delay in payment of the tax found due from it. Therefore, the order of the lower appellate authority as regards interest was to be upheld. [Para 10.1]

A ground raised for the first time before the Tribunal was based on the Circular No. 89/7/2006-ST, dated 18-12-2006. [Para 11]

The lower authorities had no occasion to examine that plea and to determine that liability of the assessee in the light of the same. The Tribunal was not in a position to decide the issue as it was not clear whether the circular applied to the assessee and if the assessee would come under the description of ‘public authority’, as envisaged in the above circular. In any case, records did not indicate that the charges collected by the assessee were deposited with the Government. The circular defines statutory authorities discharging sovereign functions, etc., to be those that deposit the ‘fees’ collected with the Government. [Para 12]

In the circumstances, the appeals were to be allowed by way of a remand. The impugned orders were to be set aside. [Para 13]

Related party transactions are generally subjected to special provisions in both direct and indirect tax laws. While VAT laws did not contain any specific procedure, excise, customs and now GST contemplate transactions with related parties and special provision from a tax law perspective.

Customs

An ancient custom of merchant offering goods as gifts to the king at the time of entering into his kingdom, evolved over a period of time to a levy at the point of entry of goods into the Country. Import by sea was governed by the Sea Customs Act, 1878; Land Customs Act, 1924; and through Rules under the Indian Aircraft Act, 1911. Post-independence, Customs Act, 1962 was passed to consolidate all other legislations. The levy of customs duty is in terms of Entry 83, Union List, Seventh Schedule which covers 'duties of customs including export duties'.

In terms of Section 12(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 the levy of customs duty shall be at the rates specified in the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 on the goods imported into or exported from India.

A common valuation code was created under Article VII of the GATT and India agreed to implement this. This agreement was implemented in 1988 through amendments in Section 14 and through the Valuation Rules, 1988. Finance Act, 2007 has completely recast Section 14 and consequently the Government has introduced Valuation Rules separately for imports and exports in 2007.

The assessee had been appointed as a custodian at the air cargo complex, under section 45 of the Customs Act, 1962. It was registered with the department as a provider of taxable services classifiable under ‘Cargo handling services’ from the year 2002. As a custodian, it handled three types of cargoes, viz., import cargo, export cargo and unaccompanied passenger baggage. As regards the import cargo and unaccompanied baggage, the assessee collected fixed charges at Rs. 4 per kg. for the consignments entrusted with it. As regards the export cargo, the amount charged by the assessee was described as terminal charge. Following inspection of its records by the internal audit party, a show-cause notice was issued to it proposing to demand service tax under various heads on account of certain other charges in addition to those mentioned above, such as destination charges, wharfage charges, demurrage charges, abandoned cargo, OT charges and penalties. In adjudication, the original authority held that by keeping in safe custody the goods involved in international trade transiting through the airport, the assessee had rendered a taxable service classifiable under ‘storage and warehousing services’. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) examined the entry storage and warehousing and found that the essential character of the activity carried out by the assessee was that of storage and warehousing services. He rejected the contention of the assessee that the activities in question were appropriately classified under ‘Cargo handling services’. He agreed with the findings of the original authority except that the following charges, viz., (i) Demurrage charges; (ii) Wharfage charges; (iii) Abandoned cargo; (iv) Destination charges and (v) OT charges/penalties were exigible under ‘Storage and Warehousing services’. The Commissioner also held that the assessee had deliberately mis-classified the services under ‘Cargo handling services’ to avail of exemptions provided under the Cargo Handling Services in respect of passenger baggage and export cargo. Therefore, he confirmed the differential service tax demand with interest and also imposed penalties upon the assessee under sections 77 and 78 by invoking longer period provided under proviso to section 73(1).

Customs Station.

Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs is authorised, vide section 8 of Customs Act, to specify the limits of 'Customs Area' and approve places for loading and unloading of goods. Thus, CBI&C appoints Customs Stations, i.e. town/city/village etc. while actual place within that city/town is approved by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014]. Inland Container Depot/Container Freight Stations - Present trend in transport is to stuff the goods in large containers and carry these containers. Such containers are easy to load and unload with help of cranes. Once the containers are unloaded at the port, these containers are carried to Inland Container Depots (ICD) and stored there. These are then cleared from such depots. Goods can also be exported from ICD. Sealing can be done at ICD. Details about ICD are given in a later chapter. An Inland Container Depot is a 'customs port' as per section 2(12). In short ICD acts like a 'Dry Port'.

CFS is a place where containers are stuffed, unstuffed and aggregation/segregation of cargo takes place. Container Freight Stations (CFS) can be taken as extended arm of the Port/ICD.

Inland Container Depots (ICDs) can be termed as 'Inland Ports' - CIT v. Container Corporation of India Ltd. (2018) 255 Taxman 334 = 93 taxmann.com 31 (SC).

Coastal Ports - Coastal ports are those which are permitted to carry trade on coastal goods. 'Coastal goods' means goods, other than imported goods, transported in a vessel from one port in India to another port in India [section 2(7) of Customs Act]. Thus, 'coastal ports' are used to transport goods by sea within India.

Warehousing stations provisions omitted - Imported Goods can be stored in public or private warehouses without payment of duty. Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBI&C) [name changed w.e.f. 29-3-2018 - earlier the name of Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBE&C)] was authorised to declare places to be warehousing stations at which public warehouses may be appointed or private warehouses may be licensed [section 9].

These powers were delegated to Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners since 1990.

This section has been omitted w.e.f. 14th May, 2016. Thus, now, warehouse can be located at any place in India after approval.

The petitioners imported a consignment of edible oils. The vessel carrying the goods approached Bombay and made its "prior entry" on July 4, 1981. It actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay on July 11, 1981, at which time the rate of duty applicable to the petitioners' goods was 12.5%. As there was no berth available and the vessel was under heavy pressure from the parties whose goods she was carrying, she left Bombay for Karachi for unloading other cargo intended for that port. The vessel returned after discharging the Karachi cargo, arrived in the Port of Bombay on July 23, 1981 and waited for a berth. On August 4, 1981 she was allowed to berth and the Customs Authorities made the "final entry" on that date. The petitioners contend that when the vessel made its original journey to Bombay and was waiting in the waters of the Port they presented the Bill of Entry to the Customs authorities on July 9, 1981, and that the Bill of Entry was accepted by the Import Department and an order was passed by the Customs Officer on the Bill of Entry on July 18, 1981 directing the examination of the consignment. The Customs authorities imposed duty on the edible oils at the rate of 150% on the footing that the import was made on July 31, 1981, the date of "Inward Entry". The case of the petitioners is that the rate of duty leviable on the import should be that ruling on July 11, 1981, when the vessel actually arrived and registered in the Port of Bombay, and that but for the fact that a berth was not available the vessel would have discharged its cargo at Bombay, and would not have left that Port and proceeded to Karachi to return to Bombay towards the end of July, 1981. Regulations framed by AAI : The AAI has framed regulations in exercise of powers conferred under the AAI Act. The regulations relied upon by the respondent CELEBI as applicable to the present case are the Airports Authority of India (storage and processing of cargo, courier and express goods and postal mail) Regulations, 2003. As per the said Regulation, the Airport Authority fixes the charges for processing of the cargo and also formulates policy for waiver of such demurrage charges. The relevant portion of the policy relating to waiver of demurrage charges (Cargo) lays down (para 10.1.10 thereof) that demurrage charges shall not be waived where : (a) Any fine/penalty/ personal penalty/warning is imposed by the Customs Authority. (b) Delay arose by reason of dispute in the assessable value or for revalidating or correcting the license in ordinary course of appraisal. [Para 36]

Policy of Waiver of AAI : The Policy framed by the AAI lays down that the authorities specified are authorised to sanction, in consultation with the finance and accounts department, remission/waiver of demurrage charges regarding cargo operation. It further lays down that Demurrage charges shall not be waived where any fine/penalty/ personal penalty/warning is imposed by the customs authority or where the delay arose by reason of dispute in the assessable value or for revalidating or correcting the license in ordinary course of appraisal. Power of customs is to control storage, removal and handling : Section 156 of the Customs Act lays down the general rule making power of the central government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act and section 157 lays down the power of the board to make regulations to carry out the purposes of the Act. Under the Customs Act, the custom authorities are concerned with the setting up of public or private warehouses and for storage, removal and handling of imported goods in a customs area. [Para 38]

HCCAR : The Handling of Cargo under Customs Area Regulations, 2009 have been framed to provide for the manner in which the imported goods/export goods shall be received, stored, delivered or otherwise handled in a customs area. The regulations also prescribe the responsibilities of the persons engaged in aforesaid activities. [Para 39]

Customs not concerned with finance of custodian : The customs authorities are concerned with the receiving, storing, delivering and handling of cargo in a customs area. 3.10 Exemption to income arising on account of storage and sale of crude oil [Section 10(48A)]

Section 10(48A) has been introduced with retrospective effect from assessment year 2016-17 to provide that the following income shall be exempt from tax:

(a)

The income is accruing or arising to a foreign company;

(b)

The income is on account of storage of crude oil in a facility in India and sale of crude oil therefrom;

(c)

The buyer is a person resident in India;

(d)

The storage and sale by the foreign company is pursuant to an agreement or an arrangement entered into by the Central Government or approved by the Central Government; and

(e)

The foreign company and the agreement or arrangement are notified by the Central Government in this behalf having regard to national interest.

The rationale behind the amendment is explained in the Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2016 as follows:

"The Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited (ISPRL) is in the process of setting up underground storage facility for storage of crude oil as part of strategic reserves. The maintenance of strategic reserves is in India's national interest and ensures price stability for Indian oil companies. The filling cost of such facility entails huge financial burden. The Government has explored the possibility of meeting a substantial part of the financial burden through participation of private players including foreign national oil companies (NOCs) and multinational companies (MNCs) storing and selling crude oil from outside India. However, the storage of crude oil by NOCs/MNCs and its sale in India would create tax liability for these entities.

In order to achieve neutrality in terms of taxation to encourage the NOCs MNCs to store their crude oil in India and to build up strategic oil reserves, it is proposed to amend the provisions of section 10 of the Act to provide that any income accruing or arising to a foreign company on account of storage of crude oil in a facility in India and sale of crude oil therefrom to any person resident in India shall not be included in the total income,

… Since the storage of oil is expected to begin in the current financial year, this exemption would be available from the previous year 2015-16, i.e. assessment year 2016-17."

It does not matter whether such costs were incurred before production or after production. [Expert Advisory Committee's Opinion - Dec. 2003 Issue of the Chartered Accountant].

The test for determining whether or not the cost of carrying out a particular activity should be included in the cost of inventories is "whether the activity contributes to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition". Where the liability for royalty arises for the company at the time of production and is payable to the Central/State Government at the rate and time specified in the Act and the Rules, the royalty charge is a necessary operational expense which must be incurred to bring the inventories to their present location and condition. Accordingly, actual royalty incurred and accounted in the books by the company should be included in the cost of finished crude oil stock. - [Expert Advisory Committee Opinion response to Query No. 36 - ICAI's website]

4.15-1 Inclusion of other costs of tank farm and pipeline, viz., depreciation/depletion, operation and maintenance cost and insurance charges of tank farm and pipeline in the cost of finished crude oil stock

The crude oil which still contains formation water is despatched from the storage tanks to tank farms, where it is processed for further separation of formation water by gravity separation process or are routed through dehydration facilities like Electrostatic Emulsion Treater and that in gravity separation process, the crude once received in the tanks is allowed to settle for a retention time of ideally 10-12 hours for free water and sludge to settle. Thus, the crude oil lying in the tank farm is subjected to certain operations and that some production process is carried out in tank farm. Accordingly, the other costs of tank farm, viz., depreciation/depletion, operation and maintenance cost and insurance charges related to tank farm are the costs necessary in the production process and that these costs are necessary for changing the condition of the inventory from unprocessed to processed. Accordingly, these costs should be included in the valuation of crude oil lying in the tank farm and pipelines. [Expert Advisory Committee Opinion response to Query No. 36 - ICAI's website]

The pipelines are used to transmit the crude oil to the custody transfer point at the refinery gate and that the sale takes place at the refinery gate with the passing of risks and rewards to the refineries. Thus, considering the refinery gate as point of sale, the pipelines are used to transmit the oil to the point of sale. Therefore, the abovementioned expenditure is incurred in changing the location of the inventories, i.e., bringing the inventories to the intended point of sale. Accordingly, depreciation/depletion, operation and maintenance cost and insurance charges of pipelines should be considered in arriving at the costs of inventories lying in the pipelines. [Expert Advisory Committee Opinion response to Query No. 36 - ICAI's website]

4.16 Exclusions from the cost of inventories

In determining the cost of inventories, the following costs shall be excluded and recognised as expenses of the period in which they are incurred, namely:—

(a)

Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;

(b)

Storage costs, unless those costs are necessary in the production process prior to a further production stage;

(c)

Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition;

(d)

Selling costs. [para 12 of ICDS-II (New)]

4.16-1 Administrative overheads

It may be noted that :

General administrative overheads (e.g. general manager's salary, rent of general administration building, printing and stationery expenses of general administrative offices etc.) generally do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition and are not treated as part of inventory costs.

Cost of factory management and administration (factory manager's salary, printing and stationery consumed at factory etc.) are clearly costs related to production activities and are treated as factory overheads and included in cost of inventory. [Expert Advisory Committee, Compendium of Opinions, Vol. XIII - page 83]

4.16-2 Demurrage - Whether includible in cost of inventories?

According to the Expert Advisory Committee, demurrage would generally be treated as abnormal loss and excluded from cost of inventories. However, if it can be demonstrated that demurrage is a normal cost in the facts and circumstances of the case, it should be included in the cost of inventories-i.e. where incurrence of demurrage is directly linked to savings in costs that are includible inventory. For example, an enterprise may, on a consideration of costs and benefits, decide to pay demurrage rather than hire additional storage space. In such a case, demurrage is includible in the cost of inventories. [Compendium of Opinions, Vol. XX - page 23]

ICDS II (New) prescribes only three cost formulae for determination of costs of inventories:

Specific identification

First-in-first-out (FIFO)

Weighted average cost

Items that are not ordinarily interchangeable; and

Goods or services produced and segregated for specific projects (whether purchased or produced).

ITC-Confiscation--Redemption fine--fine cannot be imposed when goods are simultaneously ordered to be re-exported. The appellant is therefore entitled to refund of redemption fine paid.

"When the goods are confiscated because of any ITC prohibition in terms of section 111(d) of the Act and an option to pay fine in lieu of such confiscation is given, the effect of such option is to lift the prohibition. In other words, the importer/appellant is entitled to import the goods and consume them within the country on payment of such redemption fine. Therefore, the simultaneous imposition of two conditions namely (i) imposition of fine in lieu of confiscation and (ii) directing re-export, cannot co-exist together. In view of this legal position the appellant is entitled to refund of Rs. 71,250/- on account of redemption fine paid by him if the goods have already been re-exported."

2. ITC--Penalty-- As the appellant had offered another licence for clearing the imported goods, the order regarding imposition of penalty is therefore set aside. "As regards the plea of the appellant regarding imposition of penalty, we find sufficient force in this respect because of non-entertainment of the offer of second licence produced by the importer/appellant for clearance of the goods. The penalty of Rs. 50,000/- imposed on the importer/appellant is also set aside."

The assessee company filed its return claiming deduction of demurrage paid to a non-resident shipping company.

The assessee's case was that there was no obligation to deduct tax at source as the amount was paid to non-resident shipping company engaged in operation of ships and, therefore, governed by section 172.

The Assessing Officer, however, opined that assessee was required to deduct tax at source under section 195 while making payment to non-resident shipping company. In view of assessee's failure to do so, Assessing Officer disallowed payments in question.

Reliance was also placed upon the Circular No. 723 dated 19-9-1995 issued by CBDT which interalia provides that Section 172 is a self contained code for levy and recovery of taxes ship wise and journey wise in case of ships owned or chartered by non-residents. Therefore, the requirement of deducting tax at source would not be applicable in such a case thus the consequent disallowance of expenditure under Section 40(a)(i) was not warranted.

However, the CIT(A) did not accept the contention of the assessee and held section 44B would apply as it related to computation of profits and gains and from shipping business. In the above view, the appeal of the assessee was dismissed.

The Tribunal allowed assessee's appeal by following decision in DCIT v. Orient (Goa) (P.) Ltd. [2009] 185 Taxman 131. The impugned order specifically held that section 172 was a charging as well as a machinery provision in respect of non-resident shipping companies. It provided for determination and collection of tax. Thus Chapter XVII of the Act in respect of deducting tax at source would not apply in such cases. Consequently, the disallowance of expenditure on account of section 40(a)(i) Act was deleted.

IJK Ltd has employed a contractor for construction of chemical plant. The terms of the agreement clearly specify that the liquidated damages are paid as compensation for failure to meet performance conditions in terms of the desired quality and level of output subsequent to commissioning of the plant. The damages will be calculated based on the shortfall in the output as a percentage of the contract price. Whether such liquidated damages received be deducted from the cost of the related asset or offered to tax as income under the ICDSs? Answer: In the instant case, the amount of liquidated damages received are not directly attributable to the construction of the chemical plant like trade discounts and rebates allowed by the supplier/contractor. Such damages are as a result of the inefficiencies on the part of the contractor. Further, the amount of liquidated damages is directly linked to performance parameters for the plant subsequent to commissioning of the plant. These liquidated damages are not related to costs that would be capitalised as cost of the plant. Therefore, these liquidated damages should not be deducted from the cost of related asset and the same should be offered to tax as income.

Case Study 5.10.1.8 : A public sector company is engaged in refining, transportation and sale of petroleum products. It incurs demurrage on imported plant and machinery i.e. payment made for detention of imported plant and machinery at discharge location for a period more than the period agreed with the supplier/transporter. The incidence of demurrage was on account of a nationwide transporters strike due to which the company could not take delivery of the machinery. Whether demurrage should be considered as an element of cost for the purpose of determining the actual cost of imported plant and machinery in accordance with ICDS-V(Revised)?

Answer: In the instant case, demurrage is incurred on account of a nationwide transporters strike, which represents abnormal cost. Therefore, the demurrage should not be capitalised as per AS 10 and Ind AS 16. However, unlike AS 10 and Ind AS 16, ICDS-V(Revised) does not provide that abnormal costs should not be capitalised as part of actual cost of a TFA. As per ICDS-V(Revised), directly attributable costs should be capitalised, whether normal costs or abnormal costs. Therefore, demurrage is to be capitalised as part of cost of the now imported plant and machinary for income-tax purposes though it would not be capitalised for accounting purposes. Suitable adjustments would need to be made to net profit as per P&L in statement of computation of income.
